covenants.name: Fudarus
covenants.notes:
Challenges to enter Fudarus. Chance decides which Primus hears of a visitor and so sets the test, which is suited to the visitor's abilities: too easy a task is a subtle insult of the kind Tytali relish and shows the welcome to expect, a hard one is a compliment, and a visitor who fails but bears himself well may still be asked in.

Buliste's challenges are mostly philosophical or plainly magical: argue convincingly that the Code of Hermes is outdated and harms the Order; talk a Lampaul villager into an act he thinks morally repugnant; work a ritual he does not know from a casting tablet without passing out; open the main gate without moving a muscle.

Harpax's challenges are mostly physical: fight a magically made beast; pin one of Fudarus's grogs in a wrestling bout; catch at least seven of twelve spears thrown from the ramparts; fetch something from Lampaul before a water clock runs out.

The Rod and the Circlet of the Primus, made long ago at Hariste's order, are the covenant's great treasures and the tokens of the House's leadership. The Rod (six effects, R: Touch, D: Conc, T: Structure, Pen 0, unlimited uses, any number kept up at once but one begun a round) varies a room's light from darkness to blinding glare (MuIg 25), its heat from freezing to baking (MuIg 25), opens arches or shuts doorways between rooms (MuTe 30), and fills it with sweet or foul smells (CrIm 25), soothing or clamorous noise (CrIm 25), and furnishings soft as down or sharp as thorns (MuIm 25). The Circlet (Control Spirit, ReVi 55, R: Arc, D: Conc, T: Ind, Pen 20, unlimited uses) commands one task of any spirit present or to which the wearer has an Arcane Connection; it is inscribed with the names of all Fudarus's servant spirits, and affects any whose Might is below its Penetration.
covenants.summary:
The domus magna of House Tytalus and the westernmost covenant of Normandy, whose influence reaches across the whole Tribunal like a web. Tytalus the Founder lived here, as did his filia Pralix, founder of House Ex Miscellanea, and Tasgillia, corrupted by demons in the tenth century. Few magi of other Houses have ever entered its halls, though many have reached the island, and its secrecy and its members' schemes have given it a sinister name.

Tytalus built it in 798 to defend the apprentice Hariste, whom he had stolen from his former pupil Pralix and loved; he trained her to a full maga in five years, but his refusal to show his love drove her away, and he held the magically raised fortress alone until he vanished. Hariste then claimed it and became the first Prima, and it has been the Primus's home ever since. In 961 House Guernicus caught Prima Tasgillia and many of the House in diabolism far from Fudarus; the new Prima Kalliste refused the Quaesitores and Flambeau hoplites entry, since the members left had been found clean, and when political pressure forced her to yield they found nothing. In the Schism War the Diedne came by sea and, unable to break in, laid siege with three mighty summoned spirits; after months Primus Klynoites wrested the spirits from them, destroyed his foes, and bound the spirits into the walls. Fudarus had sat with the Stonehenge Tribunal; as the only Breton covenant to survive the war, its move to Normandy in 1018 brought Brittany's rich vis into its hands, and the Tribunal favoured it in sharing the spoils.

The covenant is a sprawling grey fortress in a semicircular wall on the very edge of Ushant's landward cliffs, and it spills down the cliff face: its towers hang upside down from buttresses at the top, reaching downward like the stone tendrils of a vast ivy. Most of its people live in the part that pours over the edge. Only the Primus's tower is occupied; by custom each Primus's tower is sealed by the successor, who builds a new one. Nine towers are sealed, one for each of the eight earlier Primi and one for Tytalus, and none but Tasgillia's has been entered since; some are thought to hold the ghosts or Twilight-changed remains of their owners. Harpax's tower has been building for twenty years and, thanks to Buliste, is nowhere near done, while Harpax devises ever cleverer ways to seal Buliste's tower and lock her out of her own sanctum.

Visitors approaching by sea or land meet the defences of the Three Great Spirits, who take turns hiding the covenant from chance discovery. An invited guest or a Redcap stands facing the island, feet together and hands raised, and speaks the current password; the guarding spirit then opens a straight tunnel through its defences to the covenant. There are no steps or ropes, and the cliffs need magic to climb. Beside the gate is St Nerius's circle, where pious magi keep a yearly vigil undisturbed.

The Heusaff family, an old Breton line, own Ushant and Lampaul, the fishing village whose catch is Fudarus's main supply; the fishermen have little to do with the family and know nothing of magi. A non-Tytalan magus must earn entry by meeting a challenge set by a Primus, usually some kind of conflict, and lodges in a tumbledown house outside the walls if he fails or refuses; every Tytalus has passed the House's Gauntlet and may enter. Membership carries no special honour in the House: any Tytalus with reason to join and the strength to make the members accept him may do so. Fudarus is an autocracy whose Primus decides everything; members act on their own initiative, but a Primus who feels his authority usurped punishes swiftly with the Rod of the Primus.

For twenty-five years the two rival Primi, Buliste and Harpax, have been its only residents. Buliste was declared lost to Final Twilight and Harpax chosen in her place, but she returned a few years later, and the two have fought for the House ever since, evenly matched; the House gives both equal respect, leadership and rule of Fudarus. The other members withdrew to the vassal they renamed Exspectatio, remain members of Fudarus, and come back for books and for laboratory work in its stronger aura; Kybella casts the Aegis of the Hearth each year for both Primi, since neither trusts the other to. Within the walls the Primi stoop to pettiness; on the Order's stage their feud is as vicious as any between beloved rivals. Fudarus has two vassals, one being Exspectatio, which has its own vassal, Atramentum Renatus in Burgundy; both are bound by harsh oaths and must fight hard at the Tourney to pay their feudal dues, and Fudarus repays them with generous political support. It has a long record of vassals that win independence and then founder, and prefers no House in its vassals.

Invisible servant spirits fill every room and do the cleaning, mending, carrying and cooking, each at the last task the wearer of the Circlet set it, so the fortress seems empty and silent and needs few servants, labourers or teamsters. There is a chef, an alchemist and a glassblower for the laboratories, a barber-surgeon who rules the covenant's regimen of health, and two craftsmen. The large turb is split evenly between the Primi and wears swatches of their colours, Harpax's green and Buliste's purple; warped by the aura, each side cannot see anyone wearing a substantial amount of the other's colour, Buliste included for Harpax's men, so a green cloak lets a man stab one of Buliste's grogs unopposed. Wearing both colours cancels the effect.
covenants.what_matters:
Vis: 12 pawns a year manifest on Ushant through the Three Great Spirits, 4 each of Creo, Auram and Imaginem (seisin)
Vis: Brittany's rich vis fell largely to Fudarus after 1018; Harpax governs it as Lord Heusaff
Vis: stripped of a legacy lease in 1172, granted to House Mercere, after Atlax of Tytalus read a Redcap's messages here
Income: Lampaul's fishing, through the Heusaff family
Income: the feudal dues of two vassals, Exspectatio and one other, under harsh oaths
Library: the House's great collection, used by Exspectatio's magi (no books named)
Enchantment: the Rod of the Primus controls every room's light, heat, doorways, smells, sounds and textures, and can make the effect follow one person (held by Harpax)
Enchantment: the Circlet of the Primus commands the servant spirits and the Three Great Spirits (worn by Buliste)
Defence: the Three Great Spirits, Magic Might 40 each, bound into the walls since the Schism War
Defence: sheer 180-foot cliffs, wandering reefs and currents, and a password tunnel for guests
Boon: Natural Fortress, Magical Fortress, Mystical Allies (the spirits), Informants (Buliste's spies)
Hook: House Covenant; Fractured Council (the two Primi); Divided Loyalty (the colour-blind turb)
Mundane: Fudarus's agents run the Paris Dyers' Guild, a coup against Florum
Tension: the feud of the two Primi, to be settled before the coming Grand Tribunal, where only one may sit
Tension: Buliste holds the House's network of spies and the Order's respect; Harpax holds the covenant, its vis and coin, and more sway in Normandy
Tension: the Traitor of Confluensis bears a key said to weaken Fudarus's defences
Tension: accused in 1200 of ruining Atramentum by founding an artificers' guild at Le Conquet
Hook: visitors must win entry by a Primus's challenge; an easy task is an insult, a hard one a compliment
Hook: a covenant Fudarus favours may be given some of its colour-blind grogs
covenants.secrets:
Lord Heusaff is Harpax in disguise: he stole the identity from Buliste's sanctum along with the Rod when she seemed dead.
The Three Great Spirits obey the Circlet's wearer through the old pact, not because the Circlet compels them; their vis's form is known only inside Fudarus.
Harpax is offering generous terms to new vassals for pawns in his feud, and wants the pieces of a pre-Hermetic item; it is a Diedne relic, Buliste has steered him to it, and she means to frame him once he has it.
Harpax has a merchant of Fudarus's spy network jailed on false charges; Buliste sends a spirit to help whoever frees him.
Porphyrion of Tytalus, an archmage who came from the Rome Tribunal three years ago, may mean to take the House for himself; a third contender is the one thing that would make the Primi work together.
The Primi will not stoop to a High Crime or Wizard's War against each other, though either may put the other in mortal danger.

covenants.name: Exspectatio
covenants.oath:
Service owed by the vassal: at each Tribunal its magi hand some or all of their sigils to the liege's representative as free proxies, or vote as the liege directs on a set number of questions; it pays a tithe of vis at agreed intervals (often of a given Art); it spends seasons copying or writing books for the liege's library; and it may be bound to harvest one of the liege's legacies each year.

Protection owed by the liege: it never backs a motion at Tribunal that harms its vassal, and backs any that helps it unless it can show the harm to itself; it answers a set number of calls for aid every seven years (though not at the cost of a season or its own vis); it may gift the vassal a vis source, books or enchantments; and it lets the vassal spend seasons copying from its library, the copies protected by a Cow and Calf agreement.

The oath is part of the Peripheral Code and enforceable at Tribunal. It ends by agreement of both sides, or after one side successfully prosecutes the other for defaulting on it, which is a Low Crime: a liege that breaks faith can be made to pay damages, and either side may then cancel the oath; a vassal that wants to go refuses a duty and lets itself be convicted and fined. A vassal that breaks away usually makes enemies of its old liege and that liege's other vassals.
covenants.summary:
A covenant of six Tytalus magi in a secluded valley of the Arrée Mountains, about three days from Fudarus. When it was plain that the feud of Harpax and Buliste would not end soon, and since Tytalan rivalries are personal and private, the other magi of Fudarus looked for somewhere else to live. Their eye fell on Atramentum, a vassal Fudarus had sponsored only the year before, conveniently near: in 1201 the elder Tytali turned out its two founders and moved in, and renamed it Exspectatio, waiting in hope or in dread. Exspectatio paid the evicted magi, Helios and Gulo Midusulfis, with the means to found a new covenant in Burgundy on a former legacy of Fudarus, Atramentum Renatus, which is now Exspectatio's own vassal.

All but one of its magi are at least forty years past apprenticeship, and they are technically still members of Fudarus. It is legally Fudarus's vassal, but the oath of fealty is very generous, since its magi helped write it, and one or more of them is often away at Fudarus using the library or a specialised laboratory. Its two leading magi are Adanos and Kybella, who stand on opposite sides of the Primi's feud.
covenants.what_matters:
Vis: none given; the covenant draws on Fudarus's resources
Library: Fudarus's, to which its members return for books
Aura: not given; weaker than Fudarus's, so its magi do some laboratory work at the domus magna
Oath: vassal of Fudarus on unusually generous terms, which its own magi helped draft
Vassal: Atramentum Renatus in Burgundy, founded by the magi it evicted
Boon: Seclusion (a hidden mountain valley)
Hook: Fractured Council (Adanos for Harpax, Kybella for Buliste); Superiors (Fudarus)
Tension: Cynics say the founders of Atramentum were duped into preparing the site for them
Hook: Iasper's family, the Foutins, and his taste for turmoil
covenants.secrets:
Iasper, looking for a way into the Cabal of the Laden Cart, draws a crossroads faerie of the passage between life and death, which blurs the border: corpses walk, the living fall into a death-like pallor, and Iasper must be freed from his own death-state to break the spell.
When one of Iasper's Foutin cousins gets into trouble (perhaps a grog of the player covenant), Iasper smooths things over with the authorities by framing the player magi in a grand plot to destabilise the region, then comes to them contrite to help untangle the mess without admitting his part.
Kybella founded the Cabal of the Laden Cart and hunts the Ankeu to imprison Death itself.

covenants.name: Montverte
covenants.summary:
An Autumn covenant, one of the five great lieges of the Tribunal and among its oldest, ruled in secret by an inner council of five. Feared, hated and often reviled for its warlike ways, it all but invented Hermetic raiding, and the practice survives only because Montverte and its followers have the strength, martial and political, to keep it alive.

Two Norse brothers, kin of Rollo, came with the Viking settlers: Harivald, a master of elemental magic who joined the Order through Ex Miscellanea and then founded a Flambeau line that endures, and his un-Gifted elder brother Haland. Together they seized an old Carolingian fort and raised a Norman keep on it; the covenant's founding was announced at Tribunal in 941, and Haland's heirs became the lords of Montverte. The magi soon dominated their hosts and used their soldiers for raids and extortion, at first on the quiet and then openly. In the Schism War the castle was a rallying point for martial Tremere and Flambeau, killed many of Normandy's Diedne, and gained great prestige. Raiding went on after the war until Koilios's brazen raid on Lapis Crudus's convoy in 1113 won it the shelter of a Tribunal precedent. Sanctions and scandals mark its history, and it is blamed for the fall of several covenants, but it has thrived.

The covenant fills the castle on the green mount, a sprawling keep above terraced walls and hanging gardens in a Magic aura of 5. The pentagonal inner curtain has a square tower at each corner, one for each councillor. The central keep holds the library, the meeting rooms and the guest chambers, and on its top floor the council chamber, a dark, bare hall round the ancient council table.

The magi live as guests of the Baron of Montverte and run his house from behind the scenes; they deal with the world through him, and other magi often question whether this is lawful. The magi say, truly, that they swear him no oath, and, less truly, that they let him rule alone. The covenfolk are the baron's household, and most servants and soldiers know nothing of the Order or that they live in a covenant.

Geirlaug leads the council and only its five sit in it. A dead councillor is replaced, usually from the junior magi, sometimes from outside, such as a leading magus of a loyal vassal. The four to six junior magi (the troupe decides) owe seasons of work and suit Tremere, Flambeau, Bonisagus, Verditius and Jerbiton; a Redcap probably lives here. Montverte has usually held one to three vassals, tools of its mischief that enjoy a strong liege's protection; Atsingani is its vassal now. Raiding by it and its vassals has made it one of the richest covenants in the Tribunal, and its magi live in luxury.
covenants.what_matters:
Vis: the book names no source; the covenant's wealth comes from raiding, its vassals and its stores, which Runild keeps
Income: the baron's domain and village, and the spoils of raids by Montverte and its vassals; one of the wealthiest covenants in the Tribunal
Library: in the central keep, overseen by Runild; contents not described
Vassals: Atsingani (since 1187); in the past Nauche-Fleur (1072-1166), and usually one to three at a time
Boon: a castle on a fortified hill with concentric walls, hanging gardens and a spring
Boon: a mundane baron and his soldiers wholly under the covenant's control
Boon: contacts in the Hanse Parisienne, who supply luxuries, and dealings with the eremite Anacrôn on raids against other covenants' town storehouses
Hook: raiding sets much of the Tribunal against it; its magi are blamed for the fall of past covenants
Hook: other magi question whether living through a mundane baron breaks the Code
Tension: Geirlaug's near-irrational hatred of Oleron, over an insult from its leader decades ago, and her dislike of the other lieges
Tension: Geirlaug's mind; she is seen only in the council mirror, and the others doubt her sanity in private
Tension: the succession to the Praeco: Geirlaug is third eldest in the Tribunal, after Celeres and Somnifer
Tension: the Lotharingian Tribunal movement, which would carve covenants away from Normandy
covenants.secrets:
The inner council is largely dysfunctional: each councillor is very able alone, but they barely coordinate, and behind a polite show of deference to Geirlaug runs a quiet contest of wills.
The baron's high chair carries an old Mentem enchantment that keeps its occupant compliant, and has left several barons slightly Warped.
Through a Mirror, Darkly: Geirlaug's face in the mirror begins to show two personalities quarrelling; perhaps a demon has supplanted her and rules through her image. Only Thormod seems untroubled.
Odin's Magus: Thormod is a leading member of the Children of Odin, practises Viking magic and uses his position for the cult; he may be kin or lover of its hierophant, Queen Skuld.
The Pirate Covenant: the council has allied with Waddenzee, the pirate covenant of the Rhine; Waddenzee would join the Lotharingian secession and then declare itself Montverte's vassal in Normandy instead, crippling the new Tribunal and winning a Tribunal that tolerates its raids.

covenants.name: Oleron
covenants.summary:
A covenant descended from a faerie court of Arthur's day, whose Merinita magi love tales of deeds of arms, passionate wooing and tragic death, and take an unusual interest, for their House, in certamen and in the lives of their peasants. It lies in the Apple Mile, a Faerie regio (aura 5) over the north of the Isle of Oléron, where it is always summer; the leadership is fought for at the orchard that joins it to the mortal world. It has five magi, three of them Merinita, and is one of the five great liege lines of the Tribunal.

In Arthur's time the young knight Lanval won the love of Triamour, Faerie Queen of Oleron, and after love lost and found was taken to live there forever. Arthur's knights might challenge him at the regio's entrance any Midsummer's Day; none won, and in time the place was forgotten except in songs. In 1028 Kherion of Merinita found it, beat Lanval and married his daughter, by then Queen of the Court of the Apple Mile. Its isolation and the might of its Sleepers have let it take part in the Order's crises without reprisal. Caprican of Merinita, consort of Triamour's great-granddaughter, rules it now.

A faerie queen, who embodies the land, rules with her magus consort and his council, which takes in most of the magi. The folk are humans and faeries from many lands and ages, for faeries have carried people off to the Apple Isle for thousands of years, and abductees, their faerie doubles and their descendants mingle in a colourful culture that each new queen bends to her liking. The place mixes real chivalry with modern romances of the past, and a magus who knows history sees the seams: a castle no Roman could have built, Lanval's arms on ancient things from before knights bore arms, and his armour in the hall too modern and too bright. The magi share the romantic feudalism, are keener on war than most Merinita, and look after their common folk with noble condescension.

The champion's seat is won by challenge: whoever would claim it sinks an axe into an apple tree ringing the challenge ground on Midsummer's Day, which the queen feels at once, and the champion must meet him in a contest of arms before sunset the next day; it need not be to the death, and lately certamen has served. A beaten or fleeing challenger must apologize and perform a hard task the queen sets, enforced by the site as a Rego Mentem effect of Penetration 75 (never suicidal, but very hard for a battle-hardened magus). A victor must marry the queen's daughter, who becomes queen at the wedding; if there is none, one appears, grown and with a lifetime's memories, the next evening, and the faeries and every human without Magic Resistance remember her life. Refusing the marriage counts as defeat. Old consorts and queens usually stay; some queens travel to the great faerie courts and Merinita covenants, and some old consorts let their Parma lapse to remember the life they are supposed to have led.

The Stone Couches are the Queen's power alone: tumuli that, like kilns, grow faerie copies of folk heroes. A skeleton forms in three years and flesh over eighteen more, when the Sleeper begins to breathe; its Might keeps growing, slowly after a century and a half, and its powers are what the folk of the Atlantic shores believe of the hero. Sleepers wake when the covenant is in danger, at the queen's call, or when something suits their story, and the covenfolk say all will one day wake for a last battle against an unnamed evil. A Sleeper who stays awake leaves his Couch growing a duplicate with all his memories. An ordinary human buried in a Couch becomes a minor faerie copy of himself, a fate faerie magi think beneath them.

Oberon is the best-known: begun centuries ago as a faerie Alberich, the magician brother of Merovech, he was remade when the Capetians made that story useless and the magi spread the song of Huon of Bordeaux, in which a dwarf-king Oberon helps Huon through his impossible penance at the court of the Amir of Babylon. Once the song caught on, the Queen woke him for good. He looks like the most beautiful three-year-old ever born, which limits him in towns, and is called the son of Julius Caesar and Morgan le Fay; his horn banishes hunger and thirst, heals, draws people to it willy-nilly and lightens hearts, he captures the will of those who talk to him, and he is a master of illusion. A second Oberon now grows on his Couch, oddly taller than a man.

Oleron prefers vassals with strong defences and treats vassalage as trade: surplus vis from the regio for mundane goods the vassals obtain, beside what it buys through House Mercere. It has lately taken weaker vassals too, to profit from Fudarus's troubles, and it fears House Tytalus, whose easiest way to strike at the unassailable regio is through weak vassals outside it.
covenants.what_matters:
Vis: surplus vis harvested in the Apple Mile, traded to vassals for mundane goods (kinds and amounts not given)
Income: the vassals' mundane goods, and purchases through House Mercere
Boon: Regio (Major): the Apple Mile, a Faerie regio of aura 5
Boon: Fantastic Environment: an endless summer, looping roads and the covenant's own sea
Boon: Natural Fortress: any invader faces every Sleeper, some made for home defence
Boon: Inhuman Residents: faeries and the Sleepers of the Stone Couches
Boon: Faux Feudalism: ruled by the faerie queen and her champion consort
Hook: Faerie Aura
Hook: Hermetic Politics: liege of Nidi; at odds with Fudarus and House Tytalus
Tension: the champion's seat is open to any challenger on Midsummer's Day; an unanswered challenge would cut the regio off
Tension: magi explore the looping roads and the sea for another way out, to the world or to Arcadia, without success
Tension: censured by the chief Quaesitor of Stonehenge for trying to rescue Eleanor of Aquitaine from captivity
Tension: the Keepers of a Thousand Tales dislike the Stone Couches for fixing stories to one place and one version
Mundane: can raise gangs of sailors from the isle to make trouble in Paris, but keeps no agents there
covenants.secrets:
Caprican has helped other covenants claim Fudarus's resources while Fudarus is weak, and has added and fortified vassals; if House Tytalus learns of it there will be reprisals once it unites behind a Primus.
One ancient Sleeper, older than the Hermetic colony, may be a mighty faerie Ogier the Dane, Charlemagne's paladin whom Morgan le Fay kept two hundred years in Avalon with a rejuvenating ring and a crown of forgetfulness. He has woken and escaped at least once and might again if disaster strikes Denmark; Rhine and Norman magi who dream of colonising Denmark would like his help, but he is hard to control and would likely seek service with Philip II. Whoever puts on the ring he wears dies at once, his place taken by a faerie that believes it is, and may be, his spirit.
The prophecy of a last battle may itself be a story planted to wake every Sleeper at the covenant's hour of need.
Nidi's weakness is a lure Oleron built for Tytalus: Oleron can reinforce it by rapid travel magic and stocks it with hidden resources.

covenants.summary:
Conventio Nidi, the nest: Bjornaer and Merinita magi who, unlike most of their kind, do not see towns as wasteland. As towns grow into cities and their communities fragment, wildness creeps back into the cracks, and Nidi seeks such niches. It has no mark of its own and uses the badge of Henri, the nobleman who serves it. It takes a new name with each new leader; Nidi refers to Micropedus's starling heartbeast.

Oleron founded it as a vassal in 1100 in light woodland far from any settlement. In the twelfth century the land was cleared for crops and the port of Bergerac grew up barely an hour away; most of the Merinita members left for wilder places, and the two who stayed, Regulus of Merinita and Micropedus of Bjornaer, chose to embrace the towns. Luna of Bjornaer joined lately. It lies south of the Dordogne line but is older than the 1103 ruling, so it belongs to Normandy.

The magi live and hold council in Lord Henri's small castle, which was once the covenant's main building. When clearing made discovery certain, the magi recruited Henri's father as their nominal overlord: the family holds mundane title to the covenant's lands, hides the magi from other landowners, gives them shield grogs, and keeps the key sites as a chase its men patrol, which should keep settlement and the Dominion off them. Henri knows his guests are wizards; for his hospitality and services he is promised a long, healthy old age. He is proud, so the magi ask and never order, and though he has never refused, being treated like a grog would rankle.

Their philosophy is the starling's: a wild bird that nests in the eaves of houses, sheltered by people who drive off its predators, and lives on what they overlook. A few magi, Micropedus argued, can do the same: live unnoticed in the spaces mundanes ignore, draw unwitting protection from them and live as parasites on their communities. They see themselves as pioneers of urban territory and want more members, knowing Micropedus is near his end.
covenants.what_matters:
Vis: the lilac-grown oak grove in the chase, Herbam vis from the flowers; Regulus can turn it into honey holding Animal vis, losing a third
Vis: pays its tithes openly, through the Redcaps and at Tribunal, for show
Boon: Tame Nobleman: Lord Henri, who hosts the magi and holds their lands
Boon: Hidden Resources: unused magic items, copies of a strong Aegis, servants trained by awakened Sleepers
Hook: Urban: close beside farmland and the port of Bergerac, and seeking niches in towns
Hook: Beholden: vassal of Oleron
Tension: the faeries driven out by the Dominion may come back in hardier forms; losing the riverbank laboratories or the grove in the chase could finish the covenant
Tension: Micropedus is close to Final Twilight; his weather magic keeps the district prosperous
Tension: Henri's only child Lila must marry a man the covenant can manage, and be happy, or the arrangement fails; Henri will soon want a longevity potion
Tension: a girl found as a baby in a wild hive a few days south may be a Bee Queen; Regulus wants her raised far away
covenants.secrets:
Nidi's weakness is deliberate. Oleron means it to look a fit target for House Tytalus once the Tytalan civil war ends and its magi go back to provoking the Tribunal: Tytalus magi who attack it in earnest will underestimate it, be driven off and be exposed before the Tribunal.
Its hidden resources: many small magic items it never uses, several copies of a remarkably strong Aegis of the Hearth, and servants whom awakened Sleepers have trained. Its magi may use them only with Oleron's leave or against magi of Fudarus, and Oleron can reinforce it quickly by travel magic.
For over thirty years its tithes have been repaid, or traded at good rates for other vis, by Oleron.
Its magi are promised places in Oleron or another of its vassals should Nidi fall.

covenants.name: Atsingani
covenants.oath:
Service owed by the vassal: at each Tribunal its magi hand some or all of their sigils to the liege's representative as free proxies, or vote as the liege directs on a set number of questions; it pays a tithe of vis at agreed intervals (often of a given Art); it spends seasons copying or writing books for the liege's library; and it may be bound to harvest one of the liege's legacies each year.

Protection owed by the liege: it never backs a motion at Tribunal that harms its vassal, and backs any that helps it unless it can show the harm to itself; it answers a set number of calls for aid every seven years (though not at the cost of a season or its own vis); it may gift the vassal a vis source, books or enchantments; and it lets the vassal spend seasons copying from its library, the copies protected by a Cow and Calf agreement.

The oath is part of the Peripheral Code and enforceable at Tribunal. It ends by agreement of both sides, or after one side successfully prosecutes the other for defaulting on it, which is a Low Crime: a liege that breaks faith can be made to pay damages, and either side may then cancel the oath; a vassal that wants to go refuses a duty and lets itself be convicted and fined. A vassal that breaks away usually makes enemies of its old liege and that liege's other vassals.
covenants.summary:
A small, mobile Spring covenant, vassal of Montverte, made up mostly of soldiers of doubtful repute with wagons and tents, living by brigandage or as mercenaries. When they have stirred up enough trouble where they are, they move on to somewhere they will be noticed less. It is camped now in the uplands of the Auvergne, in the east of Aquitaine.

Its founder Aureliana came of the Atsingani, a Byzantine tradition of wandering seers who served Emperor Constantine IX in the mid-eleventh century against wild beasts and rebel peasants, then fell from favour. As Byzantium declined she left the Theban Tribunal with another magus and her apprentice Viviana and went west looking for a Tribunal that would have them: Transylvania drove them out, the Rhine would not recognise them as a covenant, and Normandy, where founding a covenant is far easier, accepted them in 1187. To survive they swore fealty to Montverte, the liege closest to their way of thinking.

Since then they have roamed the south of the Tribunal and raided weaker covenants, winning few friends and much mistrust. With no fixed base they have no steady income: they prosper when their mercenaries serve rich masters and otherwise rob villages, monasteries, merchants, pilgrims and weak covenants. They have no stone buildings or walls and only poor shared laboratories in tents, apart from Viviana's. Hardship binds them: magi and covenfolk are close and loyal, and the magi are not aloof from their servants.

About fifty people follow the covenant, three dozen of them Brabançon mercenaries, with nearly as many horses: Byzantines and Brabanters, mostly young or in middle age, since the camp can hardly keep the infirm and mothers often leave to settle down. The Brabançons are coarse, crude men but expert soldiers and riders, deadly with the crossbow. There may be one or two more magi beyond the two the book describes.

covenants.name: Eboris
covenants.summary:
Conventio Eboris, the House of the Ivory Carvers, is a small Jerbiton covenant in Paris whose members do no magical research. It was made not as a place to study but as a memorial: its founder, Archmagus Mathieus, saw Constantinople, the new Rome and in his eyes God's own instrument of civilisation, sacked in 1204, and the house is the machinery of his grief. He was away at Valnastium's library when the crusaders came, crossed their lines by magic too late to save the city, and fled with a few covenfolk and a little of his covenant's wealth by ship to Marseilles and overland to Paris, apparently to be out of the Latin Empire. His family and covenant were gone.

For two years he was legally a wanderer, a nobleman in exile patronising the artists and scholars round the court. His Primus drew him back: he guided the Itinerarium on several of its tours, graduates came back to Paris to stay with him, and his home became a covenant. A Redcap, Marcus of Paris, runs the household as majordomo. The house is on the Rue de la Tabletterie, a former pilgrims' hostel turned ivory-carving office, chosen in a poor quarter so as not to threaten the nobility and to avoid the university; its basement lacuna counted too. Some members live elsewhere in the city.

Its residents are the Sweated Shillings, a shifting band of young magi named for coins shaken in a bag until silver flakes off: always at least three besides Mathieus, many more during the Tour, interchangeable to outsiders, usually fun-loving and frantic to cram a lifetime into a year, and given to leaving Mathieus a crisis to mend. Jerbiton holds that magic tempts its practitioners to waste their lives, and that a vibrant city inoculates the young against the laboratory.

Eboris owes no feudal dues and seeks none. Because its members do not study, it wants little of what other covenants fight over, so even its modest vis income leaves a surplus to trade, and it is rich. It is more and more a neutral ground for covenants in dispute. It is the senex of Paris. Mathieus holds revels eulogising great magi, feasts and games through the Paris night, for which he buys strange items from young magi across Europe as a way of drawing them into his circle; at least one magus he eulogised never existed, a fraud he blames on an unnamed Tytalus.

Mathieus is the Warden of Paris: Jerbiton magi tell him what they do in the city and help him when it is threatened. He is also a convenient injured party for the Quaesitores, ready to say that another magus's doings caused him trouble with mundanes, which turns an unwelcome act into a breach of the Code; in Paris even small meddling with the powerful is punished. Not a hoplite, he is still a dangerous foe for young magi, with his illusions, his experience of casting in a city, his knowledge of Paris, his band of young allies and his political friends.

covenants.secrets:
Mathieus's revels may honour magi long forgotten or entirely invented; some say the maga who never existed ought to have.
Mathieus will help the Quaesitores by claiming injury when it suits him.

Seed, Rescuing Constantinopolitans: a slave of a Roman Tribunal covenant asks Mathieus to rescue survivors of his old covenant; Mathieus fears a Venetian trap and sends young magi to scout and smuggle.
Seed, Treasure in Constantinople: Mathieus sealed away his dead friends' treasures in the city and now wants sturdy young magi to bring them out; he will not go himself.
Seed, Succession: his named heir, Constantina filia Andru, was picked mostly to silence petitioners; a novel enough experience might win the player characters the place.
Seed, Tremors at the End of the World: Paris's ivory comes through Trebizond, so a sudden stop means trouble in Asia, and Andru will send magi to look; a glut of walrus ivory would also make Mathieus ask who took it and why.

covenants.name: Lapis Crudus
covenants.summary:
Once one of the great covenants of Normandy, Lapis Crudus is a shadow of itself after more than eighty years shut inside a faerie regio, and its magi, lately able to come and go after a fashion, are trying to win back their old standing. It was born of the Schism War's spoils: the Grand Tribunal sponsored it in 1063 to heal the breach between Flambeau and Tytalus, with two magi of each, a Jerbiton and a Bonisagus of Trianoma's line. Many of Normandy's Flambeau descend from its founders; for a time they were the only two Flambeau in the Tribunal. It grew more mixed, was a leading voice in Tribunal politics and culture for a century, was a liege covenant, and sponsored two vassals, both short-lived. In 1113 Koilios of Montverte raided its supply train, and the Tribunal's refusal to punish him set the precedent that allows raiding.

In 1118 a mishap betrayed its site and nature to several noble families, who tried to use the magi; threats and blackmail held them off for a while. To escape, Aries of Flambeau tricked the faerie Candidus into protecting and hiding the covenant. Candidus kept the bargain by moving it into a regio, and in resentment sealed the borders. Some vis seisins lay inside, but at first the magi had to spend them on food and tools, until one of them learned to pass non-living goods inward and they tasted meat and wine for the first time in nearly seventy years. They lived on their large vis stocks and wore out their library. Their vassals, glad of freedom, made little effort to free them, and they were forgotten.

Aries entered Final Twilight five years ago, in 1215, and Candidus agreed to new terms: anyone may leave if someone of like social standing enters in exchange, magus for magus, churchman for churchman or scholar, outcast for outcast, and the newcomer may bring whatever he can carry. The gate is a mirror in a hut that straddles the regio's edge on Les Trois Pignons in the forest of Fontainebleau; the two walk toward it from either side and change places. Laden grogs swap in and out constantly. Outside there are only a few shacks of apparent outlaws.

Inside, under a Faerie aura of 7, a dozen sandstone buildings fill a star of valleys, lit directly only at midday: a sanctum in each arm, covenfolk at the centre, the council chamber over the cavern of the Bleeding Stone. Minor Herbam and Terram enchantments made in captivity are everywhere: doors open in walls as people approach, roofs turn clear on command, the humblest cook has a magic knife. Through Somnifer's dreams the magi kept up with the world, yet they are oddly naive about the Order, eager to see it again, and see it through the twist of the strong Faerie aura. Three ancient, narrowly specialised magi remain; Somnifer's filius Languidus has spoken for the covenant at Tribunal for ten years but will not join it. It has not entered the Tourney since it was sealed, and all its legacies are held to have lapsed. Most covenfolk were born inside, some of the third generation, and are badly Warped (a score of 3 by puberty and 5 by their late forties); they assume every covenant uses magic items for everyday work.

Vis: the Bleeding Stone, in a cavern under the council chamber, Corpus and Terram (seisin; amount not given)
Vis: the vines down the valley cliffs, Herbam (seisin; amount not given)
Vis: large old stocks, much drawn down by eighty years of study
Library: large, with several rare high-quality tomes and many tractatus written in captivity
Boon: Regio; Faerie Aura 7; household enchantments everywhere (Herbam and Terram)
Hook: trapped behind Candidus's mirror; leaving needs a substitute of like standing
Hook: covenfolk heavily Warped; magi nearing Final Twilight
Hook: all legacies lapsed; no Tourney team since the sealing
Tension: means to reclaim its old vassals, now independent
Tension: Mnemon's unknown debt to Candidus
Tension: Somnifer is second in line for Praeco after Celeres of Cunfin
covenants.secrets:
Seed, Through the Looking Glass: to travel, the magi must tempt other magi to take their place, offering seasons in the library; once out, they do not want to go back.
Seed: as the price of the new terms Candidus bound Mnemon to a fearsome task once he gets out, which might destroy a player covenant's faerie-bound vis source, kill its guardian, or stir mundane politics to have it disbanded.
Seed: Lapis Crudus will try to reassert its lost Oaths of Fealty, perhaps over the player covenant.
Each magus took a Warping Point a year from the aura alone during the eighty years, and more from Longevity Rituals; the opening may have come just in time.

covenants.name: Florum
covenants.summary:
Liege of a line of covenants and the leading power of the Order in the Low Countries, Florum lives by Flanders' new industry. Its name and badge are the blue flowers of flax. The Tribunal's rules on vis have split what would elsewhere be one covenant's resources between Florum and its vassals, binding them in a close alliance; together they want out of Normandy and are the leading supporters of the proposed Lotharingian Tribunal, complaining at every meeting about the rules on mundane interference and raiding.

Founded in 907 as a small Jerbiton House covenant between Bruges and Ghent, on the site now called the Spider's Palace, it sat out the Schism War by moving most of its magi into Ghent, where an attack on them would rouse the Church. Its customs followed the Primi of House Jerbiton: when one urged city living, the magi returned to Ghent and founded a vassal at the old site to keep its resources; when another asked Jerbiton covenants to open their doors, both admitted magi of other Houses. The covenant is now in Ghent, with members from many Houses. (The chapter puts the move in the tenth century; the Tribunal's records and the timeline give 1117, when the Spider's Palace was founded.)

The covenant's real home is the Farm, an enclosed suburb on Ghent's southern edge, with smaller holdings across the city gathered over the centuries. The great factory at its centre is a blind: the cloth is made there by magic, under illusions, through the gift of a faerie-blooded family, the Spinnen, and the factory makes that wealth look ordinary and so lawful under the Peripheral Code. The tenements round it, finer than most in the new parts of Ghent, house the staff and their families; all of them know their landlords as the old de Spinnen family, now headed by Piet de Spinnen, though not all know they serve magi. The covenant poses as a few old farming families; no property is ever sold or let to an outsider.

Membership shifts, usually four to six magi. Two members are living at the Spider's Palace for its excellent laboratories; four are in residence: Rhesus of Verditius, who leads the magi, Calvinus of Jerbiton, Alroy of Flambeau, the covenant's champion, and Prunellie of Merinita. A Quaesitor, a Tytalan hoplite and a Redcap are staying as guests, using the covenant as a base while they look for a site for a House Guernicus covenant should the Lotharingian Tribunal come about.

Florum has two vassals: the Spider's Palace, nearby and vital to its work, and Requies Aeterna in Picardy, a covenant in decline. Two earlier vassals have gone: Lixivia in Champagne (1021 to 1124) and Alcuin's Auberge, the Mercer House at Tours (1124 to 1197).

Income: cloth woven by touch by the Spinnen, almost thirty of them in 1220, sold through international traders and much of it exported in secret
Income: a mundane weaving workshop of the Spinnen's relatives, and a seat in Ghent's Weavers' Guild
Vis: half the harvest of Requies Aeterna, its vassal, sent as a tithe
Vis: Prunellie harvests faeries turned to standing stones in the fields of the Low Countries (Form and amount not given)
Vis: the Spider's Palace keeps the old site's sources for the line
Library: no titles given (see its library record)
Boon: Wealth (the Spinnen's cloth)
Boon: Strong Community (the Farm's families), Mystical Allies (a kabouter tribe)
Hook: City (Ghent), Faerie Aura, Hermetic Politics (the Lotharingian movement)
Hook: Guild (the Weavers' Guild of Ghent), Dark Secret (the Spinnen and the false family)
Duty: each year a small party of covenfolk is sent, by drawing straws, to serve a year at Requies Aeterna; all dread it

covenants.secrets:
Piet de Spinnen is Petrus, Calvinus's mundane son, born at Valnastium; a mercenary in Italy who faked his death to escape his rivals and was trained by an old Redcap to play the heir of the childless Arne de Spinnen, who was himself a front. The de Spinnens are a fiction the magi keep up.
Two of Piet's children spent a year at the new university in Paris and then went secretly to Valnastium to be trained as servants of House Jerbiton.
Calvinus's 'uncle Calvin' persona, his Italian wife and his daughter brought up by her grandparents are all invented; the daughter newly arrived in Ghent is his apprentice Sophia.
The flax origin legend of the Spinnen is common knowledge in the Low Countries, so anyone with enough clues might guess what the spider-kin are.
The visiting Quaesitor, hoplite and Redcap are scouting for Confluensis's planned Quaesitorial covenant and Mercer House in a Lotharingian Tribunal.

Florum's vassal on Florum's first site, founded in 1117 when the Jerbiton magi went back to Ghent and wanted to keep their claim to the site's magical resources. Usually a single magus lives here to hold that claim; just now two members of Florum are also here, using its fine laboratories.

Its magi see the need for two covenants on two such close sites, only so that no other magus may lawfully take the resources, as proof of what is wrong with Normandy's way of sharing out vis; the covenant is an eager supporter of its liege in the Lotharingian movement.

covenants.summary:
Eternal Rest: a small Winter covenant of the Donatores Requietis Aeternae, the Givers of Eternal Rest, an Ex Miscellanea tradition that helps the dead leave the world of the living. It is a vassal of Florum and of no political weight, though the Quaesitores have watched it closely. Most Donatores have left; it is little more than a shell on the site where their tradition began.

In the eleventh century France suffered hauntings and hordes of walking dead, blamed on a cult of the dead said to be strongest in Picardy. Early in the twelfth, hedge wizards, clergy and others banded together and, guided from heaven, went to Nesle, which a band of undead warriors was ravaging. They won, at the cost of many lives and the town itself, and some of the hedge wizards stayed among the ruins lest the dead return. The Quaesitor Muirgheal arranged their admission to the Order, over the doubts of many Normandy magi; those who stayed declared a covenant in 1123 and swore fealty to Florum.

As the dead stayed quiet, most of its magi spread across western Europe to work wherever the dead walked, and the covenant slid into Winter, though it remains the tradition's spiritual centre and the home of its library. Two magi remain: the ancient founder Eulogius and his youngest filius Henri. They barely keep up their sancta and the library and ignore the world; the townsfolk have forgotten the battle and see only a haunted ruin, and the Church has lost touch. Abroad, the magi pass for monks in their plain robes.

Nearly all the covenfolk died or left, and none would come from a place of such ill repute, so the covenant pays Florum a larger vis tithe in return for a small party of servants each year, a posting Florum's covenfolk dread.

Florum expects Requies Aeterna to follow it into a Lotharingian Tribunal; its magi will go along, expecting the Rhine magi there to reject vassalage and cancel their oath, which they would not mind.
covenants.what_matters:
Vis: the site is rich in vis, Perdo and Corpus among it (amounts not given); roughly half goes to Florum as tithe

Boon: Aura (Magic 5), Hedge Tradition (the Donatores)
Hook: Haunted (reputation), Massacre Site (the battle of Nesle), Indebted (servants from Florum for a larger tithe)
Hook: Beholden (vassal of Florum), Hermetic Politics (the Quaesitores' suspicion)
Tension: the Quaesitores distrust its past dealings with the Church; several Donatores were trained clergy
Tension: magi who distrust the Donatores could plot a Wizard's War on Eulogius to break the covenant and seize its vis, which would drag Florum in
Hook: magi troubled by restless dead may seek its help, but persuading Eulogius or Henri to leave, or even finding the way in, is hard
covenants.secrets: Philip of Atramentum Renatus was formerly a member here, and other Donatores are scattered across western Europe. Without Eulogius the covenant would surely fall.

covenants.summary:
A covenant of magi sharing a Champagne valley with a Cistercian abbey of the same name, which keeps the Order in touch with the Church's affairs. It is a vassal of Confluensis, recognised by the Tribunal of 1192 though magi lived on the site long before; Eloi of Jerbiton founded it with the backing of his parens Jerome. The Presiding Quaesitor worries about trouble with the mundanes, but the covenant's ties to the Church have served the Order well.

When the old Mercer House at Tours fell to raiders in 1197, Confluensis seized on Florum's weakness and proposed Cunfin as the new one, close to the fairs, and paid for a Mercere Portal; the Redcaps agreed, handing Confluensis and its vassals a hold on Redcap services that its rivals noticed. A small band of Redcaps now lives here, the portal leads to Dragon's Rest, and from Cunfin they organise, with Confluensis, the temporary Mercer Houses at the Champagne fairs. The monks hold hospitality a holy duty and are used to travellers coming and going.

In 1199 the ancient, eccentric Celeres of Bonisagus arrived, declaring Cunfin the castle from which he and his knights would seek the Grail. Many took it as proof he was mad, but he has made himself the heart of the place: his rebuilt castle stands in the regio over the abbey, his Grail library draws scholars from across the Order, and every visitor has a story about his hospitality.

Cunfin's purpose is to stand between the Order and the Church. Eloi is the abbey's prior, Brother Eligius, with great sway over the monks and their abbot; the monks put his wonders down to holiness. All the magi but Angelus have the Gentle Gift. Abbot Martin, the cellarer and a few brothers know the truth and support the magi; the rest of the monks have met the magi without knowing what they are.
covenants.what_matters:

Library: Celeres's Grail library, said to hold every book written on the Grail and many on Arthur and Merlin

Boon: Mercer House; Hook: a Divine aura round a Magic regio

Tension: the Presiding Quaesitor fears the covenant will embroil the Order with the mundanes

The abbot knows what Eloi and the magi are and shares their aims.
Jerome of Confluensis secretly saves troublesome heirs marked for death, convincing the world they are dead and hiding them in monasteries and covenants; Eloi is his chief partner, and Artorius was one such child. It is very likely a breach of the Code.
The covenant may not survive the Church's growing hostility even with Eloi (The Specter of Rome).

covenants.name: Atramentum Renatus
covenants.oath:
Service owed by the vassal: at each Tribunal its magi hand some or all of their sigils to the liege's representative as free proxies, or vote as the liege directs on a set number of questions; it pays a tithe of vis at agreed intervals (often of a given Art); it spends seasons copying or writing books for the liege's library; and it may be bound to harvest one of the liege's legacies each year.

Protection owed by the liege: it never backs a motion at Tribunal that harms its vassal, and backs any that helps it unless it can show the harm to itself; it answers a set number of calls for aid every seven years (though not at the cost of a season or its own vis); it may gift the vassal a vis source, books or enchantments; and it lets the vassal spend seasons copying from its library, the copies protected by a Cow and Calf agreement.

The oath is part of the Peripheral Code and enforceable at Tribunal. It ends by agreement of both sides, or after one side successfully prosecutes the other for defaulting on it, which is a Low Crime: a liege that breaks faith can be made to pay damages, and either side may then cancel the oath; a vassal that wants to go refuses a duty and lets itself be convicted and fined. A vassal that breaks away usually makes enemies of its old liege and that liege's other vassals.
covenants.summary:
A young covenant in Burgundy, vassal of Exspectatio and through it bound to Fudarus. In 1200 Helios of Tytalus and Gulo Midusulfis of Bjornaer founded a vassal of Fudarus in the Arree Mountains of Brittany and named it Atramentum, ink, after a sodalis who died in the founding. A year later five of Fudarus's magi, leaving their own covenant over the feud of its Primi, threw the two young founders out and took the site as Exspectatio. By way of amends Exspectatio gave them the means to start again in Burgundy, about a vis source that had been a legacy of Fudarus, and they called the new covenant Atramentum Renatus, ink reborn.

Iacula of Bonisagus and Philip of Ex Miscellanea have since joined them. Like the other vassals of Fudarus's line, the covenant is bound by a hard oath of obligation and must compete hard at the Tourney to pay its feudal debts, in return for Fudarus's generous political support.
covenants.what_matters:
Vis: the source about which the covenant was built, formerly a legacy of Fudarus (Art and amount not given)
Library: no books are named
Oath: a harsh contract of obligation to Exspectatio and Fudarus, paid partly from Tourney winnings
Tension: Helios's theurgy probes whether Bibracte raised the spirit of Vercingetorix; Philip fears it is angering the ghosts
Tension: a Quaesitor is looking into reports of a savage wild beast near the covenant, and whether Gulo broke the Code
Tension: the founders were evicted from their first covenant by their liege's own magi
Hook: Iacula's new projectile spells have great martial potential
covenants.secrets:
Whether the ravaging beast is Gulo in his heartbeast's shape, and whether he harmed mundanes by it, is the Quaesitor's open question.
Cynics say Helios and Gulo were duped into preparing Atramentum's site for the elder Tytali of Exspectatio.

covenants.name: Confluensis
covenants.notes:
Sagas: eight starting points the book gives for a Confluensis saga.
- The Praeco is Dead, Long Live the Praeco: the players work for Proctor, who cannot be seen to take sides, to settle the succession before the next Tribunal a little over a year away. Stellatus, the eldest, has left for Iberia; next come Celeres of Cunfin, then Somnifer of Lapis Crudus or Geirlaug of Montverte, each a problem. Proctor wants a Praeco he can trust or control; many would rather see his power checked.
- Riches and Vis: as Confluensis's agents before the Grand Tribunal of 1228, the players fight the Lotharingian Tribunal, whose loss would leave Tytalus-held Brittany out-producing the rest of Normandy in vis; or they found the 'new law' there, a Quaesitorial covenant and Mercer House on a site Confluensis has already scouted.
- The Haunted Woods of Broceliande: Confluensis backs a new covenant in Brittany against Tytalus influence; the players are its magi or its senior sponsors, and faeries and magi alike harry it, as they have every covenant tried there.
- The Specter of Rome: the players keep the Order's uneasy peace with the Church as the Dominicans and the Papal letter of inquisition turn from the Cathars, which Jerome and Eloi fear will come north; troubleshooters or envoys, with enemies on both sides.
- City of God: remove the Hospitallers' settlement from the Cotentin without breaking the Code or setting a precedent, or win over its old knights.
- The Strange Saint of Cotentin: find out what makes the statue of St. Giles regrow its wood before the Hospitallers do.
- The Chapter of Cherbourg: a Fengheld chapter house magus at Cherbourg counts as a cenobite under the Peripheral Code, seeks recognition, takes Confluensis's vis and may gain housemates; skilled magi might break her from Fengheld and bring her under a local liege.
- Young and In Charge: the players take the places of some of the covenant's magi, serve Proctor for a while, then lose him to murder or a lab accident; his replacement, a respected Quaesitor new to Normandy, leans on them to run the House's business.

Story seed, the Bud and the Venelli: after a night of portents a huge stone bud rises from the swamp, and a boar-headed faerie says the covenant stands on an old pact between the marsh powers and the Venelli, which the magi must now keep. The Venelli once drowned captured kings, later a pig crowned king and trussed in a set way, shown on the coins of their last king, who hired Jersey mercenaries against Caesar. Leads run to Jersey (wreckers, ghosts and ghost-gathering faeries), the ship of drowned souls leaving Le Havre each All Hallows' Night, a coin-collecting Jerbiton magus, or a demon holding a coin. Drowning a royal pig might bring Rego or Animal vis, a valerian flower whose chambers heal, a vis-scenting gift for the Venelli's new king, boar skinchangers, the watery ghosts of past boar kings, or a white lady sent as the marsh's envoy.
covenants.summary:
The Covenant of the Confluence is the largest Quaesitorial covenant in Normandy, home of the Tribunal's Praeco and its Presiding Quaesitor, hidden in the marshes of the Cotentin. Since the Tribunal is a turbulent one, its members are mostly investigators and hoplites. Its buildings stand on huge stone flowers, meant to show both growth and stability. It sits where fresh water meets salt, and its purpose is the same kind of balance: keeping the peace among the covenants of Normandy. To that end it keeps vassals: the lesser Guernicus covenants of the Tribunal (one of them two magi, a Quaesitor and a hoplite, whose site each saga places for itself), Cunfin in Champagne, and Dragon's Rest, a Mercer House on the Seine. It has just lost its leader, and whether it is still strong enough for its role is an open question.

Guernicus himself ordered the covenant founded, in 810, to see Hermetic law kept at the Order's edges. It first stood in the lair of the dragon Gargouille, in the swamps between Rouen and the Seine's mouth, and in time took in a Mercer House. Diedne magi sacked it in the Schism War; three members who were away elsewhere in the Tribunal survived and rebuilt it. After the war the Primus of Guernicus enlarged it, and with ever more traffic on the Seine it grew too big to stay unnoticed. In 1051 it took over its own vassal, the Orchard of Sour Apples, in the Cotentin, absorbing its magi. The Mercere magi stayed behind as Dragon's Rest, keeping the old badge of a dragon spouting water; Confluensis took a stylised whirlpool. The two remain close, each using the other's laboratories and library. Confluensis has always served the Primus of Guernicus as the House's mustering point and supply base in a crisis, and it helped bring down Tasgillia, the diabolist Prima of Tytalus.

Its central buildings were shaped by magic, whimsically, on platforms that are single pieces of stone grown into flowers, which makes some think Terram magi of House Guernicus's Terrae cult settled it. The rest look like dressed granite, like that of Mont St. Michel; some were built by masons and some only made to look that way. The Sundew carries most of them: five great pads, each ringed with stone globes joined to it by covered walkways, linked by stems to a six-storey stone spike with a lookout on top, which the magi have begun carving with the covenant's history in the manner of Trajan's column. The western pad holds the Great Hall, with dining and drill space below, stores and offices on a mezzanine, and a pulley that lifts cargo from the covenant's lighters; eighteen houses for guests and senior staff stand around it. Clockwise come the Pad of Gatherers (food: seafood and chestnuts, a mill, granary, brewery and bakery), the Pad of Crafters (potters using clays from all over the swamp, and paper made from papyrus reeds that Quaesitors brought in and spread by magic), the Pad of Parades (festivals, games, the Aegis rite and often the Tribunal itself), and the Furled Pad, too narrow to live on, where the boats moor.

West of the Sundew the Bell Flower holds the magi's eight two-storey houses on its petals around an ornamental lake, with a stone disc on three stamens that is formally the council chamber but too awkward to reach without flying. South of it the square, three-storey Library Tower, the oldest building, rises straight from the ground, raised by a ritual meant for another site: its bottom floor is flooded and silting up, the second is the real council chamber, bridged to the Bell Flower, the top holds the library and the magical stores, and the roof serves sentries, ceremonies and the odd signal fire. A Mercere Portal to Dragon's Rest is here too.

The covenfolk are the last of the Venelli, the Celtic tribe whose capital was Coutances, conquered and settled by Rome. Most entered the Order's service when the Normans burned their town in 998. Once pagans, whose last king took the boar as his sign, they lost their own magic first to Rome and then to House Guernicus, after a pagan sympathiser helped House Diedne in the Schism War. Today they live by serving the magi, trading at times in the ports of southern England, with no part left in Norman life. Their tongue is close enough to Breton to be understood but has its own accent and turns of phrase, and most also speak Norman French or English. Few have been soldiers, but they know the marsh well enough to be dangerous guerrillas. They wear bright woollens dyed with herbs and minerals, from wool bought in England, and have sometimes been taken for faeries.

The Quaesitors here are known for deep knowledge of Hermetic law and for practical answers, and Presiding Quaesitors from here have been merciful when they could be and hard when they had to be. Renita of Bjornaer, Praeco and leader of the covenant, died last winter. Proctor, the ruthless Presiding Quaesitor, has taken over the covenant, but who will be Praeco is still open. Before her death Proctor, Jerome of Confluensis and Eloi of Cunfin were the three supports of her rule; the three now see themselves as what keeps the Tribunal from chaos. The covenant also houses the Traitor of House Tytalus, a volunteer exile from that House who is reckoned to have lost all its games and whose one duty is to start its quarrels again when they stall.
covenants.what_matters:
Vis: whirlpools spun up by the spring tides beneath the covenant, caught in enchanted nets (seisin; Art and amount not given)
Vis: Intellego in the sour apples of the Orchard island (seisin; amount not given)
Vis: a tithe from Dragon's Rest of one pawn a year for each of its members
Vis: Dragon's Rest and its other vassals tithe as their oaths require
Library: the covenant's own library in the Library Tower, and the Library of the Tribunal, lent only as Tourney prizes
Income: the Venelli covenfolk's crafts (pottery, papyrus paper, rope and flax) and trade with the southern English ports
Income: great influence over the shipping companies that carry Paris's food down the Seine, and friends on the University of Paris's law faculty
Boon: Difficult Access (the ring of mist and shifting currents)
Boon: Defensive Environment (the tidal marsh, and a ring of active defences)
Boon: Mystical Portal (the Mercere Portal to Dragon's Rest)
Boon: Favors Owed (liege of Dragon's Rest, Cunfin and a small Guernicus covenant)
Hook: Protector (owes its vassals support and protection under its oath)
Hook: House Covenant (it serves the policies of the Primus of Guernicus)
Hook: Hermetic Services (the Tribunal's Quaesitors, its law and its book store)
Hook: Indigenes (the Venelli, last of a Celtic tribe)
Tension: the Praeco is dead; the eldest magus would be Celeres of Cunfin, whom Proctor wants set aside
Tension: Proctor's hatred of House Tytalus, with a Tytalus Traitor under his roof
Tension: Cavillor advises the pro-Lotharingian faction, which Proctor will take as betrayal
Tension: a Fengheld chapter house magus at Cherbourg takes vis Confluensis has always gathered
Tension: the Hospitallers' City of God, with a Dominion aura of 4, on the peninsula
covenants.secrets:
One of the founders had a flaw in her Gift that made building on the tide necessary.
Jerome secretly saves 'troublesome heirs' from murder with Mentem magic and hides them in monasteries and covenants, very likely against the Code; Eloi of Cunfin is his chief partner, and Proctor does not know.
Valerian's familiar is a spirit beyond Hermetic binding, so he must belong to a Mystery Cult, probably the Guernicus Terrae cult.
Augustina belongs to the Cabal of Frankish Gold, which works for the Lotharingian Tribunal; she thinks it will fail but wants to see how the Order reacts.
The Traitor's key is thought to weaken the defences of Fudarus, or perhaps by now to be only a symbol.
The stone flowers were not made by Terram magi: they belong to an older pact between the marsh's faerie powers and the Venelli.

covenants.name: Dragon's Rest
covenants.notes:
The oath of fealty to Confluensis, in its own terms:
Each comes to the other's aid when a member of either faces Wizard's War.
Each votes with the other at Tribunal, granting that un-Gifted Redcaps are loath to vote.
Each offers membership to the other's magi if their covenant is destroyed.
Each passes on as fast as it can any news that bears on the other's fortunes, so far as the duties of Quaesitors and Redcaps allow.
Their trading ventures avoid competing where possible and help each other in hard times.
Dragon's Rest pays Confluensis a tithe of one pawn of vis a year for each member.
Dragon's Rest hosts Confluensis's magi who want its laboratories; Confluensis hosts Redcaps who want its library.

Story seed, Gargouille: townsmen are found dead near the covenant and the magi are blamed; Archbishop Robert names them the new Gargouilles and marches on them with the condemned prisoners and the shrine of St. Romanus (Faith 5). Harming him could bring a crusade against the Order in Normandy, and the magi may have been framed.
covenants.oath:
Each comes to the other's aid when a member of either faces Wizard's War.
Each votes with the other at Tribunal, granting that un-Gifted Redcaps are loath to vote.
Each offers membership to the other's magi if their covenant is destroyed.
Each passes on as fast as it can any news that bears on the other's fortunes, so far as the duties of Quaesitors and Redcaps allow.
Their trading ventures avoid competing where possible and help each other in hard times.
Dragon's Rest pays Confluensis a tithe of one pawn of vis a year for each member.
Dragon's Rest hosts Confluensis's magi who want its laboratories; Confluensis hosts Redcaps who want its library.
covenants.summary:
A Mercer House and vassal of Confluensis on the old site of its liege, around the drowned cavern of the dragon Gargouille in the estuary swamps on the Seine's north bank. When Confluensis moved to the Cotentin in 1051 its Mercere magi stayed, and kept the old badge of a dragon spouting a fountain of water. It is the hub of the Tribunal's Mercere Portals, with gates to Cunfin, Confluensis and Harco among others, and its laboratories are excellent; members of Confluensis use them, and its Redcaps use Confluensis's library.

Its covenfolk are few and live by trade. Many descend from the man who helped kill Gargouille, and the prisoners the clergy of Rouen pardon each year in St. Romanus's memory often take service here. It is home to the Evangelium, the Redcap officer who carries the Tourney results to every covenant, now Myrina. In 1123 the Tribunal found Pandion of Flambeau guilty of taking twelve horses, one of them magical, from that Redcap, and so robbing Antonin of Dragon's Rest of part of his magical power. How many Redcaps live here is not given.

Its oath to Confluensis is long-winded but fairly even-handed, since Guernicus and Mercere are on good terms; its terms are in the notes.
covenants.what_matters:
Vis: pays a tithe of one pawn a year per member to Confluensis
Income: trade by its covenfolk and the Mercere network
Laboratories: excellent, shared with Confluensis
Boon: Mystical Portal (hub of the Tribunal's Mercere Portals: Cunfin, Confluensis, Harco and others)
Boon: Powerful Ally (Confluensis, its liege)
Hook: Mercer House
Hook: Beholden (the oath of fealty to Confluensis)
Hook: Legendary Site (the Gargouille's lair, remembered by the clergy of Rouen)
Tension: Rouen's clergy keep the Gargouille's memory, and a mob led by the archbishop with St. Romanus's shrine could be roused against magi near the city

tribunals.name: The Normandy Tribunal
tribunals.summary:
The old Tribunal of the West Franks, renamed for the Norman duchy in 983, covers the French-speaking north of France: from the Atlantic east some four hundred miles to the edge of Lorraine and the Saône, where the lands owing fealty to the Emperor begin, and from the Channel south as far as the Dordogne, where its border with Provençal has been settled by language since 1102 (a place belongs to Normandy if its nearest settlement speaks the langue d'oïl). It takes in Brittany, claimed after the Schism War, and Flanders, but not imperial Lorraine or Arelat; the Massif Central at its south-eastern corner is uncertain ground that no covenant presently quarrels over.

It is a land of crowded fields, great cities, cathedrals and castles, and the Dominion presses hard on the magi. Vis is scarce, and the rules for sharing it out (the Perthean Compact) shape everything: covenants are easy to found and hard to keep, so Normandy has perhaps more covenants than any other Tribunal but only a little over a hundred magi, most covenants holding about four. Three in four covenants are a liege, a vassal or both, bound by oaths of fealty copied from the feudal world around them, and five great lines rule its politics: Fudarus (the Domus Magna of House Tytalus, on its island off Brittany), Confluensis (the Quaesitores' covenant in the Cotentin), Florum in Flanders, Oleron in Aquitaine and Montverte in Normandy. A few eremites and the odd coenobium live outside the covenants. The countryside is strewn with the ruins of covenants that failed, and young ones keep rising in their place.

Its magi are hard and competitive by other Tribunals' standards. Raiding a rival covenant's mundane supplies is lawful here; meddling with mundanes is only a crime once mundane reprisals actually fall on magi, so covenants work through mundane 'masks'; and the Tytalan spirit of contest runs through its customs. Young magi go errant like knights, far beyond the Tribunal, to win vis and a name before settling down. Old fears linger too: the Order of Odin from the Viking raids, and House Diedne, whose records the Guernicus censors cut from the archives and whose sealed Domus Magna, Branugurix, may not be empty. Regional quarrels between Breton, Norman, Parisian and Aquitanian grogs have even come to blows at Tribunal, and a few magi still follow Metrodorus's discredited belief that Mythic Blood makes an aristocracy of magi.

The Tribunal meets every seven years, and since the Schism War the host is drawn by lot from the covenants rather than being the Praeco's home, so the next meeting's place is not yet known. Even a new Spring covenant may draw it, and must then provide a secluded ground for the Tourney, an excellent Aegis and lavish hospitality, while crowds of Quaesitores use the preparations as cover to look into its affairs; hosting can ruin a young covenant, which usually borrows from its liege or another great covenant, though many guests bring a pawn of vis or a Lab Text as a gift. Business comes first, then the Hermetic Tourney, where covenant teams compete for the Tribunal's vis sources and books for the next seven years.

The next meeting is in 1221. Renita of Bjornaer, Praeco and leader of Confluensis, died last winter, and the post stands vacant: by custom the eldest magus succeeds, but her sept-mate Stellatus, the eldest, has gone to Iberia, leaving Celeres of Cunfin, then Somnifer of Lapis Crudus, then Geirlaug of Montverte. Proctor of Guernicus, Presiding Quaesitor these two meetings and now acting head of Confluensis, holds the Tribunal together with the two Jerbiton, Jerome of Confluensis (its envoy to the nobility) and Eloi of Cunfin (its link to the Church). Library books won at the Tourney and the list of the Tribunal's luctationes are kept at Confluensis.

The Noble Life. Living cheek by jowl with the mundane world, some Normandy covenants put their lands in a companion's name, since a magus may not swear fealty and a castle or manor is hard to hold without a liege. The knight still owes his own lord forty days of armed service a year and attendance at court at the great feasts, Easter, Pentecost and Christmas, and a rich one may pay écuage instead. Knights also do justice under Frankish customary law (the Common Law Ability), where trial by combat, often by champion, is still claimed. They hunt, write verse (some are trouvères), fight in tournaments the Church and king distrust, ride out young as knights errant, and pursue courtly love, the devotion to a lady glimpsed and unattainable; in time they settle on a manor to marry well, raise an heir and enlarge the family estate, and expect their magi to help, which can strain the Code. Montverte lives this way; Cunfin shelters by a Cistercian abbey and Florum behind a merchant's front. Iola of Guernicus held in 1047 that living in a lord's house is no breach without an oath of vassalage, so magic may serve the companion lord as a consors; the rulings against Florum in 1088, on mundane resources in 1116, for Infelicitas in 1130 and for Pernix in 1179 mark how far that goes.

Tytalus Schemes. With Fudarus in the Tribunal, Tytali are everywhere, but each nurses her own schemes and the Primi are too busy with their feud to direct any grand plot. For a shared end they form cabals, anonymous by agreement, meeting in disguise or by letter, often drawn from more than one Tribunal, each member with her own reasons: the Cabal of the Laden Cart, founded by Kybella after a Twilight vision of Death reaping Europe, which hunts the Ankeu to hold Death to ransom; the Cabal of the Crushed Viper, mostly Stonehenge magi under Arthurian names ('Lancelot', 'Vivian', 'Pellinore') working against the chivalric ideal; the Cabal of Frankish Gold, behind the Lotharingian movement; and the Cabal of the Golden Coin, which fixes the Tourney. Over all hangs the twenty-year feud of Primus Harpax (whose Decimi hold sway in Normandy) and Prima Buliste (whose Fideli and spies reach beyond it), which must be settled, by surrender, death or a third contender, before the Grand Tribunal of 1228 seats only one of them.

Salvirius's quests. The Boar King's adviser grants Virtues: he sets the seeker a mystical quest that demands a sacrifice, a Flaw taken on, and the Virtue follows. He offers Strong Faerie Blood, Shapeshifter, Animal Ken, Faerie Blood, Second Sight and Wilderness Sense, and the troupe may let him teach Hermetic Virtues. To one magus he offers Diedne Magic, taught in a season, which brings the Major Story Flaw Dark Secret with it (part of the Virtue, not counted in the balance) and a Major Hermetic Flaw besides.
tribunals.history:
Ancient Gaul. The Gauls who once held these lands sacrificed to the mighty spirits and faeries of the country, revered the boar as the beast of their tribal kings, and followed druids who may have been forerunners of House Diedne. Julius Caesar conquered them between 58 and 50 BC, beating Vercingetorix at Alesia, and wrote his commentaries on the war. Rome's rule reached as far as Brittany and its ruins still dot the land. Many druids withdrew into the wilds, the Gauls kept their own gods beside Rome's, and a prosperous Gallo-Roman culture grew up around the great capital of Lugdunum.

The saints of Gaul. Christianity reached Paris about 250 with Denis and his companions Eleutherius and Rusticus, who won many converts until the governor imprisoned them; after years in a dungeon they were beheaded on Montmartre in 275 and thrown into the Seine. The abbey of Saint-Denis honours them, and Denis is the king's own patron and a patron of France and of Paris. St Martin, who shared his cloak with a freezing beggar in 337, became bishop of Tours in 371 and died in 397. When the Huns came in 450 St Geneviève's prayers turned them from Paris, and in 464 she broke Childeric's siege of the city by leading boats down the Seine at night with food. In 451 Romans, Franks and Visigoths under the legendary Merovech defeated Attila at Châlons and ended his push west. In the fifth and sixth centuries Britons fleeing the fall of Arthur's kingdom and the Saxon raids settled Armorica, which became Brittany, with its own tongue and culture.

The Merovingian Franks. The Franks, first settled as Rome's treaty allies, rose under Merovech, said to be the child of a Frankish queen and a sea-beast like the Quinotaur, and his son Childeric. Clovis, king from 481 to 511, beat the governor Syagrius in 486 and built an empire by war, guile and marriage. His Christian wife Clotilde's prayers healed their son, and when he vowed to give up Mercury and Jupiter for victory over the Alemanni in 496 and won, St Rémi baptised him at Reims; a dove brought the holy oil from Heaven, and that never-emptying ampoule has anointed every king since. By 507 he had beaten Romans, Burgundians and Visigoths and ruled from Paris. The long-haired Merovingian kings were held to be sorcerers. After Clovis the kingdom was split among his sons and wracked by civil war; Chlotar II reunited it in 613 and Dagobert I briefly ruled it all, but the mayors of the palace grew until, by 687, Pepin of Herstal ruled in all but name. Gregory, bishop of Tours from 573, wrote the history of the Franks that tells these tales.
