In 732 Charles Martel turned back a Muslim army near Tours and Poitiers, and in 751 his son Pepin the Short took the crown and sent the last Merovingian, shorn of his magical hair, to a monastery. Legend says other heirs of the blood escaped.

The Carolingians. The new dynasty sought the Church's backing: the abbot of Saint-Denis supported it, and in 754 Pope Stephen II threatened excommunication on anyone who made a Frankish king of any other line. Charlemagne, king from 768, conquered Lombardy, founded the kingdom of Aquitaine in 778, set up schools with the help of the scholar Alcuin, and was crowned emperor in Rome in 800. Tales of him and his paladins, Roland at Roncesvalles above all, are sung by every minstrel of 1220. His empire did not outlast him long: his grandsons fought for four years and divided it at Verdun in 843, Brittany won its independence from Charles the Bald in 846, and after Charles the Fat briefly reunited the empire it broke apart in 887. Kings of the old line and of rival houses followed one another amid feuding nobles.

The Northmen. Viking raids on Breton monasteries began in the late eighth century. In 845 a hundred and twenty longships rowed up the Seine and extorted seven thousand pounds from Paris; monkish chroniclers saw the hand of God punishing the civil wars that followed Louis the Pious's death. Aquitaine was nearly ruined, Paris was besieged again in 885, and Count Odo's defence of it won him the crown in 888. The Norse wintered in Neustria until in 911 Charles the Simple granted Rouen, Lisieux and Évreux to their leader Rollo, who was baptised, married the king's daughter and was meant to hold off his kin. Instead his line drew in more settlers and seized more land, and the Land of the Northmen became Normandy. Monasteries learned to carry their relics and books inland each spring. In 1066 Duke William conquered England.

The Capetians. Hugh Capet, descended from Robert the Strong, became king in 987 with the help of the scholar Gerbert of Aurillac, reputed to have some small magic, whom he made archbishop of Reims, and he made Paris his capital. Pope Stephen's ban hung over him until he recovered the relics of St Valéry and St Riquier, earning his line seven generations on the throne, of which Philip Augustus is the last so far. His successors were weak kings among strong vassals: Robert the Pious, Henry I, who saw the emperor crush Odo of Champagne at Bar in 1037, Philip I, and Louis VI, crowned at Orléans in 1108 because he could not reach Reims. Meanwhile the Church grew in strength: Cluny was founded in 910, Cîteaux in 1098 and St Bernard's Clairvaux in 1115, the First Crusade set out in 1096, Abélard came to Paris in 1118, and work on Notre-Dame began in 1163. In 1134 a great flood reshaped the Flemish coast and gave Bruges back its way to the sea.

The Lions and the Lily. In 1137 the young Louis VII married Eleanor, heiress of Aquitaine, Gascony and Poitou. The match soured: the monkish king and his worldly southern queen fell out on the Second Crusade, which St Bernard preached, amid rumours of her affair with her uncle Raymond of Antioch, and the marriage was annulled. Eleanor at once wed Henry of Anjou, son of Geoffrey V, who had married Matilda of England in 1127 and conquered Normandy in 1144. Henry inherited Normandy in 1151, married Eleanor in 1152 without his lord's leave and became King of England in 1154, master of half of France, and later took Brittany too. The Angevin lion seemed ready to maul the Capetian lily, but Henry's sons, egged on by their mother, rebelled against him again and again with French help, Eleanor was kept in comfortable captivity, and the barons of Aquitaine rose whenever they could. The Angevins boasted of descent from Melusine, a faerie or demon bride who could not abide the Mass.

Philip Augustus and Richard. Philip, son of Louis VII and Adèle of Champagne, was crowned in 1179 after his father's pilgrimage to Becket's shrine saved him from a grave illness, and ruled alone from 1180: clever, combative and devoted to administration, he favoured clerks and lawyers over the old nobility. Henry the Young King died in 1183 and Geoffrey of Brittany in 1186, and in 1189 Richard, with Philip's help, beat his father and took England, Normandy and Anjou. Both kings went on the Third Crusade, but Philip came home after Acre, to whispers of cowardice, and built the Louvre. Returning, Richard was taken by Leopold of Austria, whom he had insulted, and handed to the emperor; Philip and Richard's brother John offered money to keep him jailed, but Eleanor paid his ransom in 1194. Richard then beat Philip at Fréteval and at Gisors in 1198, where the French king had to be fished out of a river, and built great castles such as Château Gaillard. In 1199 he died of a crossbow wound while besieging Châlus over a buried hoard, and on his deathbed named John, not his nephew Arthur of Brittany, as heir.

The fall of Angevin France. John seized and married Isabella of Angoulême, already promised to Hugh de Lusignan, and seemed spellbound by her while his vassals rebelled. Summoned to Philip's court in 1202 he did not come, and Philip declared his French lands forfeit and backed Arthur of Brittany. John roused himself to rescue his mother at Mirebeau and capture Arthur, who vanished at Rouen in 1203, almost surely murdered, by John's own hand it is said, driving many vassals over to Philip. Eleanor died in 1204, Château Gaillard fell and Normandy with it, and Poitou followed in 1205. England was laid under interdict, and John, allied with the emperor, was crushed at Bouvines in 1214. His barons forced Magna Carta on him in 1215 and rebelled again in 1216; Prince Louis invaded England, but John's death that year rallied the barons behind the boy Henry III, now ruled for by a regency council.

France in 1220. Philip has made the University of Paris a chartered body (1200) and fortified his capital; Chartres is rebuilding after its great fire of 1194, and the pope banned the teaching of law in Paris in 1219. The Tribunal's lands are at peace, though still split between French and Angevin lords, and the Angevins are no longer feared. Philip has not yet anointed his heir Louis, born in 1187 to Isabella of Hainault; he also has a daughter Mary and a son Philip by Agnès of Méranie. Many northern knights and mercenaries have fought in the Albigensian Crusade against the Cathars of the Langue d'oc since 1209, Philip letting his nobles go without leading them. In 1212 a shepherd boy of Châteaudun worked miracles at Saint-Denis and set the Children's Crusade moving, and the Fifth Crusade left in 1217. Magi of Normandy tend to frown on those who dig too deep into the past, and the Quaesitores watch anyone curious about the Schism War.

cases.title: The Praeco's succession
cases.charge: Renita of Bjornaer, Praeco and leader of Confluensis, died last winter. By custom the eldest magus succeeds: Stellatus, her sept-mate, has left for Iberia, so the next are Celeres of Cunfin, then Somnifer of Lapis Crudus, then Geirlaug of Montverte. Proctor fears Celeres's eccentricity and his sway over Cunfin's Redcaps and wants him set aside for someone he can trust or control, without seeming partial; many magi would rather see Proctor's own power checked.

cases.title: Augustina of Tytalus, the Traitor
cases.charge: The Traitor, exiled by her own choice from House Tytalus with the single duty of restarting its conflicts when they stall, serves Confluensis as hoplite. Twenty-five years into the stalled feud of the Primi Harpax and Buliste, and with the Traitor's key thought to weaken Fudarus's defences, Proctor, who distrusts every Tytalus, gives her the riskiest and least trusted tasks and questions whether she can be trusted with Quaesitorial work at all.

cases.title: Fengheld's chapter at Cherbourg
cases.charge: The lone maga of Fengheld's chapter house near Cherbourg, a coenobite under Normandy's Code, harvests vis sources that once belonged to Pagus and that Confluensis has traditionally gathered, and seeks recognition as a covenant. Chapter houses may not be used to sidestep the Perthean Compact.

cases.title: A Provençal claim by language
cases.brought_by: A magus of the Provençal Tribunal
cases.charge: A rich vis source in Normandy's southern reaches is claimed for Provençal on the ground that the nearby villagers say 'oc', not 'oïl', which under the ruling of 1102 would make the land Provençal's. Whether the village is truly of the langue d'oc, or the claim a fraud, is unproven.

cases.title: Praeda's vis auction
cases.charge: Praeda auctions vis smuggled in from the southern Tribunals to a paying consortium of covenants. Plundering another Tribunal is no crime here, but vis gathered this way is a luctatio and should be open to all, so selling it to a closed club breaches the Perthean Compact.

cases.title: Raiders from over the border
cases.charge: Magi of the Rhine and Iberian Tribunals have raided Normandy covenants under Normandy's own Code. The Tribunal at large thinks it minor and can only punish foreign raiders harshly when they break the Code; covenants within reach of another Tribunal want more done.

cases.title: A covenant at the vacant castle
cases.charge: A castle in the Cotentin, empty since 1204 and now the lair of a monster akin to Grendel's kin, holds a strong Magic aura; the magi who explored it in 1218 will propose sending colonists to found a covenant there. French officials would seek influence over a repopulated castle unless a royal grant comes first.

rulings.title: The Perthean Compact: seisins
rulings.says: Every vis source belongs to a covenant, never to a magus. A source within a day's return march of an established covenant is its seisin, harvested by it alone. Since 1109 the test is exact: a man on foot, with no magic, must go from the covenant's council chamber to the source and back between sunrise and sunset on a day within a month of an equinox. Covenants keep trained runners (cursores) to prove it before the Quaesitores (a fit man covers about 10 + twice his Athletics miles a day cross country, five fewer in wild country and five more on good roads). An unchallenged claim stands; roads built, forests cleared and even a hill moved have stretched the march, and rivals have done the reverse.

rulings.title: The Perthean Compact: legacies
rulings.says: A source too far away to be a seisin may be voted the discoverer's legacy: exclusive harvest for seven years. Since 1032 the lease must be renewed by vote at each meeting, and fewer than half the renewals succeed; a source refused becomes a tropaeum. A new find is usually granted without contest, and a legacy may last for many terms when only its holders can reach it. Harvesting another's legacy is the High Crime of depriving a magus of his power, though pleas for mercy are nearly always granted. The holder may grant the harvest to whom it likes, including new magi settling within a day's march, which is how most covenants are founded.

rulings.title: The Perthean Compact: tropaea
rulings.says: Known sources that are neither seisins nor legacies, and need little effort to harvest, are tropaea, owned by the Tribunal in common and leased for seven years as prizes at the Tourney, with the same exclusive harvest as a legacy. A covenant that would settle within a day's march of one needs the Tribunal's vote, and if it wins, the tropaeum becomes its seisin.

rulings.title: The Perthean Compact: luctationes
rulings.says: A Tribunal source whose harvest depends on the harvester's skill or daring is a luctatio, a contest open to any magus willing to try; success gives no right to later harvests. The list is public and a copy is kept at Confluensis, though how to win the vis need not be written down. Settling near one needs the Tribunal's leave, which is a little easier to get than for a tropaeum.

rulings.title: Interim leases and plundering
rulings.says: Whoever finds a vis source reports it to a Quaesitor, who grants an interim lease until the next meeting declares it. An interim lease is not exclusive: a second finder may get one too, and the holders settle it between themselves until the Tribunal rules. Harvesting an unknown source without declaring it is plundering, a Low Crime punished harshly, with fines above three times the vis taken. Vis traded or lent by the Redcaps, once it belongs to magi, is outside the Compact, which governs only gathering.

rulings.title: The Library of the Tribunal
rulings.says: Books given to the Tribunal in common, a custom begun by Perpauca of Bonisagus, are kept at Confluensis, their list public, and no one may read them unless they win them at the Tourney. A book won is leased for seven years under a Cow and Calf oath (copies made belong to the Tribunal) and must come back in good order before the next meeting. A magus who gives an original book wins at the next Tourney the lease of one of similar worth, settled by certamen when two authors want the same book. Pamphlets on each spine tell a reader its Quality and Level.

rulings.title: Mundane resources and raiding
rulings.says: Confirming the rulings of 1081 and 1088: a covenant's food, consumables, building supplies, arms and armour and luxuries are not part of its magi's magical power, so raiding them is no Hermetic crime; books (finished or not), vis, enchanted items and laboratory supplies are. Livestock and covenfolk have no protection (1123), but apprentices, familiars and magical beasts do. A raider may not damage the covenant's buildings (1130) or break the Code in any way during the raid, and must challenge any magus escorting the goods to certamen: losing ends the raid, winning sends the escort a mile off until sunrise. Raids by magi of other Tribunals fall under this Code too, and the Tribunal judges foreign raiders who break it especially harshly.

rulings.title: The town senex
rulings.says: The covenant nearest a town, its senex, has the better right there: if the senex's agents harm another covenant's interests in the town as a side effect, no ruin has been caused. The senex is the covenant where the town's church bells sound loudest, as a Quaesitor judges; a covenant that cannot hear them has no claim, so many towns have none. Made in Fudarus's favour against its vassal Atramentum over the artificers' guild of Le Conquet, and sometimes used to settle rival claims to urban vis.

rulings.title: Urban covenants
rulings.says: A covenant may sit in a town, and its magi's ordinary dealings with townsfolk ruin no one. A lord may grant a covenant a charter, but the magi may take none of its privileges, which would be fealty in all but name; paying a tax as a covenant is allowed, and seeking a charter to fix the limits of a lord's power is commended. Eligible covenfolk may vote and hold town office; magi may not. Made after several covenants took charters from King John and were then asked for soldiers. Fluvius's The Order and Towns (1208) is the standard commentary.

rulings.title: Mundane interference
rulings.says: No ruling has ever been made. By long precedent a covenant is rarely convicted of meddling unless its actions bring mundane reprisals down on magi, and acting through a mundane 'mask' who never names his Hermetic sponsors protects it even when the mask is punished. Masks give no protection against a charge of depriving a magus of his power, so they cannot be used against a town's senex.

rulings.title: Founding a covenant
rulings.says: A new covenant needs exclusive access to vis sources yielding at least a pawn a year for each of its magi, and never fewer than four, at its founding (aura vis does not count; losing the source or gaining magi later does not undo it), and a council chamber named to the Tribunal: any meeting place will do, a room, a cave or a grove, but not within a day's journey of another covenant's, by tradition out of reach of the Seven League Stride. Chapter houses may not be used to dodge the Compact; Fengheld's at Cherbourg is treated as a coenobium. Vis owed to a liege still counts.

rulings.title: Eremites and coenobia
rulings.says: A solitary magus (an eremite) may own no seisin and lives on Tourney leases and luctationes. Magi who band together without meeting the vis rule are a coenobium, not a covenant: they own no seisin, rarely win a legacy, and enter the Tourney as solitary magi, and are looked down on for flouting the Tribunal's ways.

rulings.title: Oaths of fealty between covenants
rulings.says: A liege covenant has one oath that all its vassals swear: support from the vassal (usually a vis tithe and its magi's sigils as free proxies), protection from the liege (using those proxies wisely and answering calls for aid on stated terms). The oath is part of the Peripheral Code and enforceable; it ends by agreement or after one side wins a prosecution of the other for default. Covenants still may not swear fealty to a mundane lord. When a liege dies out, all its vassals are free.

rulings.title: Personal vis
rulings.says: Vis that grows in a magus's own person, in his hair, blood and so on, is his alone and outside the Compact. A personal source outside him is still subject to it.

rulings.title: The host drawn by lot
rulings.says: Since the Schism War the covenant that hosts the next meeting, and the Tourney after it, is drawn by lot from the Tribunal's covenants, not chosen as the Praeco's home. The host finds a secluded Tourney ground within a day's travel, hidden from mundane eyes (the Tribunal can lend a casting tablet for a Moon-duration Shrouded Glen), and must declare its own event to Confluensis by Redcap by the summer solstice before the meeting.

rulings.title: The Hermetic Tourney: entry and events
rulings.says: Held after the meeting's business, usually over three days, with an even number of teams (the Redcaps recruit visitors to make it so) of at most five magi each, besides grogs and companions. A team that is not a recognised Normandy covenant stakes five pawns a magus, added to the prizes. A team starts with a point per member of its covenant (a coenobium's or visitor's magi one each). Six events: the hastiludium, a magical charge on village 'mounts' (20, 10 and 5 points to the semi-finalists); the certamen tournament (25, 15, 8); the dimicatio, forceless spells against a fast-cast defence, penetrating a Parma being a crime (23, 12, 6); each with a point for taking part; the melee of grogs rushing Creo Imaginem 'castles' with blunt weapons and no magic (6, then 2 for second to fourth, 1 for fifth; serious injury forfeits and is fined); the host's choice, a true test of magic it should not win (12, 8, 3, 3); and the deadly joust (20, 8, 3, 3), each with a point for taking part.

rulings.title: The Hermetic Tourney: ranks and prizes
rulings.says: Teams are ranked by points, ties going to the older covenant (or the earlier Gauntlet). Ranks win gold prize pawns, spent in rank order for leases until the next Tourney: at first one tropaeum or lump of one Art's vis and one book or item each, then again while pawns remain. A tropaeum costs a pawn for each pawn it yields; a book or item a pawn per 5 Build Points (no charged or limited items); a pawn buys at once 5 pawns of Form vis or 3 of Technique. First is the Siege of Normandy (31 pawns), second the Siege of Valor (24), seventh the Siege of Notatus (17), thirteenth the Siege of Shame (nothing, its prize going to the fourteenth, since an Iberian team disgraced the Tourney in 1151) and twenty-first the Siege of Alms (6 kept and 6 given to the teams below); each named rank brings a Hermetic Reputation of 2 for seven years. A prize not returned brings charges and a ban from the next Tourney.

rulings.title: The first meeting
rulings.says: The Tribunal of the West Franks first meets with Confluensis, Pagus, Baiocassium, Bibracte and Sinapis; Fudarus and Branugurix attend the Britannian Tribunal instead.

rulings.title: Adela of Jerbiton acquitted
rulings.says: Accused by a long-standing enemy of being court wizard to King Louis III from 879 to 881, Adela was acquitted, as nothing showed any danger to the Order from her friendship with the late king.

rulings.title: Lotharingia divided
rulings.says: The Tribunal accepts the Grand Tribunal's decision, takes in part of the old Provençal lands and reaches east to the Rhine Tribunal.

rulings.title: The Normandy Tribunal
rulings.says: On Adrianus of Montverte's proposal, the Tribunal of the West Franks is renamed for the Duke of Normandy, foremost lord of its lands.

rulings.title: Brittany claimed
rulings.says: Fudarus, the last Breton covenant left after the Schism War, is welcomed to the 22nd meeting, and the Tribunal claims Brittany and all its magical resources.

rulings.title: Nauche-Fleur and the baron
rulings.says: Nauche-Fleur was found innocent of swearing fealty to its baron, as the oath was taken by an unGifted companion acting as lord of the manor for the magi.

rulings.title: The border by language
rulings.says: On a complaint from three Flambeau of Provençal: where no clear border exists, disputed land goes by the language of its nearest settlement, langue d'oïl to Normandy and otherwise to Provençal. Upheld against Provençal's protest at the Grand Tribunal of 1129.

rulings.title: The Donatores admitted
rulings.says: Quaesitor Muirgheal brings into the Order the hedge wizards he found fighting a plague of restless dead, as the Ex Miscellanea tradition of the Donatores Requietis Aeternae.

rulings.title: Koilios's raid; Praecepsus acquitted
rulings.says: Quaesitor Lothaire upheld Koilios of Tytalus's raid of 1113 on Lapis Crudus's convoy of food and luxuries as no breach of the Code, fixing the custom of lawful raiding. Praecepsus of Flambeau, accused of cutting down the king's enemies with a Perdo sword in 1111, had no charge to answer, as no mundane could tell magic was involved.

rulings.title: Pandion's horses
rulings.says: Pandion of Flambeau, who stole twelve horses from Antonin of Dragon's Rest, returned the one magical horse and paid ten pawns, keeping the other eleven as the spoils of a lawful raid: enchanted creatures count toward a magus's power, ordinary livestock and (as Lothaire added) covenfolk do not.

rulings.title: Jacinth and Infelicitas
rulings.says: Jacinth of Oleron, raiding Infelicitas, brought down its upper storey and two laboratories: convicted of deprivation (the charge of trying to kill a magus failed), he lost his familiar, and raiders were forbidden to damage a covenant's buildings.

rulings.title: Lothaire accused
rulings.says: Jacinth of Oleron accused Quaesitor Lothaire of profiting from raids by Montverte, Fudarus and their allies. He was cleared for want of substance but never regained his place as chief Quaesitor, and went to Magvillus.

rulings.title: Atlax and the Redcap's letters
rulings.says: Atlax of Tytalus read the messages Redcap Camille carried while a guest at Fudarus. Quaesitor Whent held the covenant responsible and gave one of its legacies to House Mercere.

rulings.title: Pernix acquitted; Camille fined
rulings.says: Pernix of Merinita, accused by Visurgis of Tytalus of healing a fallen nobleman by magic, was acquitted, as only the man and three friendly monks knew. Camille of Mercere, accused by Buliste of using a knight to gather a legacy's vis (the knight confessed to doing devils' work, and only Atlax of Fudarus averted ruin), paid fifteen pawns to Fudarus, and the source was closed for thirty years.

rulings.title: Pugnatis expelled
rulings.says: Convicted at the previous meeting of controlling the mayor of Laval by magic to reach a vis source and fined in enchanted items, Pugnatis came to neither this meeting nor with the items, and was expelled from the Order.

diary.title: Trianoma's travels begin
diary.details: For more than thirty years Trianoma journeys across Europe, seeking out wizards and bringing them to meet Bonisagus. Many of those she finds become Founders of the Order.

diary.title: Foundation of the Order of Hermes
diary.details: Bonisagus and the other Founders take the Oath of Hermes, and the first gathering of the Order is held at Durenmar.

diary.title: Second Grand Tribunal: what a Tribunal is
diary.details: The Order settles how lesser Tribunals work: one needs at least twelve magi drawn from at least four covenants.

diary.title: Jerbiton meets Charlemagne
diary.details: The Founder Jerbiton, who has taken on several apprentices of the emperor's mage-smith Carolinus, meets Charlemagne. The emperor's decree against sorcery and paganism that year spares magic of a kindly sort, such as Jerbiton's.

diary.title: Branugurix founded
diary.details: House Diedne raises its domus magna, Branugurix (in Breton Bren Gwrac'h), in a regio near Mount Dol in Brittany. It becomes the head of a line of Diedne vassal covenants.

diary.title: Tytalus founds Fudarus
diary.details: Tytalus carries off Hariste, the apprentice of his own former pupil Pralix, and raises the fortress of Fudarus on Ushant to keep her safe from Pralix's anger. He trains her to the Gauntlet in five years. Pralix takes over the running of House Tytalus.

diary.title: Third Grand Tribunal
diary.details: The Order's third Grand Tribunal meets.

diary.title: Tytalus vanishes; Hariste first Prima
diary.details: Tytalus walks out of Fudarus in a leper's robe and veil, staff in hand, visits his followers one last time and disappears into the Maddenhofen Woods of Bohemia. Hariste claims Fudarus and becomes the first Prima of House Tytalus; the covenant has housed the Primus ever since.

diary.title: Confluensis founded
diary.details: Confluensis is founded at the mouth of the Seine, on the site Dragon's Rest holds today.

diary.title: Fourth Grand Tribunal
diary.details: The Order's fourth Grand Tribunal meets.

diary.title: Bibracte founded
diary.details: Bibracte, a vassal of Fudarus, is founded on Mount Beuvray in the Morvan by a few Diedne magi and one Tytalan.

diary.title: Fifth Grand Tribunal: the seven-year cycle
diary.details: The Grand Tribunal fixes its own meetings at every thirty-three years, and those of the regional Tribunals at every seven years from 836.

diary.title: Pagus founded
diary.details: Confluensis sponsors the vassal covenant of Pagus in a ruined Roman outpost near Cherbourg, overlooking the Channel. Its magi pour vis into restoring the Roman buildings and a dock.

diary.title: Viking raids on the covenants
diary.details: As Norse fleets sack Paris and the coasts, covenants suffer with the monasteries. Confluensis, then at the Seine's mouth, is raided a dozen times in a hundred years and its magi grow skilled at battle magic; Pagus loses many vis sources and never recovers; the Diedne covenants of the Breton coast are struck too. Some raids are led by Gifted shapechangers using runes, and talk of a Norse 'Order of Odin' begins, much of it from Confluensis.

diary.title: Baiocassium founded
diary.details: Baiocassium, a Diedne vassal of Branugurix, is founded in the forest near Bayeux. Its magi, heirs of Gaulish druids, stay on good terms with the local faeries.

diary.title: Sinapis founded
diary.details: Sinapis is founded in Anjou, near the heart of France. It grows into an important liege covenant, head of a line of its own.

diary.title: The Tribunals are drawn
diary.details: A stormy Grand Tribunal divides the Order into regional Tribunals, each free to make its own Peripheral Code, on House Mercere's argument that Redcaps should serve a region they know. The Tribunal of the West Franks is one of them. It takes in Gascony but neither Flanders nor Brittany: Brittany, independent since 846 and steeped in Celtic and druidic tradition, goes to the Britannian Tribunal. The eastern lands fall to a new Lotharingian Tribunal.

diary.title: Inaugural meeting of the Tribunal of the West Franks
diary.details: The first meeting gathers Confluensis, Pagus, Baiocassium, Bibracte and Sinapis. Fudarus and Branugurix attend the Britannian Tribunal instead.

diary.title: Rotomagus founded
diary.details: The first generation of Sinapis's apprentices found Rotomagus near Rouen.

diary.title: 3rd meeting: Adela of Jerbiton acquitted
diary.details: Adela of Jerbiton, often at court, is charged with having been court wizard to King Louis III from 879 to 881. She blames a long feud with her accuser; nothing shows the Order was ever endangered by her friendship with the late king, and she is acquitted.

diary.title: Rotomagus destroyed
diary.details: The Vikings sack Rouen and Rotomagus with it, less than a generation after its founding. Its one survivor leaves House Flambeau in shame for Ex Miscellanea.

diary.title: The Lotharingian Tribunal dissolved
diary.details: Following the mundane partition of Lotharingia at Meersen in 870, the Rhine and West Frankish Tribunals had taken in its covenants, which welcomed the move. The seventh Grand Tribunal confirms it: the Lotharingian Tribunal ends, and its southern part becomes the Provençal Tribunal.

diary.title: 5th meeting: the Tribunal reaches the Rhine
diary.details: The West Franks vote to accept the Grand Tribunal's decision, take in part of the former Lotharingian lands and extend east to border the Rhine Tribunal.

diary.title: Florum founded
diary.details: Florum is founded in Flanders, on the site Spider's Palace now holds. Like Confluensis it suffers several Viking raids in its early years.

diary.title: Ligurio founded
diary.details: Fudarus sponsors Ligurio, a vassal on the border of Aquitaine and Brittany in the Vendée.

diary.title: Kerguntuil founded
diary.details: Branugurix founds Kerguntuil on the Rose Coast of Brittany, by the stone said to be a petrified giant. Its magi study the Breton tales of giants, and its covenfolk grow larger than common folk.

diary.title: Eighth Grand Tribunal
diary.details: The Order's eighth Grand Tribunal meets.

diary.title: Baiocassium Minor founded
diary.details: Tired of Viking raids on their forest covenant, magi of Baiocassium make a spring sanctuary in a regio inside Bayeux. It becomes a covenant of its own, Baiocassium Minor, a vassal of Baiocassium.

diary.title: Montverte founded
diary.details: Scandinavian converts to the Order found Montverte in Normandy. It becomes the head of one of the Tribunal's great lines.

diary.title: The Betrayal of House Tytalus
diary.details: House Guernicus finds Prima Tasgillia corrupted by the Infernal and seizes her, and a large share of her House, far from Fudarus; she is executed for diabolism. Her filia Kalliste, the new Prima, refuses the Quaesitores and Flambeau hoplites entry to a covenant whose members have already been cleared, but is made to give way; the search finds nothing. The wounds between Tytalus and Flambeau last for a century.

diary.title: Ninth Grand Tribunal
diary.details: The Order's ninth Grand Tribunal meets.

diary.title: Bibracte sacked by Montverte
diary.details: Bibracte had revived a cult of Vercingetorix and turned against all things Roman, banning Latin for Brythonic and then refusing to deal with magi of the 'Roman' Houses. With Fudarus weakened after the Betrayal, four Flambeau and Tremere magi of Montverte declare Wizard's War on its magi at once, charging them with devil-worship, and destroy the covenant.

diary.title: Caput Capra founded
diary.details: Branugurix founds its youngest and easternmost vassal, Caput Capra, on the Loire near Fleury, to guard the old druidic site there from the lawlessness of the age.

diary.title: 17th meeting: the Normandy Tribunal
diary.details: With the Duke of Normandy foremost in the Tribunal's lands and the Franks fading as a people, the Tribunal adopts the proposal of Adrianus of Montverte and renames itself the Normandy Tribunal.

diary.title: Tenth Grand Tribunal
diary.details: The Order's tenth Grand Tribunal meets.

diary.title: Aedes Salii founded
diary.details: Sinapis founds Aedes Salii on Jersey, named for the priests of Mars, as a base to coordinate the coming war in Normandy and the Stonehenge Tribunal.

diary.title: The Schism War declared
diary.details: War is declared on House Diedne. Some of its worst battles are fought in Normandy and Brittany, and for a long while the Diedne have the upper hand. A Diedne force comes by sea to Fudarus, cannot break in and besieges it for months with three great summoned spirits, until Primus Klynoites wrests the spirits from them, destroys the besiegers and binds the spirits into the covenant's walls.

diary.title: Caput Capra and Baiocassium Minor destroyed
diary.details: Caput Capra is the war's first casualty in the Tribunal; Confluensis still brings its apprentices to the scant ruins for their history lessons. Baiocassium Minor falls the same year.

diary.title: Kerguntuil destroyed
diary.details:
The Diedne covenant on the Rose Coast is wiped out.

Secrets
Rumour says a Quaesitor later steered the Templars into building their chapel at Lanleff, to cleanse the district of the Diedne's supposed diabolic taint.

diary.title: Pagus destroyed
diary.details: Pagus, never recovered from the Viking raids, is destroyed by the magi of Baiocassium.

diary.title: Baiocassium and Ligurio destroyed
diary.details: Baiocassium falls to the Order. Ligurio, Fudarus's vassal in the Vendée, is crushed by giants hurling great boulders, thought to have been sent by Kerguntuil's magi before their end.

diary.title: The Tempest: Branugurix falls
diary.details:
The war's last battle is fought at Branugurix. In its final moments the Diedne Primus somehow seals every entrance to the regio, and some of the Flambeau and Tremere attackers are never seen again. Diedne history and alleged crimes are later struck from the Tribunal's records, and House Guernicus guards the site's secrets.

Secrets
Guernicus's records hold the regio's exact location and the old way in. Rumour has it that some Diedne survive inside, and that someone is working to free them; the Quaesitores watch anyone who lingers around Mount Dol.

diary.title: 22nd meeting: Brittany joins; the spoils
diary.details: The Schism War over, the Quaesitores list the vis sources and books taken from the fallen covenants. Fudarus, the only Breton covenant left, comes to the Normandy Tribunal, which claims Brittany and its magical wealth. Pertheus of Tytalus wins the victors the right of conquest over the spoils, on condition that a contest be held in seven years to share them out again. The old Tytalus-Flambeau quarrel flares over the spoils.

diary.title: Orchard of Sour Apples founded
diary.details: Confluensis sponsors a new vassal after the war, the Orchard of Sour Apples, on the Cotentin peninsula.

diary.title: Lixivia founded
diary.details: Florum founds Lixivia in Champagne as the great fairs begin, a covenant of Redcaps and Gentle Gifted magi meant to broker trade between the Order and merchants and fetch whatever any covenant wanted.

diary.title: 23rd meeting: the Perthean Compact
diary.details: With Northern Tytali and Southern Flambeau close to open war over the Diedne spoils, the Quaesitores back Pertheus of Tytalus, whose statutes pass over this and the next two meetings. Contested vis becomes the Tribunal's, competed for every seven years, and magi gain set rights over the vis near their covenants with a way to win more as they grow. The Compact is refined at later meetings. Three Flambeau-led covenants of the south call it a Tytalan swindle and go over to the Provençal Tribunal.

diary.title: Oleron founded
diary.details: Oleron is founded on its island off Aquitaine. It becomes the head of one of the Tribunal's great lines.

diary.title: Eleventh Grand Tribunal
diary.details: The Order's eleventh Grand Tribunal meets.

diary.title: Vexatores founded
diary.details: Fudarus founds Vexatores purely to goad Sinapis, twenty-one miles north of it, the least distance the law allows, on a vis source taken from the Diedne.

diary.title: Confluensis moves; Dragon's Rest founded
diary.details: Confluensis moves to the Orchard of Sour Apples on the Cotentin, whose magi join their liege as the vassal covenant is wound up. Dragon's Rest is founded as a vassal of Confluensis on its old site at the Seine's mouth. By about this time the Tribunal has its modern borders.

diary.title: Twelfth Grand Tribunal: Flambeau withdraws
diary.details: The feud of Tytalus and Flambeau formally ends with House Flambeau withdrawing from all hostilities. Sinapis is abandoned as its members leave for Provence and Iberia, ending its line; Aedes Salii, left to the Flambeau after the Tremere went home, is disbanded, and two of its magi help found Lapis Crudus, a covenant shared by the two Houses and counted in the line of Sinapis.

diary.title: Vexatores abandoned
diary.details: Never meant to last, Vexatores is abandoned once the quarrel it was built to serve is over.

diary.title: Nauche-Fleur founded
diary.details: Montverte sponsors Nauche-Fleur near Niort in Aquitaine, a covenant that keeps a school of arms and letters whose fees pay for its magi's lavish living.

diary.title: The Library of the Tribunal begun
diary.details: Perpauca of Bonisagus, whose own covenant kept her great books from visitors, starts giving books to the Tribunal as a whole. Hers are declared the first books of the Library of the Normandy Tribunal, kept at Confluensis, and the right to read them becomes a prize of the Tourney. Other authors follow her lead.

diary.title: 33rd meeting: Nauche-Fleur acquitted
diary.details: Nauche-Fleur is accused of swearing fealty to its local baron. The magi answer that the oath was taken by an unGifted companion standing as lord of the manor in their name, and the Tribunal finds them innocent.

diary.title: Thirteenth Grand Tribunal
diary.details: The Order's thirteenth Grand Tribunal meets.

diary.title: Infelicitas founded
diary.details: Rancrax of Tytalus loses a wager to his rival and, under its terms, must leave Fudarus; he founds Infelicitas as a vassal of Fudarus.

diary.title: Nidi founded
diary.details: Conventio Nidi is founded as a vassal of Oleron.

diary.title: 34th meeting: the language border
diary.details: At the request of three Provençal Flambeau, the Tribunal rules that, without any clear natural frontier, disputed ground belongs to Normandy if the nearest settlement speaks the langue d'oeil and to Provençal if it speaks the langue d'oc.

diary.title: 35th meeting: the Donatores join the Order
diary.details: In Picardy Quaesitor Muirgheal finds hedge wizards fighting a plague of restless dead. Once the dead are laid, many of them are taken into the Order as the Donatores Requietis Aeternae, a tradition of House Ex Miscellanea.

diary.title: 36th meeting: mundane raiding; Praecepsus cleared
diary.details: Building on an earlier ruling on mundane resources, Quaesitor Lothaire holds that raiding a covenant's mundane resources is allowed. At the same meeting Praecepsus of Flambeau, accused of wielding a Perdo-enchanted sword for the king when the count of Meulan raided Paris in 1111, is cleared: nothing showed magic to mundane eyes, so there is no case to answer.

diary.title: Florum moves; Spider's Palace founded
diary.details: Florum leaves its first site, and Spider's Palace is founded there as its vassal.

diary.title: Lapis Crudus lost
diary.details: Lapis Crudus becomes trapped in its own regio and is given up for lost.

diary.title: 37th meeting: Pandion and the Redcap's horses
diary.details: Pandion of Flambeau is found guilty of taking twelve horses, one a magical beast, from Antonin of Dragon's Rest, a Redcap, and so lessening his magical power. He must return that one and pay ten pawns, but keeps the other eleven as spoils of a lawful raid. Enchanted creatures, familiars or not, count toward a magus's power and ordinary livestock does not; Quaesitor Lothaire later adds that covenfolk do not count either. The same year the Donatores found Requies Aeterna as a vassal of Florum.

diary.title: Lixivia disbanded; Alcuin's Auberge founded
diary.details: Distrusted by magi who doubted its motives, Lixivia became everyone's favourite target for raids and is driven into poverty and disbanded. Its Redcaps found Alcuin's Auberge, a small Mercer House in Tours, as a vassal of Florum.

diary.title: Fourteenth Grand Tribunal: the border upheld
diary.details: Despite Provençal protests, the Grand Tribunal upholds Normandy's ruling that language marks the border between the two Tribunals.

diary.title: 38th meeting: Jacinth of Oleron convicted
diary.details: Raiding Infelicitas, Jacinth of Oleron brought down its upper storey and wrecked two laboratories. The charge of trying to kill a magus by destroying the covenant is not proved, but he is convicted of deprivation. Quaesitor Lothaire rules that raiders may never damage a covenant's buildings and that a lawful raid does not excuse a breach of the Code. Jacinth escapes a March but loses his familiar.

diary.title: Moles Magna founded
diary.details: Oleron sponsors Moles Magna on the edge of the Morvan, a covenant built inside a dam across a small tributary of the Yonne, hidden behind its own waterfall.

diary.title: 40th meeting: Lothaire accused
diary.details: Jacinth of Oleron accuses Quaesitor Lothaire of partisanship, naming raids by Montverte, Fudarus and their allies from which he profited. An inquiry clears him for want of substance, but he never regains his place as chief Quaesitor of Normandy and is invited to Magvillus in honour of his long service.

diary.title: Infelicitas abandoned
diary.details: Rancrax is killed in Wizard's War by a magus of Moles Magna, and the two magi left at Infelicitas have no wish to stay.

diary.title: Fifteenth Grand Tribunal
diary.details: The Order's fifteenth Grand Tribunal meets.

diary.title: Nauche-Fleur ends
diary.details: Its mundane dealings always controversial, Nauche-Fleur kept none of the apprentices it trained, and it dies when the last of its founders enters Final Twilight.

diary.title: 44th meeting: Fudarus loses a legacy
diary.details: Atlax of Tytalus is charged with stealing and reading the messages the Redcap Camille carried while a guest at Fudarus. Quaesitor Whent holds the covenant answerable for its magus, strips Fudarus of the lease of a legacy and gives it to House Mercere.

diary.title: 45th meeting: Pernix acquitted, Camille fined
diary.details: Pernix of Merinita, accused by Visurgis of Tytalus of interfering with mundanes for healing a young noble thrown from his horse, is acquitted: only the noble and the abbot, prior and infirmarian of a friendly monastery knew. Camille of Mercere, accused by Buliste of Tytalus of using a local knight to gather the vis of one of his legacies, is convicted after the knight confessed to doing the devil's work and Atlax of Fudarus had to avert the ruin; Camille pays fifteen pawns to Fudarus and the source is closed for thirty years or more.

diary.title: Moles Magna destroyed
diary.details: After heavy rain the river bursts the dam that housed Moles Magna and the covenant is swept away. Since its magi had magically strengthened the dam against exactly that, most think they angered some power of the river they held back.

diary.title: Atsingani founded
diary.details: Atsingani is founded in Anjou as a vassal of Montverte.

diary.title: Cunfin founded
diary.details: Cunfin is founded in Champagne as a vassal of Confluensis.

diary.title: Sixteenth Grand Tribunal; Harpax made Primus
diary.details: The Order's sixteenth Grand Tribunal meets. About this time Prima Buliste of House Tytalus falls into a Twilight so deep she is taken for dead, and her rival Harpax, her fellow apprentice, is chosen as Primus and takes the Rod of the Primus from her sanctum.

diary.title: Alcuin's Auberge falls
diary.details: The Mercer House in Tours falls to raiders no one has identified.

diary.title: Two Primi of Tytalus; Atramentum founded
diary.details:
Buliste returns from Twilight, still wearing the Circlet of the Primus, and she and Harpax begin their struggle for the House; both are honoured as Primus and both rule Fudarus. Just as their battle begins, Fudarus sponsors the young vassal covenant of Atramentum.

Secrets
Cynics hold that Atramentum's founders were duped into readying the site for the magi who would soon take it.

diary.title: Exspectatio takes Atramentum's site
diary.details: The other magi of Fudarus leave the two Primi to their quarrel and settle at Atramentum, ousting its young magi and renaming it Exspectatio, still counting themselves members of Fudarus. Atramentum's founders form Atramentum Renatus, a vassal of Exspectatio, in Champagne.

diary.title: Eboris founded
diary.details: The covenant of Eboris is founded in Paris.

diary.title: 49th meeting: Pugnatis expelled
diary.details: The previous meeting convicted Pugnatis of controlling the mayor of Laval by magic to reach a vis source, and fined her a number of enchanted items. Neither she nor the items appear at this meeting, and she is cast out of the Order. Proctor of Guernicus presides, as he does again in 1214.

diary.title: Lapis Crudus returns
diary.details: After nearly a century trapped in its regio, Lapis Crudus wins a kind of freedom and comes back into Hermetic affairs, reminding the Tribunal that the Diedne may still be waiting in theirs.

diary.title: Death of Renita, the Praeco
diary.details: Renita of Bjornaer, Praeco of the Tribunal and leader of Confluensis, dies in the winter. Proctor, the Presiding Quaesitor, takes charge of Confluensis; who will be the next Praeco is open. Stellatus, the next eldest, has left for Iberia, leaving Celeres of Cunfin first in line.

tenures.source: Grove of St. Lie (Creo)
tenures.notes: A Gaulish mound in an oak grove above Reims with a hermit-saint's chapel: its pale flowers give a few pawns of Creo vis.

tenures.source: Ushant: the Three Great Spirits, 4 Creo, 4 Auram and 4 Imaginem a year
tenures.notes: On Fudarus's own island; its form is known only inside the covenant.

tenures.source: Fountain of Barenton (Brocéliande): Vim
tenures.notes: A druids' spring; amount not given.

tenures.source: Lake Comper (Brocéliande): up to 5 Aquam a year
tenures.notes: None in a drought year, when a priest blesses the lake for rain. The book gives no tenure; a known source that is neither a seisin nor under a legacy lease is a tropaeum under the ruling of 1032.

tenures.source: The Faeries' Mirror (Brocéliande): a little Imaginem
tenures.notes: Only if the mirror has gone unused for a month. The book gives no tenure; a known source that is neither a seisin nor under a legacy lease is a tropaeum under the ruling of 1032.

tenures.source: The Singing Stones (Arguenon estuary): Imaginem
tenures.notes: The stones must be struck just so with a stone of their kind. The book gives no tenure; a Tribunal source whose harvest rests on the harvester's skill is a luctatio under the ruling of 1039.

tenures.source: The oak of Pléchâtel: vis in large acorns
tenures.notes: A few acorns; the Art is not given. The book gives no tenure; a known source that is neither a seisin nor under a legacy lease is a tropaeum under the ruling of 1032.

tenures.source: Bréhat Isles: thrift in the cleft, up to 5 Intellego a year
tenures.notes: Taking more than 3 ruins the cleft's prophecies for years. The book gives no tenure; a known source that is neither a seisin nor under a legacy lease is a tropaeum under the ruling of 1032.

tenures.source: The Seven Isles: 6 Herbam and 5 Animal a year
tenures.notes: From the weeds and creatures of the clear waters. The book gives no tenure; a known source that is neither a seisin nor under a legacy lease is a tropaeum under the ruling of 1032.

tenures.source: Karreg an Tan (Black Mountains): Ignem lichen
tenures.notes: The rust-red lichen grows slowly. The book gives no tenure; a known source that is neither a seisin nor under a legacy lease is a tropaeum under the ruling of 1032.

tenures.source: The hawthorn of Rostrenen: Herbam, Divinely tainted
tenures.notes: Dedicated to Our Lady and always in bloom. The book gives no tenure; a known source that is neither a seisin nor under a legacy lease is a tropaeum under the ruling of 1032.

tenures.source: Roh-en-Aod (Quiberon): Auram
tenures.notes: Only a woman can gather it. The book gives no tenure; a Tribunal source whose harvest rests on the harvester's skill is a luctatio under the ruling of 1039.

tenures.source: Port-Goulphar (Belle-Île): Herbam algae
tenures.notes: The book gives no tenure; a known source that is neither a seisin nor under a legacy lease is a tropaeum under the ruling of 1032.

tenures.source: The Needles (Belle-Île): Aquam sea foam
tenures.notes: The book gives no tenure; a known source that is neither a seisin nor under a legacy lease is a tropaeum under the ruling of 1032.

tenures.source: St Cado's pillar (near Ploëmel): Creo
tenures.notes: The book gives no tenure; a known source that is neither a seisin nor under a legacy lease is a tropaeum under the ruling of 1032.

tenures.source: The surplus vis of the Apple Mile (kinds and amounts not given)
tenures.notes: Harvested in the covenant's own regio and traded to its vassals.

tenures.source: The lilac grove in Lord Henri's chase (Herbam; amount not given)
tenures.notes: The source that justified the covenant's founding.

tenures.source: The vis of Atsingani's ruined council tower (kind and amount not given)
tenures.notes: Gathered each summer at Atsingani's Council Tower, Montverte's gift.

tenures.source: The hot springs of the Auvergne: Aquam vis
tenures.notes: Gathered at Royat, le Mont-Dore and la Bourboule.

tenures.source: The hot springs of the Auvergne: Auram vis
tenures.notes: Gathered at Royat, le Mont-Dore and la Bourboule.

tenures.source: The hot springs of the Auvergne: Creo vis
tenures.notes: Gathered at Royat, le Mont-Dore and la Bourboule.

tenures.source: The hot springs of the Auvergne: Ignem vis
tenures.notes: Gathered at Royat, le Mont-Dore and la Bourboule.

tenures.source: The Bleeding Stone (Corpus and Terram)
tenures.notes: In a cavern under the council chamber, inside the regio

tenures.source: The cliff vines of Lapis Crudus (Herbam)
tenures.notes: On the valley walls inside the regio

tenures.source: Spider's Palace's sources (amounts not given)
tenures.notes: The reason the vassal exists: it keeps Florum's old site's vis lawfully in the line.

tenures.source: Graveyard of old Nesle (Perdo and Corpus, rich)
tenures.notes: About half goes to Florum as the vassal's tithe, raised in return for servants.

tenures.source: Cliffs of Laon (a small source of Terram)
tenures.notes: Granted to Norlanus of Jerbiton, an eremite with no covenant, and renewed for many years for his wisdom; up for renewal at the next meeting.

tenures.source: Footprints on the Seven Roads, Bavacum (Rego, a pawn an imprint)
tenures.notes: Dug up on the Mercuralia, 15 May. The book gives no tenure; entered as a luctatio since the harvest rests on the day and careful digging.

tenures.source: Cave of Sabinus: Aquam vis from the source of the Marne, by the genius loci's leave
tenures.notes: The spirit of the spring is notoriously hard to please, so the Tribunal leaves the source to any magus who dares.

tenures.source: Atramentum Renatus: the source the covenant was built about
tenures.notes: Formerly a legacy of Fudarus; Exspectatio gave it to Helios and Gulo as amends in 1201, and the covenant now stands by it. Its Art and yield are not given.

tenures.source: The tidal whirlpools beneath Confluensis
tenures.notes: Spun up on spring tides where fresh water meets salt and caught in enchanted nets; Art and yield not given.

tenures.source: The sour apples of the Orchard
tenures.notes: Intellego vis in the island's apples; yield not given.

tribunals.secrets:
The Cabal of the Golden Coin, begun by Tytalus magi and now drawn from many Houses, fixes Tourney events between its members and pushed through several of the odd prize levels to profit by them; the young three-magus team that has finished 14th at the last three Tourneys, just past the prizeless Siege of Shame, is one of its fronts. The Siege of Notatus's large prize may have a more practical origin than the tale of Notatus's love of seven, buried in the Tribunal's records. Three Normandy covenants back the Lotharingian movement, which would take some of the Tribunal's richest vis sources away and leave Tytalan Brittany producing more vis than the rest combined; a Tytalan Cabal of Frankish Gold works for it, with Augustina the Traitor among its members and at least one saboteur inside. Proctor's inherited hatred of House Tytalus may yet drive him to extremes. Rumour that Diedne survivors wait inside Branugurix's sealed regio, and that someone means to free them, may be true.

If the saga follows real history: Frederick II is crowned emperor in 1220. Louis VIII becomes king in 1223, and his son Louis IX, the future St Louis, in 1226. The seventeenth Grand Tribunal meets in 1228, the year of the Sixth Crusade and a papal ban on teaching Aristotle at Paris. The Albigensian Crusade ends in 1229. Orléans's cathedral school becomes a university in 1235 and Angers gains one in 1250. The Seventh Crusade runs from 1248 to 1254, and the Treaty of Corbeil settles France's claims against Aragon in 1258. The eighteenth Grand Tribunal meets in 1261, when a Troyes cobbler's son becomes Pope Urban IV; France takes a single coinage in 1263, and Guido le Gros of Saint-Gilles becomes Clement IV in 1265. The Eighth Crusade sails in 1270 and Philip III takes the throne. Simon de Brie of Touraine becomes Martin IV in 1281, Philip IV the Fair is crowned in 1285, the nineteenth Grand Tribunal meets in 1294, and Louis IX is made a saint in 1297. The Tribunal next meets in 1221, then 1227 (moved a year for the Grand Tribunal), 1235 and every seven years after.

The seven generations granted to Hugh Capet's line end with Philip Augustus, so some sudden change of dynasty is due at his death. The Royal Touch that cures scrofula comes from the holy oil, not from Merovech's blood; most Merovingian heirs carry a hidden immunity to drowning and a red cross birthmark. And Arthur of Brittany may not be dead: if he had the Gift and was hidden away in a late apprenticeship, his memory altered by Mentem, he would only now have passed his Gauntlet, unaware of his birthright.

neighbours.name: Branugurix (Mount Dol)
neighbours.summary:
Founded 791, sealed 1012. The Domus Magna of House Diedne, properly Bren Gwrac'h, hidden in a regio on Mount Dol, a low granite outcrop in the county of Rennes sacred to the Gallic druids. In the last great battle of the Schism War the Diedne Primus somehow closed every entrance to the regio, and some of the Flambeau and Tremere attackers were shut inside and never seen again. Its vassals were Baiocassium, Kerguntuil and Caput Capra.

Christians shun the mount; their tale of St. Michael hurling the Devil down here, and leaping after him to Mont St. Michel, remembers the assault. House Guernicus's records hold the regio's exact place and the old way in, and the House watches anyone who spends long around Mount Dol.

levels.name: Bren Gwrac'h
levels.see: Sealed: no way in is known outside the Guernicus records.
levels.enter: Closed by the Diedne Primus in 1012.
levels.notes: The Diedne Domus Magna as it was sealed, with whatever attackers and defenders were trapped there. The book gives no aura.

neighbours.secrets: Rumour says some Diedne survived inside the sealed regio and that someone is working to free them after two centuries; Lapis Crudus's return from its own regio has made the Tribunal fear this again.

neighbours.name: Bibracte
neighbours.summary: Founded 822, sacked 969. A vassal of Fudarus on Mont Beuvray in the southern Morvan near Autun, the Gallic hill-city where Vercingetorix raised the tribes and Caesar wintered. A few Diedne and one Tytalus rebuilt its double ramparts and revived a cult of Vercingetorix, then turned against all things Roman: they banned Latin for Brythonic and refused to deal with the 'Roman' Houses. With Fudarus weakened after the corruption of House Tytalus, four Flambeau and Tremere of Montverte declared Wizard War on them together, calling them devil-worshippers, and destroyed the covenant. The overgrown ruins are mostly forgotten, though Helios of Atramentum Renatus now studies them and Philip of the Donatores fears he is angering the ghosts.
neighbours.secrets: Whether the cult succeeded in raising Vercingetorix's spirit is unknown; Helios means to find out.

neighbours.name: Pagus
neighbours.summary: Founded 840, destroyed 1008. A vassal of Confluensis at a ruined Roman outpost near Cherbourg, overlooking the Channel, whose magi spent heavily restoring the Roman buildings and a dock. The Viking raids wrecked it and cost it many vis sources; it never recovered, and the Diedne magi of Baiocassium destroyed it in the Schism War. Some of its old vis sources are now claimed, controversially, by Fengheld's chapter house at Cherbourg.

neighbours.name: Baiocassium
neighbours.summary: Founded 851, destroyed 1011. A vassal of Branugurix in the forest near Bayeux, its magi mostly Diedne descended from Gallic druids and friendly with the local faeries. Raided several times by Vikings, it founded a refuge in the town that became Baiocassium Minor; it destroyed Pagus in the Schism War and was itself destroyed in 1011. The ruin still lies in the shrinking forest of Bayeux.

neighbours.name: Sinapis (the church at Tavant)
neighbours.summary: Founded 855, abandoned 1063. Once a great liege in Anjou and head of its own line (Rotomagus, Aedes Salii and Lapis Crudus were its vassals), it was abandoned when the quarrel between Houses Tytalus and Flambeau ended and its magi left for Provençal and Iberia. All that remains is a small church at Tavant, six miles up the Vienne from Chinon, which a poor parish took over unaware of its past: lifelike paintings, lily-bearing figures by the crypt door, and carvings of griffins, sirens, a two-bodied monster and a serpent in a tree. Its old Magic aura shows only when the Dominion is at its weakest. Lapis Crudus counts itself of Sinapis's line.

neighbours.name: Rotomagus
neighbours.summary: Founded 875, destroyed 892. Founded near Rouen by Sinapis's first apprentices and destroyed when the Vikings sacked the city less than twenty years later. Its one survivor left House Flambeau in shame for Ex Miscellanea.

neighbours.name: Ligurio
neighbours.summary: Founded 913, destroyed 1011. A vassal of Fudarus in the great marsh of the Vendée on the Aquitaine-Brittany border, lasting about a century until giants hurling boulders smashed it, sent, it is thought, by the Diedne of Kerguntuil. Little is left: its buildings have sunk into the marsh among fishers and fowlers, near the priory at Sallertaine and the abbey at Chauvet.

neighbours.name: Kerguntuil
neighbours.summary: Founded 920, destroyed 1007. A Diedne vassal of Branugurix on the Rose Coast, named for the dolmen on a hilltop above the Trégastel headland, said to be a petrified giant. Its magi studied the Breton giant tales and many of its covenfolk were unusually large. Raided by Vikings, it was obliterated in the Schism War. The Templars' round chapel at Lanleff and the church at Lannion were built nearby, by rumour at a Quaesitor's suggestion, to cleanse the coast of Diedne taint.

neighbours.name: Baiocassium Minor
neighbours.summary: Founded 936, destroyed 1005. A vassal of Baiocassium, begun as a spring sanctuary in a regio inside the town of Bayeux after the Viking raids, and destroyed in the Schism War. No living magus admits to knowing where the regio is.

neighbours.name: Caput Capra
neighbours.summary: Founded 981, destroyed 1005. The youngest and easternmost vassal of Branugurix, on the Loire near Fleury, founded to guard the old druids' assembly ground there through the lawless late tenth century. It was the first covenant in the Tribunal to fall in the Schism War. Confluensis brings its apprentices to the scant ruins for their history lessons.

neighbours.name: Aedes Salii
neighbours.summary: Founded 998, disbanded 1063. A vassal of Sinapis on Jersey, named for the priests of Mars and founded to run the Schism War in Normandy and Stonehenge. Its Tremere went home after the war, leaving it to House Flambeau, and it was disbanded when the Flambeau withdrew from the Tribunal; two of its magi joined Lapis Crudus.

neighbours.name: Orchard of Sour Apples
neighbours.summary: Founded 1020, absorbed 1051. A vassal of Confluensis founded after the Schism War and named for a nearby vis source. When Confluensis had to move, it took over the site and the Orchard's magi joined their liege; Confluensis stands there now.

neighbours.name: Lixivia
neighbours.summary: Founded 1021, disbanded 1124. A vassal of Florum in Champagne, set up as the fairs began to deal between the Order and mundane merchants. Its Redcaps and Gentle Gifted magi offered to find anything any covenant wanted, but magi distrusted them, raided them freely, and drove them into poverty until they disbanded. Its Redcaps went on to found Alcuin's Auberge.

neighbours.name: Vexatores
neighbours.summary: Founded 1048, abandoned 1064. A vassal of Fudarus founded only to provoke Sinapis in the quarrel between Tytalus and Flambeau, 21 miles north of it (the least the law allowed) at one of the vis sources taken from House Diedne. Never meant to last, it was abandoned once the quarrel ended.

neighbours.name: Nauche-Fleur
neighbours.summary: Founded 1072, ended 1166. A vassal of Montverte near Niort in Aquitaine that ran a school of arms and letters whose fees kept its magi in luxury. Cleared in 1095 of swearing fealty to its baron, it was always controversial for its part in mundane politics, so none of its apprentices stayed, and it died when the last founder went into Final Twilight.

neighbours.name: Infelicitas
neighbours.summary: Founded 1099, abandoned 1158. A vassal of Fudarus in Flanders, founded when Rancrax of Tytalus lost a wager to his rival and had to leave Fudarus. Jacinth of Oleron's raid in 1130 brought down its upper storey and two laboratories. It foundered when Rancrax was killed in Wizard War by a magus of Moles Magna and the other two magi did not care to stay. Some once suspected it, or Florum, of raising the tidal wave that struck the Flemish coast.

neighbours.name: Alcuin's Auberge
neighbours.summary: Founded 1124, destroyed 1197. A small Mercer House of Florum's line in Tours, founded by Redcaps from Lixivia in rooms dug beneath a pilgrim hostel, home to two Redcaps and a stopping place for others and passing magi. It prospered, drew the wrong attention, and fell to unknown raiders; some blame Fudarus, unproven.

neighbours.name: Moles Magna
neighbours.summary: Founded 1136, destroyed 1182. A vassal of Oleron on the edge of the Morvan, built inside a dam on a small tributary of the Yonne, the lake behind and the waterfall in front hiding it. One of its magi killed Rancrax of Infelicitas in Wizard War. The dam burst after heavy rain despite the magic that held it, and the covenant was swept away; most think the magi had angered a spirit of the river they penned.

neighbours.name: Atramentum
neighbours.summary: Founded 1200, taken 1201. A vassal of Fudarus in the Arrée Mountains of Brittany, founded by Helios of Tytalus and Gulo Midusulfis of Bjornaer and named 'Ink' for a sodalis who died at the founding, just as the two Tytalus Primi began their feud. It lost a case against Fudarus over the artificers' guild of Le Conquet (the town senex ruling of 1200), and a year after its founding the elder Tytali leaving Fudarus evicted its founders and made it Exspectatio. Cynics say the young magi were used to prepare the ground. The founders went on to found Atramentum Renatus.

neighbours.name: Brittany
neighbours.summary:
A peninsula of hard crystalline rock thrust into the Atlantic at the Tribunal's western edge. The north-west wind brings fog, mist and rain most days, more in the north than in the sunnier south, and the sea keeps the land free of frost. The Armor, the country by the sea, is a long, ragged coast of high cliffs, drowned river valleys and countless islands, where great tides bare mud flats and rock shelves twice a day. The Argoat, the country of the wood, is an upland cut by deep valleys, forested or, where the trees went long ago, moorland; its thin soils over granite, schist and gneiss make its peasants among the poorest in the Tribunal, though the sheltered valleys farm well.

Faeries, giants and magical beasts held the land first, served by a few pagans. Rome ruled for four centuries; then Celts from Britain settled it and saints crossed from Wales to convert it. Louis the Pious made it a duchy under Nominoé, who won its independence from Charles the Bald; Erispoë took the title of king, Salomon seized the throne by murder, and the kings held off the Norsemen until Alain Crookbeard died in 952. A century of noble feuding ended with Alain IV Fergent; marriage and fealty then drew the duchy to Anjou, and Henry II of England took it between 1158 and 1166. It slipped free of the English crown after King John was rumoured to have murdered his nephew Arthur of Brittany, and Peter of Dreux now rules it as regent for his wife Alice's son.

The east speaks a French dialect close to its neighbours'; the west speaks Breton, seldom written, and in the countryside often nothing else. The harp and the Breton pipes play for dances in lines and rings; sports are lifting a heavy beam like a chariot axle, putting heavy stones, and a seated tug for a short stick with the feet braced on a low board. The great feasts are the pardons: processions with prayers, then feasting, each old parish keeping its own saint's day. Bretons hold that Welsh monks brought the faith, and every Breton should once in life make the Tro Briez, the round of the eight founders' cathedrals (St Malo, St Brieuc for St Broch, Perros-Guirec for St Guirec, St-Pol-de-Léon for St Paul, Dol for St Samson, Tréguier for St Tugdual, Quimper for St Corentine and Vannes for St Patern); whoever fails must make it after death, creeping a coffin's length every seven years.

Brittany is the least civilised and emptiest part of the Tribunal and the richest in vis, much of it unclaimed, with only Fudarus and its vassals near; covenants founded here, in Brocéliande above all, have all failed. Megaliths are everywhere, many with an aura: a dolmen (flat slabs on upright stones) may be a giants' table, a faerie meeting place or an old altar; a menhir (one standing stone) may have been raised by saints, angels, demons, giants or faeries; a tumulus (a mound) may be a clod a giant threw or earth heaped over a faerie door, and many hide a dolmen. Every acre still has a lord, so a covenant on a lonely isle, a firm patch of marsh or a forest hollow must still deal with the feudal order and the Church.

Across the duchy roam the Ankeu, Death as a shrouded skeleton with a scythe driving a creaking cart heaped with the dead (on the islands he comes by the Bag Noz, the night boat): to hear the cart foretells a loved one's death, and to meet it is nearly always one's own. A folk rite traps a ghost that will not leave its house in a black dog, to be drowned at once: the dog (Divine Might 10 at most, usually 5; Infernal for a sinner's ghost, Magic for a pagan's) barks fear and howls despair, and if it dies any way but drowning the spirit stays bound where it fell, with a pawn or two of vis in its tongue. Korrigan, hunched manikins with cat's claws and goat's hooves, dance at crossroads and hoard treasure in woods, caves and dolmens; outside Brocéliande they are more fond of dancing and riches than of harm, but quick to punish.

Folk tales across the duchy hint at what magi might find: two quarrelling trees that are a bewitched husband and wife; a king of fishes, a king of birds and a bound demon king who each repay a rescue; three hermits whose advice adds up to an answer; starved beasts on rich grass beside fat beasts on bare ground; a loaf that never grows less; a silver whistle that calls the birds; a shirt that freezes an unwanted lover till dawn; apples of sleep; a honey cake that brings a maiden a helpful magic cat and a good husband; a cloth that lays a meal when spread. Other tales tell of the Princess of the Shining Star, kept from men in a tower of a green glass castle hung in the air on gold and silver chains inside a Magic regio, who steals young women as companions; of the Mother of Winds, a bearded old woman by her forest fire who keeps her four giant sons in order with a sack; and of a white Magic fox by a stone with an aura, whose ivory ball, if followed, rolls to a forest hermit.

neighbours.name: County of Rennes
neighbours.summary: The duchy's east, gentler, drier and richer than the rest, largely wooded, and studded with strong castles from the recent wars against the Normans and the Franks. Its northern shore, the Emerald Coast, runs low and marshy toward the sands of Mont St Michel; west of the marshes to St Brieuc Bay it turns to high, rocky cliffs with a few small beaches. Inland the Rance leads to the forested hills of Hunaudaye, deep ravines and scattered granite boulders crossed by a single trade road from Rennes to St Brieuc. At the centre stands Rennes on the Vilaine, which runs south-west between red stone hills; to the west lies Brocéliande, and near the Normandy border the forest round Fougères is thick with megaliths even for Brittany.

neighbours.name: Mount Dol
neighbours.summary:
A granite knoll only about two hundred feet high that nonetheless commands the marshes, a holy place of the Gallic druids. Branugurix, the domus magna of House Diedne, lay hidden in a regio here. Christians shun the hill: they say St Michael fought the Devil on it and flung him down so hard that the hollow and the claw marks still show on its north side, beside the cleft of the saint's sword; when the Devil reappeared on Mont St Michel, the saint leapt after him and left a footprint on the summit.

South of the town of Dol stands the menhir of Champ-Dolent.
neighbours.secrets: The legend of St Michael is a garbled memory of the Order's assault on Branugurix. The regio's entrances were closed in the last battle of the Schism War.

neighbours.name: The Menhir of Champ-Dolent
neighbours.summary: The Field of Pain, south of Dol: a single stone thirty feet tall, square at the base and tapering to a point, which marks the ground of the last battle of the Schism War.

neighbours.name: The Siren's Cave at Décollé Point
neighbours.summary: A cave at the foot of the first headland west of the Rance mouth, home to a siren. She guards a natural rock bridge between the cliffs and Décollé Point, and nobody has learned why she protects the point.

neighbours.name: The Singing Stones
neighbours.summary: A heap of rocks on the coast above the Arguenon estuary that rings like metal when struck. Struck the right way with a stone of the same kind, the sound can be harvested as Imaginem vis.

neighbours.name: The Temple of Mars at Corseul
neighbours.summary: A Roman settlement about five miles west of Dinan, where the round wall of a temple of Mars, of thin Roman brick, still rises above the treetops; nothing else of it shows. The ruin has a Magic aura of 3, and through the regio boundary the temple stands whole.

levels.name: The temple whole
levels.notes: Inside the walls, past the regio boundary, the building is intact.

neighbours.name: St Broch's Fountain
neighbours.summary: The spring at St Brieuc beside which the saint lived. Once a week, leaving the cathedral after Sunday Mass, a person may dip the right hand in it and devoutly cross himself for a blessing that shifts one Personality Trait a step until sunset (no further than +3 or -3): a lowered step falls on the trait likeliest to lead to sin, a raised one on the trait likeliest to lead to good.

neighbours.name: The Caves and Oak of Pléchâtel
neighbours.summary: Well-hidden caves near the village of Pléchâtel in the Vilaine valley, with a weak Magic aura (its strength is not given), and an ancient oak whose few unusually large acorns are vis (the book does not name the Art).

neighbours.name: The Young Ladies of Langon
neighbours.summary: About thirty standing stones on the moor by Langon, a village on terraces above the Vilaine whose chapel of St Agatha is built into the walls of a Romano-Gallic temple of Venus. Locals say the stones are girls who danced on the moor instead of going to vespers and were turned to stone by God.
neighbours.secrets: The stones are far older than the tale and belong with the temple: they record the fate of the women who served it.

neighbours.name: Faeries' Rock
neighbours.summary:
Forty-two huge slabs of purple schist in the forest south-east of Rennes, halfway to the Normandy border: a broad, low doorway facing the midwinter sunrise opens on a passage and a tall chamber divided into stalls.

Each year on the eve of the winter solstice a faerie court sits here to judge faeries, and sometimes mortals, who have broken its seemingly arbitrary laws. The accused are snatched from their beds and set down in the chamber almost at once; anyone present, the accused included, may speak briefly for or against, and the presiding faerie noble gives verdict and sentence, rewards and punishments as capricious as the laws. However long the hearing seems, it ends when the first ray of dawn enters the chamber, and mortals must find their own way home.

neighbours.name: The Forest of Brocéliande
neighbours.summary:
A vast, mysterious and perilous forest west of Rennes and the Vilaine, under a Faerie aura of 2 that runs much higher in places. A small monastery at Paimpont tries to counter its influences and makes little headway. Brittany's richest faerie and vis sites lie here, and every covenant founded in it has failed, whether to territorial faeries or territorial magi.

The korrigan of Brocéliande are the most dangerous in Brittany since their queen Viviane lost interest in them and the forest. A korred is a hunched manikin about three feet tall with cat's claws and goat's hooves (Faerie Might usually 5 to 10, rarely 15, Animal): a tireless dancer and a magician, greedy, capricious and short-tempered, quick with claws, club and thrown stones, and the stronger ones can spend Might to become a beautiful young woman for an hour. They punish whoever annoys them severely, sometimes reward from their hoards, invite passers-by to their moonlit crossroads dances and punish those who refuse. Each carries a pawn of Animal vis in its hooves. Anyone gathering vis or prying into the forest's secrets will meet them.

neighbours.name: The Fountain of Youth and the Stone of Merlin
neighbours.summary:
A spring ringed with stones at the heart of the forest, in a glade with a Faerie aura of 5. Washing the face in it smooths an old person's wrinkles for a few hours, a faerie glamour no magus has yet learned to prolong or use. Merlin came here for solitude and met Viviane, the Lady of the Lake; tired of him, she put him into a deep sleep, and many think he sleeps still under the nearby pair of slabs called the Stone of Merlin. A drop of the fountain's water let fall on the stone turns to vapour, and the air fills with shadows and thunder.

A magus following the Path of Aging may drink here for the second quest.

levels.name: Merlin's sleeping place
levels.enter: Perhaps by a rite that begins with fountain water dropped on the Stone of Merlin
levels.notes: Rumoured; its aura is not given.

neighbours.secrets: The drop on the stone is probably the first step of the rite that opens the Faerie regio where Merlin may lie sleeping.

neighbours.name: Lake Comper and the Joyous Garden
neighbours.summary:
Viviane's home deep in the forest. Merlin raised the Joyous Garden and the Crystal Castle there for her, peopled with faerie knights, ladies and maids, and where she is said to have raised Lancelot. She probably still lives in the Faerie regio that hides her estate; research suggests it can be found and entered on the night before Midsummer's Day. Given how she has treated suitors and great magicians, a senior magus risks being kept there, and one with the Curse of Venus is courting trouble.

The lake yields up to 5 pawns of Aquam vis in a normal year; in a drought a local priest comes to dip a cross in the water for rain, and that season no vis can be gathered.

levels.name: The Joyous Garden and the Crystal Castle
levels.enter: Perhaps on the night before Midsummer's Day
levels.notes: Viviane's estate, with faerie knights, ladies and maids; aura not given.

neighbours.name: The Bridge of Secrets
neighbours.summary: A bridge near the village of Beignon, about four miles south of Comper, where Lancelot and Guinevere are said to have shared their first kiss. The ruin that betrayal brought suggests Perdo vis may be had here on its anniversary, if anyone discovers how to harvest it.

neighbours.name: The Fountain of Barenton
neighbours.summary: A spring about four miles west-south-west of the Fountain of Youth, sacred to the druids. Tales say that its water splashed on the stone called Merlin's Step calls up wild storms and a fierce knight in black armour. It is a source of Vim vis, held by the Tribunal as a tropaeum.

neighbours.name: The Faeries' Mirror
neighbours.summary: A small lake about four miles south of Barenton that the faeries use as a looking glass. If it has gone unused for a month, a little Imaginem vis can be gathered from it.

neighbours.name: The Valley of No Return
neighbours.summary: A deep valley just past the Faeries' Mirror, where Morgan le Fay, Arthur's half-sister, imprisoned her faithless lover Guyomart at False Lover's Rock. Legend says no wrongdoer can leave it.
neighbours.secrets: Only those unfaithful in love are actually held.

neighbours.name: Lordship of Penthièvre
neighbours.summary: A barony along the rugged middle of the north coast that climbs inland over forested hills, thinly peopled. The Central Argoat inland is nearly all forest with a few small settlements: Loudéac, a crossroads market with two animal fairs a year; Moncontour under its castle where two valleys meet; Quintin among its flax fields, with the Long Rock menhir nearby and a small castle at Robien. Cistercian houses at Boquen, Quenécan and Gouarec, a Benedictine house in the Lorge Forest and St Briac's chapel at Bourbriac hide in the woods.

neighbours.name: The Rose Coast
neighbours.summary:
The cliffs of pink granite, topped with moor, between St Brieuc Bay and Morlaix Bay, round small sandy beaches and creeks. Many of the oddly worn rocks look like beasts and people, and a few of them really were. Small islands lie offshore in great number. Tréguier stands on terraces between the Jaudy and the Guindy; beyond it the coast breaks into massive headlands split by deep clefts, and on the largest island nearby a dolmen stands on blue rock, for a giant hauled the whole isle here from south-west Wales.

On a hill above the Trégastel headland stands the Dolmen of Kerguntuil, thought to be a giant turned to stone, which gave its name to a Diedne covenant destroyed in 1007. The Templars, it is rumoured at a Quaesitor's prompting, built along this coast to cleanse the Diedne taint: a round chapel at Lanleff in the eleventh century and Brélévenez church at Lannion on the Léguer in the twelfth. Behind the dunes north of the Léguer mouth lies the fifty-five-acre Quellen Marsh.

neighbours.name: The Bréhat Isles
neighbours.summary:
