Two isles off the coast's eastern point, each about a mile across but deeply indented and almost touching, under a Magic aura of 4, with a mild, dry climate: pink cliffs on the wilder northern isle, low pink and grey sand and shingle on the east, and sea of many blues and greens over pink rocks bared only at low tide.

At the far end is a deep cleft in the cliff. Once a year a maiden may drop a pebble into it: if it falls clean into the water she will marry within the year, and otherwise she waits a year for every bounce. The thrift clinging to the cleft holds Intellego vis, up to 5 pawns a year, but taking more than 3 spoils the prophecies for several years after.

neighbours.name: The Seven Isles
neighbours.summary: An archipelago east of Trégastel Head, far enough out to be troubled only by the seabirds of its high cliffs and the seals on the rocks below. Its clear waters, full of feathery weed and bright clinging creatures, usually yield 6 pawns of Herbam and 5 of Animal vis a year, along with eels, crabs, lobsters and crayfish. Each isle has its own Magic aura: one 4, one 3, two 2 and three 1.

neighbours.name: Yaudet
neighbours.summary: A round hilltop above the sea on the south side of the Léguer estuary, its humps and ditches the remains of a Romano-Gallic settlement. Locals sometimes glimpse oddly dressed men and women there and now and then wander into a regio. A surer way in lies a little along the coast at Plestin-les-Grèves, in the ruined Romano-Gallic bathhouse, through the alcove whose inscription says it held a statue of Teutates, or Mars.

levels.name: The Romano-Gallic town
levels.enter: By chance on the hill, or through the alcove of the bathhouse at Plestin-les-Grèves
levels.notes: Its strangely dressed people are glimpsed from outside; aura not given.

neighbours.name: The Long Rock
neighbours.summary: A menhir on a hilltop near Quintin that takes on a Faerie aura for a time, at intervals nobody can predict.

neighbours.name: Lordship of Léon
neighbours.summary:
Brittany's north-western tip, woodland and bleak moor ringed on three sides by muddy estuaries, exposed beaches and islands; its far end is rightly called Finistère, Land's End. The coast of the Abers is drowned river mouths, small beaches and countless rocks awash at high tide; salt-laden westerlies poison the soil, and few people live there. The coast near Pontusval is known for lingering pagan ways tied to its many shipwrecks.

Brest guards the north shore of its sheltered bay; the Crozon peninsula, all high cliffs, stacks and arches, closes it to the south. To the south and east the Arrée Mountains curve round the county.

neighbours.name: The Monster's Hole on Batz
neighbours.summary: A low rock shelf on the isle of Batz, off St-Pol-de-Léon, covering the pit where St Paul the Aurelian penned the dragon that terrorised the island, after leading it there tamed on his stole. He founded a monastery on the island.

neighbours.name: The Barnenez Tumulus
neighbours.summary: An enormous cairn of green, pink and grey stones across the estuary east of St-Pol. No door shows, but searchers find openings on the south-east side, each a passage of twenty to forty feet into one of eleven chambers.

neighbours.name: The Men-Marz Menhir
neighbours.summary: A standing stone on Pontusval Point with a Celtic cross on top, where prayers are said from time to time, on a coast notorious for shipwrecks and the pagan practices bound up with them.

neighbours.name: Tolente
neighbours.summary: A Romano-Gallic town near Plougerneau, the westernmost village of the north coast, which vanished in 875 while Vikings attacked it; the village church stands on a pagan cairn. The Quaesitores investigate anyone known to be looking for a way in.

levels.name: The hidden town
levels.enter: Unknown; the Quaesitores watch for anyone seeking it
levels.notes: Hidden since 875; aura not given.

neighbours.secrets: Druids almost certainly hid the town in a regio by magic.

neighbours.name: The Isle of Ushant
neighbours.summary:
A small island ten miles off Brittany's western tip, four miles by two and a half, its sheer cliffs rising 180 feet to a nearly flat top, ringed by treacherous currents and by reefs that sailors swear wander. The storm-beaten mainland opposite is empty. The fishing village of Lampaul lies on the gentler south-western shore; the rest is deserted but for Fudarus, the domus magna of House Tytalus, which crouches on the landward cliff edge in a Magic aura of 7. Without magic no one climbs the cliffs.

Three Great Spirits bound into Fudarus's walls guard the island in turn (Magic Might 40, Auram), invisible and intangible, aware of all that happens on Ushant, and touchable by magic only by a caster who can sense them: Mogidell of mist and sea fog, a vast grey bird whose spread wings bring down the mist; Kerseenn of misdirection, always shifting between monstrous blends of man and beast; and Arnev of storms, a huge serpent with a horse's head. Each can match any non-Ritual spell of its kind up to level 40 at a point of Might a magnitude. Their presence makes 12 pawns of vis appear on the island each year, 4 each of Creo, Auram and Imaginem. They obey whoever bears the Circlet of the Primus, through an old pact that made them the island's genii loci.
neighbours.secrets: Only the people of Fudarus know what form the spirits' vis takes.

neighbours.name: St Nerius's Circle
neighbours.summary: A clean ring of grass just left of the gates of Fudarus, set in blackened, blasted ground: the place where St Nerius was martyred, with a Divine aura of 1. Every year on the anniversary a single blue flower of no known kind blooms in the burnt turf for a day. A few pious magi come to keep vigil and let no one pick it; Fudarus lets them come, does not interfere, and some of its magi have even joined the devotions with due solemnity.

neighbours.name: The Menhirs of Camaret
neighbours.summary: An array of 143 standing stones in a Magic aura of 3 near Camaret, the tiny village at the west end of Crozon where pilgrims bound by sea for Rocamadour land and give thanks for their passage in a little chapel.

neighbours.name: The Caves of Morgat
neighbours.summary: Many caves on Crozon's south shore, their roofs and walls brightly coloured by nature. Of the two groups of great caverns, one holds the cave called the Devil's Chamber and the other the cave called the Altar; many small caves can be reached only at low tide.

neighbours.name: The Arrée Mountains
neighbours.summary:
The duchy's highest ground, an arc round the south and east of Léon, often lost in mist: rounded summits a little over 1,200 feet, mostly under deciduous forest thick with moss and fern, home to deer, boar and wolves, broken by bare saw-toothed crags, gorse and heather moor and a few sheltered fields. Its small, scattered folk mix Christian and pagan ways, and civilisation keeps to the edges: the Cistercians of Le Relecq to the east, a castle over the Élorn valley to the north-west, the church of King Salomon's martyrdom on the south-east fringe and the port of Landerneau at the head of the Élorn estuary.

Exspectatio lies in a secluded valley of these mountains.

neighbours.name: Exspectatio's Valley
neighbours.summary: A secluded valley in the Arrée Mountains, about three days' journey from Fudarus, where the young magi of Atramentum founded their covenant in 1200 and the elder Tytali of Exspectatio took it from them a year later. Its aura is not given, but it is weaker than Fudarus's.

neighbours.name: The Rocks of Huelgoat
neighbours.summary: Piles of boulders left when the hamlets of Plouyé and Berrien went to war and pelted each other with stones that all fell between them. Nearby are the Devil's Cave, the huge Trembling Rock that rocks when pushed in the right spot, the Virgin's Kitchen, a chasm where the River Argent goes underground, a pool the faeries haunt and a cave where King Arthur once slept.

neighbours.name: Youdig in the Yeun Elez
neighbours.summary: A peat bog spreading east from the foot of St Michael's Mount near Brennilis, said to hide Youdig, a gate of Hell, which can be reached only in winter when mist lies on the bog. A short way to the north lies Mougau-Bihan, a giant's tomb: a covered walk of megaliths forty-five feet long.

neighbours.name: County of Cornouaille
neighbours.summary:
A broad peninsula with points to north and south and wooded hills and valleys inland. At Locronan pilgrims climb the hill by the path St Ronan walked daily, fasting and barefoot. The Black Mountains, lower and softer than the Arrée across the broad Aulne valley, still shelter hermits' woods; from Ménez-Hom at their west end one sees Cornouaille, Crozon, the bay of Brest, St Matthew's Point and both ranges. Carhaix, the Roman Vorgium where seven roads met, is the only sizeable place for miles; further east lie the healing springs of Bulat-Pestivien and desolate Burthulet, so cold in winter that a demon froze to death there.

Between Raz Point and Van Point opens the dreaded Bay of Troubled Souls, where the drowned wash ashore; south of it a twelve-mile shingle beach runs to the cliffs of Penmarch, with a yearly torchlit blessing of the sea halfway along.

neighbours.name: Sein Island
neighbours.summary: A low island off Raz Point, drowned by the highest tides, with two menhirs and a dolmen. The druids who died on the mainland were ferried here by boat for burial, and that keeps the locals away. Pomponius Mela wrote that nine virgin witches who could raise winds and storms lived on it.

neighbours.name: The Drowned Town of Is
neighbours.summary:
King Gradlon's lovely capital in the sixth century, guarded from the sea by a dyke whose floodgates only the king could open. The Devil, as a handsome youth, seduced his daughter Dahut into stealing the key while Gradlon slept and opened the gates at high tide. The king fled with her on horseback, and when a voice told him to cast off the wicked woman he threw her into the flood; the waters drew back far enough for the townsfolk to escape, but Is sank. Gradlon founded Quimper in its place.

Dahut became Marie-Morgane, an evil siren who still sings sailors to their deaths and peoples her sunken town with them. A Mass said in one of the drowned churches on Good Friday is said to banish her.

neighbours.name: Karreg an Tan
neighbours.summary: Fire Rock, a summit in the Black Mountains east of Ménez-Hom, where a rust-red lichen grows slowly on the stone; it is Ignem vis.

neighbours.name: The Hawthorn of Rostrenen
neighbours.summary: A hawthorn at Rostrenen in the east of the Black Mountains, dedicated to Our Lady, which blooms all year; it yields Herbam vis tainted by the Divine.

neighbours.name: The Gorges of Corong and Toul Goulic
neighbours.summary: Two gorges where a river vanishes under tumbled rocks, Corong's spilling out lower down in cascades, Toul Goulic's further east. Each has a temperamental genius loci, and the two have feuded so long neither remembers why; whichever has the upper hand has its river running above ground. Both would gladly end it and would reward whoever managed it without either seeming to give way.

neighbours.name: Broërec
neighbours.summary:
Low forested plateaus cut by many rivers that widen into drowned estuaries on the coast; crops grow in the sheltered valleys, and the sea feeds the rest. By the Étel estuary a sailor's wife drops a crust into Ste Hélène's fountain and reads her husband's safe return in whether it floats or sinks; nearby, deaf petitioners sleep on St Cado's stone bed and pillow hoping for a cure.

The Gulf of Morbihan is nearly closed by land, about twelve miles across and nine deep, fringed with mud and salt marsh and scattered with low islands. Inland Vannes stands on the Marle, and beyond it the Lanvaux Moors, a crescent of bare flaking rock dotted with megaliths; Ploëmel lies past them, founded by St Arthmael, who slew a dragon there. At Castennac, near the Cornouaille border, a statue the locals call their Venus serves lewd pagan rites; churchmen have thrown it in the river several times, and it always comes back.

neighbours.name: The Tumiac Tumulus
neighbours.summary: A mound on the arm of land south of the gulf from which Julius Caesar watched his fleet fight the Veneti, the strongest Gallic tribe: more than two hundred Gallic sailing ships against Roman galleys. Interesting relics very likely lie on the sea floor.

neighbours.name: The Gavrinis Tumulus and Er Lanic
neighbours.summary:
A cairn about twenty feet high on an islet near the gulf's mouth, over a passage and a chamber roofed with huge slabs on uprights carved with spirals, cups and rings; the chamber is eight great slabs of a dark, fine-grained stone not found nearby. It has an evil name for dark magic done there long ago, and a Faerie aura of 3, and in the right conditions it opens on a dark Faerie realm.

Just south, on the isle of Er Lanic, stones stand in a figure of eight, one ring drowned at high tide, in a Magic aura of 5.

levels.name: The dark Faerie realm
levels.enter: Under the right circumstances, through the chamber
levels.notes: Aura not given.

neighbours.name: The Megaliths of Locmariaquer
neighbours.summary: A remarkable gathering of ancient monuments toward the end of the Rhuys peninsula. The greatest, once over sixty feet tall, lies broken in two; the slabs called the Merchants' Table are carved with crooks and an ox, so the place probably served old animal magic. Er-Grah, Mané-er-Hroech, Mané-Lud, Mané-Rethual, Kerlud and the Flat Stones are other dolmens of huge dressed and often carved stone, mostly a covered passage into a great chamber, likely giants' homes.

neighbours.name: Quiberon and Roh-en-Aod
neighbours.summary: A long isle cut off from the mainland only at high tide: dunes at the north, cliffs, caves and reefs pounded by the ocean on the west, long gentle beaches on the sheltered east, where twenty-two menhirs stand in rows. At the north end of the west cliffs the stone Roh-en-Aod has five cup-shaped hollows; women who tap them with hammers by night win fair winds for their husbands' boats, and Auram vis can be had from it, but only by a woman.

neighbours.name: Belle-Île
neighbours.summary:
The largest Breton island, five miles out from Quiberon: a schist plateau cut by fast streams ending in creeks and small beaches, swept by westerly wind and rain, with trees only where sheltered. At Port-Goulphar on the south-west coast, bright algae gathering on the rocks of a deep, calm chasm are an unusual Herbam vis; a little further, the surf at the rocks called the Needles throws up foam that is Aquam vis.

Two menhirs called Jean and Jeanne stand on a gorse moor in the north of the island, one of pale granite and one of dark schist: a betrothed couple turned to stone for not waiting for their wedding.
neighbours.secrets: A suitable Hermetic ritual could restore Jean and Jeanne, who would be glad to join a covenant since their world is long gone. Jeanne is pregnant and gives birth three months after the spell ends, to a Gifted child with a close affinity for Terram.

neighbours.name: Carnac
neighbours.summary:
One of the mightiest magical sites in Mythic Europe: more than a thousand rough menhirs, from a child's height to over twenty feet, in broken avenues across the heath by the village of Carnac, on a scale that dwarfs Stonehenge. By day a Magic aura of 5 covers the heath, one of the largest the Order knows, rising to 6 or more on the avenues, with many regiones; the place is brighter and more real than the land round it, and its birds, flowers and beasts show odd cleverness, strange powers or speech. As the light goes the aura fades, and by night it is Infernal. No covenant has ever been built here, and none likely will be.

The Order's legends set Trianoma's meeting with Diedne the Founder here on a bright summer afternoon, and here a fleeing remnant of the Diedne was hunted down and killed; some say that blood brought the curse. Locals credit faeries with the stones and try hedge charms to make them build houses overnight; the pious say St Cornelius, fleeing in his ox cart, prayed at the shore and God turned his faerie pursuers to stone. Most who live nearby agree that demons haunt it by night. Processions of the ancient dead are seen, and every Midsummer night the villagers bar themselves into St Cornelius's church to pray till dawn, for even the churchyard's aura turns Infernal 5.

The Nains guard the stones' mysteries: child-sized, misshapen imps with filthy long hair, bandy goat legs and burning red eyes (Infernal Might 10, Animal), once korrigan corrupted by their own wickedness. They read the strange letters on the rocks that show only by starlight on moonless nights, dance orgies among the stones and vanish into regiones by dawn. They make moon-bright silver coins that vanish at daybreak to lure the greedy into ambush, conjure false vis that answers a simple Intellego Vim but melts away under closer study, and compel up to ten victims to dance with them till sunrise, often to death. They attack three to a victim, often with worse demons. Their unholy night is the first Wednesday in May, when they make blood sacrifice and the Infernal aura reaches 6; to come near then is suicide.

Magi of Hermetic geometry and astrology come seeking insight, others suspect fertility magic, and a Breakthrough might unlock the stones. Jacques Vert of Merinita suggested the Nains were dead Diedne dreaming in faerie flesh; nobody believed him, and about fifty years ago he disappeared among the stones one moonless night, hunting the legendary, unnamed treasure of Carnac.

levels.name: The avenues
levels.notes: Among the stones themselves the aura is 6 or higher by day, and many regiones are known.

levels.name: The heath by night
levels.notes: After dusk the Magic aura gives way to an Infernal one; it reaches 6 on the first Wednesday in May.

neighbours.secrets: Rumours say Diedne fled into the regiones, or that the stones hold portals, like Mercere Portals, to other far-off stone rows, through which the surviving Diedne may one day return for revenge.

neighbours.name: St Cado's Pillar and the Giant of Kerderf
neighbours.summary: North-east of Ploëmel, beside the petrified Giant of Kerderf, stands a lone pillar named for St Cado, which women who wish to conceive rub themselves against. The pillar yields Creo vis, of interest for what it shows of fertility cults, and perhaps a link to a magic that could undo the sterility a longevity ritual brings.

neighbours.name: County of Nantes
neighbours.summary: The country round Nantes on the Loire, hardly Breton at all: few Bretons live there, and its Frankish people feel closer to Anjou and Poitou. The road to Rennes runs through forest with little settlement; at Blain two minor trade roads cross, the old Roman one better than one would expect, and a leper house hides in the Gâvre Forest nearby. Redon, where several rivers meet, is the Vilaine's highest seaport and a market for a wide area.

neighbours.name: The Grey Stones of St Just
neighbours.summary: Several groups of grey stones on the high ground by the village of St Just, north of Redon and west of the Vilaine, in a small Magic aura of 3.

neighbours.name: The Grande Brière
neighbours.summary: A huge peat marsh behind the coastal sands between the Loire and Vilaine estuaries, rich in fish, eels and wildfowl but almost empty of people, with a few firm islands. On one, Kerbourg in the south-west, stands a covered alley of megaliths with a weak Magic aura (its strength is not given). The fortress of Ranrouët is being built on the north side; Guérande overlooks the south-west edge, and on the rocky ridge between its salt marsh and the sea salt is worked in a small way.

neighbours.name: Duke of Brittany
neighbours.summary:
Peter I of Dreux holds the duchy by his marriage to Alice, heir of the old ducal house, and rules as regent for her son. Brittany won free of the English crown after King John was rumoured to have murdered his nephew Arthur of Brittany, the duke whom Philip Augustus had backed against him. Rennes, famous for holding out against Normandy, is the capital now; Nantes was Alain Crookbeard's and Vannes Nominoé's.

The arms shown are the plain ermine Brittany bears in later years; Peter's own shield is the checky of Dreux with an ermine quarter. The duchy holds over six hundred mottes and forty great castles, and the barons were bloodily brought to heel by Henry II.

neighbours.name: Baron of Penthièvre
neighbours.summary: Lord of the barony along the rugged middle of the north coast and the forested hills behind it, from his seat at Lamballe on the trade road from Rennes to St Brieuc. His land is sparsely peopled, and Bréhat, the Seven Isles and the Rose Coast lie within it.

neighbours.name: Baron of Fougères
neighbours.summary: Lords of the strong castle on a spit of land in a bend of the Nançon below the town of Fougères, long the frontier with France. Raoul II of Fougères led the Breton barons who rose against Henry II's takeover; his castle was razed after a three-month siege, but he survived and began rebuilding at once.

neighbours.name: Count of Léon
neighbours.summary: Lord of Brittany's poor north-western tip, woodland and bleak moor round muddy estuaries and wreck-strewn coasts, with his home at the see of St-Pol-de-Léon. Brest castle, lately strengthened on Roman foundations, guards his bay.

neighbours.name: Lord Heusaff of Ushant
neighbours.summary: Head of the Heusaff family, an ancient Breton line that owns the Isle of Ushant and its only village, Lampaul, whose fishing keeps the family. The lord is a dashing young nobleman with some off-putting habits; the fishermen have little to do with the family and do not know its 'castle' is a magical place.
neighbours.secrets: Lord Heusaff is Harpax, Primus of House Tytalus, in a deep cover disguise taken from Buliste. Through the role he governs Fudarus's vis and coin.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Dol
neighbours.summary: The see of St Samson, one of the seven Welsh founders and a station of the Tro Briez, in the small town of Dol on a cliff above the marsh. A fortified cathedral to the saint is being built. Mount Dol, just north, is shunned by Christians.

neighbours.name: Bishop of St Malo
neighbours.summary: The see seated since 1144 in the Church of St Vincent, when the new town on the point took the name of St Malo and old Aleth, where the Welsh St Maclou converted the Gauls in the sixth century, was rededicated to St Servan. A station of the Tro Briez.

neighbours.name: Bishop of St Brieuc
neighbours.summary: The see of St Stephen's Cathedral in St Brieuc, a station of the Tro Briez for St Broch, whose blessed fountain is beside the place where he lived.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Tréguier
neighbours.summary: The see of the Church of St Tugdual at Tréguier, on terraces between the Jaudy and the Guindy; a station of the Tro Briez.

neighbours.name: Bishop of St-Pol-de-Léon
neighbours.summary: The bishopric St Paul the Aurelian founded; its twelfth-century cathedral bears his name; a station of the Tro Briez. The saint tamed the dragon of Batz with his stole. When Duke Mark refused him one of the seven bells that summoned his castle, a fisherman soon landed a great fish with a bell in its mouth and gave it to the saint; that bell and the others are lost.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Quimper
neighbours.summary: The see of St Corentine, first bishop of King Gradlon's new capital and a station of the Tro Briez. The saint lived on a magic fish caught daily from the river: he ate half and threw the rest back, and next morning it was whole. The fish (Divine Might 2, Animal) may still be nearby and might show itself to a deserving seeker.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Vannes
neighbours.summary: The see of the Cathedral of St Peter in Vannes, the largest town of Brittany, and the station of the Tro Briez for St Patern.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Rennes
neighbours.summary: The church of St Peter inside the walls of Rennes, the ducal capital, founded in the sixth century on a Romano-Gallic temple.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Nantes
neighbours.summary: The cathedral of Nantes, a place of martyrdom: in 843 pagan raiders slaughtered the bishop and his whole congregation there. Nantes is a political and church centre.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St Mélaine
neighbours.summary: An abbey within the walls of Rennes.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St Magloire, Léhon
neighbours.summary: A monastery beside a castle at Léhon, just up the Rance from Dinan, founded by Nominoé in 850. Badly damaged by the Vikings and soon rebuilt, it has lately been enlarged in the new style by Geoffroy of Corseul.

neighbours.name: Basilica of St Savior, Dinan
neighbours.summary: Raised in the twelfth century by a crusader in thanks for his safe return from the Holy Land, it shows eastern features of building unknown elsewhere in these parts.

neighbours.name: Monastery of Paimpont
neighbours.summary: A small monastery set inside Brocéliande to counter the forest's other powers, with little success so far.

neighbours.name: Priory of Marmoutier, Lamballe
neighbours.summary: A priory at Lamballe, the Baron of Penthièvre's seat, which also has a church of Our Lady.

neighbours.name: Chapel of Our Lady, Fougères
neighbours.summary: A chapel in Fougères whose statue shows Our Lady suckling the Christ child; some mothers praying before it have been miraculously helped.

neighbours.name: Churches of Langon
neighbours.summary: Langon's church of St Peter and its chapel of St Agatha, whose fabric takes in the walls of a Romano-Gallic temple of Venus; the Young Ladies stand on the moor nearby.

neighbours.name: Templar chapels of Lanleff and Brélévenez
neighbours.summary: A round chapel built by the Templars at Lanleff in the eleventh century and the church of Brélévenez at Lannion in the twelfth, raised to cleanse the coast of the Diedne's diabolic taint.
neighbours.secrets: Rumour says a Quaesitor suggested the building to the Templars.

neighbours.name: Chapel of Our Lady of Haut
neighbours.summary: A chapel two miles south-east of Moncontour where an unusual number of healing saints are petitioned: St Mamertus for colic, St Livertin and St Eugenia for headaches, St Leobinus for the eyes, St Méen for madness, St Hubert for sores and St Houarniaule for fear. It is hung with offerings, mostly wooden carvings of the body parts healed, and has a Dominion aura of 5, higher than a chapel's usual.

neighbours.name: Our Lady of Deliverance, Quintin
neighbours.summary: The main church of Quintin, whose statue of Our Lady of Deliverance draws expectant mothers praying for her protection in childbirth.

neighbours.name: Cistercians of Boquen, Quenécan and Gouarec
neighbours.summary: Three Cistercian monasteries hidden deep in the forests of the Central Argoat.

neighbours.name: Monastery of the Lorge Forest
neighbours.summary: A Benedictine house hidden in the Lorge Forest.

neighbours.name: Chapel of St Briac, Bourbriac
neighbours.summary: A forest chapel where St Briac is prayed to for those who suffer fits.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St Matthew's Point
neighbours.summary: A sixth-century monastery at the western point of Léon, with a village grown round it. It once held the head of St Matthew, a relic that calms storms at sea, but no one has seen it for centuries.

neighbours.name: Abbey of Daoulas
neighbours.summary: An abbey on the east shore of the bay of Brest, founded in 500 by followers of St Columba, destroyed by Vikings in the tenth century and lately rebuilt; a few men live there under the Rule of St Augustine.

neighbours.name: Abbey of Landévennec
neighbours.summary: The abbey St Guénolé founded in the fifth century at the east end of the Crozon peninsula.

neighbours.name: Abbey of Le Relecq
neighbours.summary: A Cistercian monastery on the eastern edge of the Arrée Mountains.

neighbours.name: Church of King Salomon's Martyrdom
neighbours.summary: A small church on the south-eastern fringe of the Arrée Mountains where King Salomon was martyred in the ninth century.

neighbours.name: Monastery of Locronan
neighbours.summary: A monastery by the pilgrimage of Locronan, where pilgrims climb the hill on St Ronan's daily path; it lodges them, stands in a forest the druids held sacred, and takes in brothers from other houses who need a change of scene.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St-Gildas-de-Rhuys
neighbours.summary: The monastery St Gildas founded in the sixth century on the southern arm of the Gulf of Morbihan. Peter Abélard withdrew here and found it wild and full of dangerous beasts, its language strange and ugly, and its monks unruly.

neighbours.name: Chapel of St Cado
neighbours.summary: A chapel by the Étel estuary where the deaf spend a night on a stone bed with a stone pillow, hoping for a cure.

neighbours.name: Church of St Cornelius, Carnac
neighbours.summary: The village church of Carnac, where the people bar the doors and pray till dawn every Midsummer night while the dead process outside; even its churchyard then falls under an Infernal aura of 5.

neighbours.name: Our Lady of Josselin
neighbours.summary: A wooden statue of the Virgin found in a bramble bush near Josselin castle on the Oust. Our Lady once came as a ragged beggar asking for water; the village women set their dogs on her, and their shouting turned to dogs' howls. Every Pentecost the women must beg forgiveness before the statue or the curse returns.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St Savior, Redon
neighbours.summary: The abbey founded in 832 at Redon, where several rivers meet.

neighbours.name: Church of St Aubin, Guérande
neighbours.summary: Built over a baptistery used in converting the local pagans, with a Merovingian sarcophagus in its crypt.

neighbours.name: Rennes
neighbours.summary: A small city on the Vilaine at the heart of the duchy, known for its resistance to Normandy and now the ducal capital, with the church of St Peter and the Abbey of St Mélaine inside its walls.

neighbours.name: Nantes
neighbours.summary: A city on the Loire, important in Roman times and before, now a political and church centre with a Frankish people closer in feeling to Anjou and Poitou than to Brittany. Alain Crookbeard made it his capital.

neighbours.name: Vannes
neighbours.summary: Brittany's largest town, on the Marle near the Gulf of Morbihan, Nominoé's capital in the ninth century, with its Cathedral of St Peter.

neighbours.name: St Malo
neighbours.summary: A small port on the point where the drowned Rance meets the sea, pushed out toward the water and walled against the Vikings; a bishop's seat since 1144, beside old Aleth, now St Servan.

neighbours.name: Dinan
neighbours.summary: A small port at the head of the Rance, with the crusader's Basilica of St Savior; the castle and abbey of Léhon are just upriver, and Roman Corseul five miles west.

neighbours.name: Dol
neighbours.summary: A small town on a cliff at the south edge of the marsh, where a fortified cathedral of St Samson is being built; Mount Dol rises to the north and the menhir of Champ-Dolent stands to the south.

neighbours.name: St Brieuc
neighbours.summary: A small port on a plateau cut by the Gouet and the Gouëdic, with a weekly market, two fairs a year, St Stephen's Cathedral and St Broch's fountain.

neighbours.name: Fougères
neighbours.summary: A town clinging to steep slopes above its baron's castle, on the old border with France in a forest crowded with megaliths.

neighbours.name: Lamballe
neighbours.summary: The Baron of Penthièvre's seat on the one trade road through the forest of Hunaudaye, with a church of Our Lady and a priory of Marmoutier.

neighbours.name: Tréguier
neighbours.summary: A town on terraces above the Jaudy and the Guindy, round the Church of St Tugdual.

neighbours.name: Lannion
neighbours.summary: A small town on the Léguer, with the Templars' church of Brélévenez.

neighbours.name: Loudéac
neighbours.summary: A small market town at a central crossroads, the trading hub of a wide forest country, with an animal fair twice a year.

neighbours.name: Moncontour
neighbours.summary: A market town under a castle on a spur where two valleys meet, near the chapel of Our Lady of Haut.

neighbours.name: Quintin
neighbours.summary: A small market town on terraces of the Gouët valley, where flax is grown, with Our Lady of Deliverance and the Long Rock nearby and a small castle at Robien.

neighbours.name: St-Pol-de-Léon
neighbours.summary: The Count of Léon's home and the see of St Paul the Aurelian, across the water from the isle of Batz.

neighbours.name: Brest
neighbours.summary: A port at the mouth of the Élorn on the north shore of a nearly landlocked bay; the Romans fortified it, and the castle built there in the eleventh century has lately been strengthened.

neighbours.name: Landerneau
neighbours.summary: The main port of the Arrée country, at the head of the Élorn estuary.

neighbours.name: Lampaul
neighbours.summary: Ushant's only settlement, a small fishing village owned by the Heusaff family; its catch is Fudarus's main supply.

neighbours.name: Quimper
neighbours.summary: The chief town of Cornouaille, founded by King Gradlon after Is drowned; the see of St Corentine.

neighbours.name: Carhaix-Plouguer
neighbours.summary: The Roman Vorgium, grown where seven roads met in the valley between the Arrée and the Black Mountains, and the only sizeable settlement for miles.

neighbours.name: Redon
neighbours.summary: The highest port on the Vilaine for seagoing ships, where several rivers meet, a market for a wide area, round the Abbey of St Savior.

neighbours.name: Blain
neighbours.summary: A small castle and a busy market where two minor trade roads cross on the forest road from Nantes to Rennes.

neighbours.name: Guérande
neighbours.summary: A settlement overlooking the south-west edge of the Grande Brière, with St Aubin's church and small salt workings on the ridge toward the sea.

neighbours.name: The Foutins
neighbours.summary: Iasper of Exspectatio's mundane family, a big clan of local roustabouts and ne'er-do-wells: not criminals by nature, but gifted at finding trouble. Iasper stays close to them and is often called on to settle things with the authorities.

details.wants: A good brawl and a way out of the trouble that follows
details.offers: Muscle and local connections; their kinsman Iasper smooths things over

neighbours.name: The Cabal of the Laden Cart
neighbours.summary: A secret cabal of Tytalus magi, from Normandy and beyond, formed to entrap Death. Some members mean it literally, others as a fight against disease and the ravages of time. Its agents listen across Brittany for anyone who hears the creak of the Ankeu's cart, and a member soon calls on whoever does.

details.rules: Members are anonymous, meet in disguise or not at all, and write rather than meet
details.wants: To trap Death and hold it to ransom, or to defeat disease and age

neighbours.secrets: Kybella founded it twelve years ago after a Twilight vision of Death reaping all Europe; the others assume she is a member but never know which disguise is hers. She and another theurgist of her line mean to imprison the Ankeu. If they succeed, Death will not take kindly to being tamed; the cabal may already have caught a night spirit that is not Death, which must be freed far from Brittany. Iasper is seeking to join.

neighbours.name: The Web of Fudarus
neighbours.summary: House Tytalus's vast network of spies, informants, mercenaries and suppliers of unusual goods and services, run from Fudarus and the root of much of the House's strength. Agents rarely know one another: in Paris two merchant partners scheme against each other for patrons who are secretly the same magus, and the Dyers' Guild, won from Florum's agents, is Fudarus's.

details.wants: Knowledge of everything that moves in the Order and the Tribunal
details.offers: Information, unusual goods and services, mercenaries

neighbours.secrets: Buliste controls the network and speaks mind to mind with several key agents; Harpax, without it, cannot steer much of the House's business and has jailed at least one agent on false charges.

neighbours.name: The Decimi
neighbours.summary: The Tytali who back Harpax and wear the tenth Primus's sigil, the stronger party in the Normandy Tribunal, where Harpax buys loyalty with Fudarus's vis and coin. Choosing a side is a matter of taste rather than merit, and Tytali of the two camps praise their champions so loudly that outsiders who try to mediate suspect a joke at their expense.

details.wants: Harpax recognised as sole Primus of House Tytalus

neighbours.name: The Fideli
neighbours.summary: The Tytali loyal to Buliste's purple banner, strongest across the Order as a whole, where her web of spies keeps her at the centre of Fudarus's power. Normandy's Tytali have mostly declared for one Primus or the other but leave the two to settle it between themselves.

details.wants: Buliste recognised as sole Prima of House Tytalus

neighbours.name: The Duchy of Normandy
neighbours.summary:
The northern duchy on the Channel coast, its shore a mix of sand and sheer white cliffs with England a hazy enemy across the water. Brittany and Maine lie south, the royal demesne and Flanders east. It is a land of heavy forest and many castles, cleared for farming mainly in the Seine basin in the east; its regions are the Seine basin, the county of Bayeux, the Cotentin peninsula and the small county of Avranches, with uplands in the south.

Gallic tribes held it first, and the faerie folk they once worshipped still remember them fondly. Rome made it Secunda Provincia Lugdunensis; the Franks made it part of Neustria; in the ninth and tenth centuries Norse raiders overran it, settled, and their chief became its duke. Since then it has been the French crown's sometime ally and frequent enemy, until Philip II took it from the English king in 1203 and 1204.

Lutins, small servile goblins (Faerie Might 5, Aquam), are common in the Norman faerie courts and in villages without a church. They clean houses in return for offal or clean water, avoid being seen, know everything in the room they stand in, can make a floor slick with suds, and carry a pawn of Aquam vis in the heart. All of them dread a 'goblin duke of Normandy' of whom the Order knows nothing.

Living covenants: Confluensis on the Cotentin, its vassal Dragon's Rest at the mouth of the Seine, and Montverte in the southern uplands. The ruins of Aedes Salii, Baiocassium, Baiocassium Minor, Pagus, Rotomagus and the Orchard of Sour Apples (where Confluensis now stands) lie here too.

neighbours.name: The Seine Basin
neighbours.summary:
The fertile heart of the duchy: the counties of Rouen, Lisieux and Evreux along the winding Seine, the river road from Paris to the sea, with Dragon's Rest at its mouth. Prosperous towns line the river and its tributaries. Most of the old forest was felled long ago, leaving fragments such as the Forest of Lyons.

Low stone walls split the fields into small plots, the bocage that sets Normandy apart from the Paris country. Wheat and oats make the bread; barley for beer is fickle and its failures leave peasants in debt, and frost often kills the autumn wheat, so the fields are resown with oats in spring. Cattle thrive on the grass, and the monks brought vines: much thin Norman wine goes downriver by barge to the towns but is not exported. A covenant that boosts its farms or its wine with Creo Herbam may find peasants at its gate wanting the same.

neighbours.name: The Forest of Lyons
neighbours.summary: A surviving fragment of the primordial forest of the Seine basin, a favourite hunting ground of the Norman nobility. A castle stands at its heart, and building it destroyed the spirit of the forest.
neighbours.secrets: The wild woodsmen say the forest is not dead and will rise one day to take back its heart.

neighbours.name: The Haunted Bridges of the Seine
neighbours.summary: Ruined fortified bridges at the Seine's narrows, built to stop Viking ships rowing upstream. Most have been quarried for farms and town houses, but a few are kept up as tollhouses. Ghosts of Norse and Frankish warriors are said to haunt several of them, and silently act out their deaths again by the light of the waning moon.

neighbours.name: The County of Bayeux
neighbours.summary:
A forested county west of the Seine basin, its villages set in cleared valleys round a monastery or a manor; its two large towns, Caen and Bayeux, lie near the coast. The ruin of the Diedne covenant Baiocassium is in the forest. The people grow more numerous each generation and the forest shrinks before them.

Pigs outnumber every other beast and run half wild in the woods. Each autumn the villages cull and salt them for winter, but woodland faeries claim the swine as theirs, and wise headmen honour the local court with a feast or a payment before the cull begins, a custom the Church distrusts and discourages.

St Vigor, bishop here in the early sixth century, destroyed a pagan temple that was still in use. The faeries of Bayeux have never forgiven it and have schemed ever since to break the Divine's hold on the county.

neighbours.name: Courts of the White Ladies
neighbours.summary:
A scatter of faerie regiones near the town of Bayeux, ruled by the white ladies, a coterie of Sidhe said to be sisters of the Lady of the Lake. They live for dancing and are always hunting for mortal partners: a lady and her minstrels wait at a narrow place near their court, a bridge, a ford or a gorge, and stop a passing man to ask him to dance.

A man who refuses, or treads on her feet, is flung from the road by her mocking court; a fine dancer is rewarded, and may be asked to the great ball one of the ladies holds for the others every spring equinox. Who brings the best partner there decides which lady is foremost for the coming year.

neighbours.name: The Cotentin Peninsula
neighbours.summary:
A thinly peopled, poor peninsula, much of it foul swamp and marsh, with a few castles and towns on the dry ground. Confluensis, the great Quaesitorial covenant, stands on the peninsula; the ruin of Pagus lies near Cherbourg, and a chapter house of the Rhine's Fengheld at Cherbourg controversially harvests some of Pagus's old vis sources.

Anyone crossing the swamps rolls Stamina against 3 or catches the fen ague: a Heavy Wound with shaking, chills and endless fever. Hermetic magic can cure it.

neighbours.name: The Forest of Brix
neighbours.summary: Forest south of Cherbourg where packs of savage faerie wolves ambush travellers. The villagers who live in it walk its paths safely.

neighbours.name: The Hague-Dicke
neighbours.summary: A Norse earthwork of the ninth century cutting off the north-west tip of the Cotentin, once barracks for raiders stranded by winter seas and a staging post in the raiding season. Now it is overgrown and unmanned, and even its line is uncertain. Rumour says raiders too laden with monastery loot buried treasure along it.

neighbours.name: The Vacant Castle
neighbours.summary:
A castle on the Cotentin left empty since 1204, now the lair of a monstrous she-creature of Grendel's kin, freed by one of King John's vassals as he fled, who stalks its corridors for human flesh. A Hermetic expedition in 1218 lost several grogs without finding her for certain, but found a strong Magic aura.

The expedition means to propose at the next Tribunal that colonists found a covenant here. The crown's officials would want the castle back in the feudal order, so settlers would do well to get a royal grant first.

neighbours.name: The County of Avranches
neighbours.summary: The small county on Normandy's southern border with Brittany. Its see is the town of Avranches on the Couesnon, but its great holy place is the Benedictine abbey of Mont St. Michel at the river's mouth.

neighbours.name: Mont St. Michel
neighbours.summary:
A rocky islet at the mouth of the Couesnon on the Breton border, crowned by a Benedictine abbey that draws many pilgrims. Once called Mount Tombe, it was a ritual site of the druids who came before House Diedne, until in 708 the archangel Michael appeared to Aubert, bishop of Avranches, and bade him desecrate the pagan graves and build a chapel. Aubert was slow to obey but finished in 709. His relics, kept here, include his skull, pierced where the angel struck him for his delay.

Hermetic scholars think Aubert destroyed a Magic aura and that taking his relics away might in time revive it, but fear of the Divine and of the Diedne taint has kept every magus away.

At low tide pilgrims cross less than a mile of sand to it, dangerous with quicksand (William the Conqueror had to be pulled out). Then its Divine aura is 4; at high tide it is a regio of 8.

levels.name: The Mont at high tide
levels.see: From the shore an image of the abbey is still seen, but it does not show what happens inside.
levels.enter: Only at low tide: at high tide no one may enter or leave, not even by flying or swimming.
levels.notes: When the tide is in and the sands lie under thirty feet of water, the whole abbey passes into a Divine regio.

neighbours.secrets: The Uncovered Crypt: a magus dreams of the archangel pointing to the Mont, with headaches that halve her Study and Lab Totals until she goes. As she arrives, builders open a crypt under a tower: a dozen skeletons and an untitled Holy Magic Theory summa (Level 3, Quality 17). Whoever studies it is visited by Michael, who means to replace Hermetic magic, which he thinks pagan, with a Divine kind.

neighbours.name: The Green Mount of Montverte
neighbours.summary: A rocky hill in the uplands of southern Normandy, crowned by a sprawling Norman keep built on an old Carolingian fort, a smaller copy of the mount of Laon. Concentric walls step down the slopes with exotic hanging gardens among them, watered by a spring near the top that an early magus is said to have called forth, running down in a web of little streams. The hill is at once lovely and grim. The baron's large village lies in the valley below.

neighbours.name: Duke of Normandy (held by the Crown)
neighbours.summary:
The Normans held their duchy to be an allod, given outright to the duke, which the French crown did not always accept. Since the conquest of 1203 to 1204 there has been no duke: the King rules Normandy directly and simply takes the duke's seat at the head of the feudal table, leaving the vassals' ties much as they were. Many lesser Anglo-Norman lords still hold land on both sides of the Channel, but Philip keeps the strategic places for himself and a few close allies. The English claimant is Henry III.

The duchy was always heavily armed. The dukes hired Flemish, Norse and German mercenaries for great campaigns, whose captains often became vassals, and the bishop of Bayeux alone has a hundred knights. The dukes tried to keep their vassals from private war, judging quarrels in their court, where the usual penalty was loss of land; when war came anyway, the beaten could not be ransomed or plundered nor their houses and mills burnt. Philip upholds these rules.

Most large towns hold charters letting their burgesses elect mayors, councils and courts for a collective rent; Philip has confirmed the great towns' charters, but many small ones were sold by King John in his last scramble for money before 1204 and the crown likes them less. A covenant that sheltered under a small town's easily led magistrates, or was itself chartered by John, may need new arrangements if the charter goes.
neighbours.ruler: King Philip II of France, in the duke's place

neighbours.name: Henry III of England
neighbours.summary: The young King of England, who still claims the duchy of Normandy his father John lost to the French in 1204. England, conquered by the Normans in 1066, broods across the Channel as France's troublesome enemy.

neighbours.name: Bailli of Rouen
neighbours.summary:
Jean de la Porte, appointed in 1219: one of the King's bailli, the salaried professional administrators of the bailliages that roughly follow the old Norman counties. Bailli are paid several hundred pounds a year, are drawn on purpose from neither the great families nor the Church (some are minor nobles or former officers), and are as a rule honest and loyal to the King. None is a Norman. From the 1220s, if history holds, they serve only three or four years.

The bailli know the Order exists and where some covenants are, though nothing more. If magic brings disaster on the duchy, they may come to those covenants for help, or for suspects; otherwise a covenant that pays its taxes and leaves the feudal order alone is of no interest to them.

None is a Norman. From the 1220s, if history holds, they serve only three or four years.

The bailli know the Order exists and where some covenants are, though nothing more. If magic brings disaster on the duchy, they may come to those covenants for help, or for suspects; otherwise a covenant that pays its taxes and leaves the feudal order alone is of no interest to them.

neighbours.name: Baron of Montverte
neighbours.summary:
Lord of the green mount, descended from Haland, the un-Gifted Norse elder brother of the founding magus Harivald. His family took their name from the hilltop castle the brothers seized, and the magi of Montverte have lived in it beside them since 941. His household is the covenant's covenfolk, and his soldiers are rather too many and too well armed for a baron. The magi are called 'the resident scholars' or 'our valued guests', and the steward Edward sits at his side.

His peers have quarrelled with him often over what the castle does, but its walls have won every war. The magi swear him no oath and say he runs his own affairs.
neighbours.secrets: For generations the family has been wholly, and unknowingly, ruled by the magi through persuasion and subtle magic. The baron's high chair, centuries old, was enchanted by an early magus with a Mentem effect that keeps whoever sits in it compliant; long use has left a line of slightly Warped barons.

neighbours.name: Archbishop of Rouen
neighbours.summary:
Metropolitan of a province whose borders almost match the duchy's, a hard-fought field in the conversion of the pagans. The first bishop, Nicaise, was martyred on arrival from Rome in the mid-third century; St Mellon founded the see, which became an archdiocese in 744. Sainted bishops include St Ouen (641-684), who converted or destroyed many pagans, and St Romanus, who overcame the Gargouille.

The archbishop since 1208 is Master Robert Poulain, a theologian; if history holds, Thibaud d'Amiens follows him in 1222. He holds the Order of Hermes heretical but has only argued the point with his bishops, who are not persuaded. The Norman church accepted Philip as king, by the Pope's leave; Philip has not meddled in elections and has given generously to religious houses, but in 1218 he made the archbishop yield the King's officers from excommunication.

Each year Rouen's clergy pick one condemned prisoner to be pardoned before St Romanus's relics, remembering the prisoner who helped the saint drag the Gargouille, a scaled beast of the Seine with pale blue eyes, back to the town to be burned.
neighbours.secrets: The Gargouille: townsmen are found dead near a covenant and the magi blamed. Archbishop Robert calls the magi the Gargouilles of the age, frees half a dozen condemned men and marches with them on the covenant behind the shrine of St Romanus (Faith Points 5). Harming him could start a crusade against the Order in Normandy; if the magi are innocent, someone framed them.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Bayeux
neighbours.summary: A theologian elected in 1206, one of the Jumieges-trained scholar bishops who know of the Order and have met Hermetic scholars. The see, founded by St Exuperius in the first century, is one of the oldest in Mythic Europe; Bishop Odo of Conteville, the Conqueror's brother, built the fortified cathedral, fought at Hastings and had the great tapestry made. The bishop has the service of a hundred knights: twenty owed to the ducal host, ten to the royal host and seventy for his own use.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Coutances
neighbours.summary: A canonist elected in 1208, one of the Jumieges-trained scholar bishops who know of the Order and have met Hermetic scholars. His diocese takes in the Cotentin.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Lisieux
neighbours.summary: A canonist elected in 1218, one of the Jumieges-trained scholar bishops who know of the Order and have met Hermetic scholars.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Avranches
neighbours.summary: A former local dean, elected in 1212. Mont St. Michel lies in his diocese; his predecessor Aubert built its first chapel at the archangel's command in 709.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Evreux
neighbours.summary: A former local dean, elected in 1203 and now old. If history holds, he dies in 1220 and the chapter elects another local dean, Ralph de Cierrey.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Sées
neighbours.summary: The see's former archdeacon, elected in 1201 and now old. If history holds, he dies in 1220 and Gervase of Chichester, a foreigner the Pope favours, is elected: a sore point, since the foreign bishops before Sylvester squandered the diocese's treasury.

neighbours.name: Rouen Cathedral
neighbours.summary:
The seat of the archdiocese, on a site where the Romans built a church in the third century and every age since has added to it. Many Norman nobles lie in its crypt, Rollo among them; some magi guess the noble dead are rich in Rego vis, but no one has dared dig them up.

It keeps the original copies of works written at Rouen: St Victricius's De Laude Sanctorum (Theology summa, Level 5, Quality 11) and Liber Regularum (Civil and Canon Law summa, Level 3, Quality 10), and Hugh of Amiens's Contra Haereticos (Divine Lore summa, Level 3, Quality 10, bound with an Infernal Lore tractatus of Quality 8).

neighbours.name: Abbey of Jumieges
neighbours.summary:
A Benedictine abbey on the north bank of the Seine below Rouen, founded by St Philibert in 634, burned by the Norsemen in the ninth century and lavishly endowed by the Norman dukes since. More than a thousand monks live there, with a sizeable town outside the walls to feed them. It is a great house of learning with large libraries of religious and philosophical works, and so many French bishops studied there that its abbot is a power in the kingdom's politics.

Norman histories are found in its library as in any cathedral or monastic library: William of Newburgh's Historia rerum Anglicarum (Area Lore: England summa L5 Q7, Area Lore: Normandy tractatus Q8); Orderic Vitalis's Ecclesiastical History (Area Lore: Normandy summa L4 Q8, Area Lore: England summa L3 Q8, Civil and Canon Law tractatus Q7); William of Jumieges's Historia Normannorum (Area Lore: Normandy summa L5 Q9, Area Lore: England tractatus Q7, some copies with a later Normandy tractatus Q8 bringing it to 1137); and Dudo of St Quentin's History of the Normans (Area Lore: Normandy summa L4 Q8 and two Normandy tractatus of Q8).

neighbours.name: Abbey of St. Wandrille
neighbours.summary: A large Benedictine abbey a day downstream of Jumieges. A Frankish count of the seventh century founded it; he and his wife renounced the world on the day they wed. It competes with Jumieges for noble patrons but is otherwise on good terms with it. Its monks first settled Mont St. Michel in 966.

neighbours.name: Bayeux Cathedral
neighbours.summary: Bishop Odo's fortified cathedral, which keeps his tapestry: really an embroidery nearly a hundred yards long and a yard high, its pictures captioned in Latin, telling the life of King Harold to his death at Norman hands. Magic was worked into its threads, and it is a +2 Sympathetic Connection to the Duke of Normandy and to the King of England.

neighbours.name: The Men's Abbey of Caen
neighbours.summary:
The fortified abbey William the Conqueror built at Caen, as Matilda built the Women's Abbey, the price of lifting the excommunication Pope Nicholas II laid on the cousins for marrying.

William lies here. He died at the priory of St Gervais in Rouen in 1087 after a fall from his horse; his body rotted and stank, his servants defiled it and his courtiers fled, an omen of the anarchy that followed. A fire broke out as the corpse reached Caen, and at the funeral the swollen body burst from its coffin and the bishops, choking, botched the rite.
neighbours.secrets: The Infernal Grave: an infernalist's belongings hold The Conquered Bastard (Infernal Lore tractatus, Quality 6), which says a demon inhabits William's corpse, helped him to his conquests and rotted his body, and was trapped in it by the botched rite; the infernalist's notes show he was trying to free her. Freeing or destroying her means digging William up and crossing the Church in Caen. The text may be a forgery, by demons or by rivals in the Tribunal, to drag the magi into an infernal plot.

neighbours.name: The Women's Abbey of Caen
neighbours.summary: The fortified abbey Matilda built at Caen, as William built the Men's Abbey, to win the lifting of their excommunication for marrying within the forbidden degrees.

neighbours.name: Abbey of Mont St. Michel
neighbours.summary:
The archangel's own foundation of the early eighth century, settled by Benedictines from St. Wandrille under Abbot Maynard in 966 with Duke Richard I's backing. Abbot Hildebert enlarged it from 1020; in 1203 the Duke of Brittany set a fire that ruined much of it, and Abbot Jordan has been rebuilding since 1210, work that if history holds will finish about 1230 (extra hands are always wanted). Its relics include St Aubert's holed skull and right arm.

Its founding is told in the anonymous Apparitio Sancti Michaelis Archangelis in Monte Tumba, a widely copied Divine Lore tractatus of Quality 11.

neighbours.name: Rouen
neighbours.summary:
Capital of the duchy, on the Seine, founded by the Romans beside a Gallic village as Rotomagus, chief city of Secunda Provincia Lugdunensis; a short-lived ninth-century covenant near it took the same name. Philip II took the town in 1203. Paris's Baltic shipping passes through, but the cross-Channel trade that made it rich has dwindled since the annexation, and in 1207 the slump led Philip to grant it a very generous charter to win support. It has many churches and the archbishop's cathedral.

A large community of Jewish moneylenders lived here until renegade knights of the Third Crusade killed many who would not convert. The survivors prospered for a while practising their faith in secret, but Philip's laws against the Jews have made them ever less safe. A few remain in trade, less openly than before; a magus who floods the markets with magical wealth will earn their anger.
neighbours.ruler: Mayor and council, under the King

neighbours.name: The Jewish families of Rouen
neighbours.summary: The few Jewish merchant families left in Rouen after the Third Crusade's massacres, now quietly in business under Philip II's harsh laws.

details.wants: Safety, and if the persecution becomes unbearable, flight to Iberia
details.offers: A large holding of Arabic and Hebrew texts, which they might trade for magical help to escape; ruthless magi might simply join the persecution and seize them

neighbours.name: Caen
neighbours.summary:
A town on the Orne that served William the Conqueror as his real capital, for its distance from Paris, and as the staging ground for his campaigns, the invasion of England among them. Caen Castle, begun in 1060, dominates it: some five hectares inside a high crenellated wall and dry moat, with a hall and keep of the 1120s and new towers and an inner wall round the keep added by Philip II.

In 1220 workmen are pulling down the old north gatehouse and tower and building new gates in the south and east walls; labourers, engineers and architects are always wanted. William's Men's Abbey and Matilda's Women's Abbey stand in the town.

neighbours.name: Bayeux
neighbours.summary: Once Baiocasses, chief town of the Gauls, taken by Rome in the first century BC. Fragments of Roman buildings still stand and much of the town is built of their stone; nothing Gallic remains, but the land remembers where it stood. In the duchy's early years it was the seat of rival Norse settlers who sometimes rose against Rouen; it is quiet now. Its mills serve the country round, and its cathedral keeps Odo's tapestry.
neighbours.secrets: Rumour puts a regio somewhere in the town that held the small Diedne vassal covenant Baiocassium Minor; no living magus admits to knowing where.

neighbours.name: Avranches
neighbours.summary: The seat of the diocese of Avranches, on the Couesnon near the Breton border, the town pilgrims pass through on the way to Mont St. Michel.

neighbours.name: Barfleur
neighbours.summary: A harbour town of the Cotentin whose shipyards built much of William the Conqueror's invasion fleet and have built warships and merchantmen ever since. Its waters are dangerous: in 1120 William, son of Henry I of England, drowned when his ship struck a rock leaving harbour. Sea ghosts haunt it, among them a spectral fleet that sails past in the worst winter storms, searching in vain for a berth.

neighbours.name: Cherbourg
neighbours.summary: The town at the north of the Cotentin, south of which lies the Forest of Brix. The ruined covenant of Pagus stood near it, and the Rhine covenant Fengheld has a chapter house here that claims some of Pagus's vis sources, to Confluensis's displeasure.

neighbours.name: Beauvoir
neighbours.summary: A chartered Norman community, a small forest community. Its charter is one of the many King John sold before 1204, which Philip II has not confirmed; a covenant that leans on its magistrates would be exposed if it were revoked.

neighbours.name: Laigle
neighbours.summary: A chartered Norman community, a small forest community. Its charter is one of the many King John sold before 1204, which Philip II has not confirmed; a covenant that leans on its magistrates would be exposed if it were revoked.

neighbours.summary: A chartered Norman community, a small forest community. Its charter is one of the many King John sold before 1204, which Philip II has not confirmed; a covenant that leans on its magistrates would be exposed if it were revoked.

neighbours.name: Conches
neighbours.summary: A chartered Norman community, little more than a village outside an abbey. Its charter is one of the many King John sold before 1204, which Philip II has not confirmed; a covenant that leans on its magistrates would be exposed if it were revoked.

neighbours.summary: A chartered Norman community, little more than a village outside an abbey. Its charter is one of the many King John sold before 1204, which Philip II has not confirmed; a covenant that leans on its magistrates would be exposed if it were revoked.

neighbours.summary: A chartered Norman community, little more than a village outside an abbey. Its charter is one of the many King John sold before 1204, which Philip II has not confirmed; a covenant that leans on its magistrates would be exposed if it were revoked.

neighbours.name: Claville
neighbours.summary: A chartered Norman community, really a large manor. Its charter is one of the many King John sold before 1204, which Philip II has not confirmed; a covenant that leans on its magistrates would be exposed if it were revoked.

neighbours.name: The White Ladies
neighbours.summary: Sidhe sisters, said to be kin of the Lady of the Lake, who rule faerie regiones about Bayeux and waylay men at bridges and fords to dance. Whoever brings the best partner to the spring equinox ball is foremost among them for a year.

details.wants: Excellent mortal dance partners
details.offers: Rewards for a fine dancer; a place at the equinox ball

neighbours.name: The Swine Court of Bayeux
neighbours.summary: The woodland faeries who claim the half-wild pigs of the Bayeux forest as theirs. Wise villages honour them before the autumn cull; they still nurse the grudge of St Vigor's broken temple and plot against the Divine in the county.

details.wants: Tribute before the cull; the Church's hold on Bayeux broken
details.offers: A peaceful cull

neighbours.name: Anjou
neighbours.summary:
The counties of Anjou, Touraine and Maine on the lower Loire, the heart of the old Angevin lands. Druid-led tribes fought the Romans here, every city keeps Roman traces, and Norse raids in the ninth and tenth centuries sacked the towns and filled the land with fortresses. Its greatest counts were Fulk Nerra, the Black Falcon (987 to 1040), and Henry, who became Henry II of England and ruled from the Scottish border to the Pyrenees. Philip II took Anjou from King John and had to win many of its castles one by one; there has been no count since 1203, the crown claims every comital right, and royal bailli govern it district by district, as in Normandy.

Castles, abbeys and churches crowd the river valleys, so that little besides the Church and the nobility seems to hold power; the forested uplands between (pine to the north, broadleaf to the south) are noble hunting grounds, full of menhirs and dolmens. The Loire is the great road, shrunk to braided streams round sandbanks in summer and flooding in spring and autumn, plied by flat-bottomed square-sailed boats and fished for eels and fowl. Its tributaries cut through soft white tufa to gravels that grow fine vines, and along many of them as many as half the people live in caves dug into the limestone cliffs.

The Hermetic covenants of the chapter are Oleron, Nidi and Atsingani; the ruins of Sinapis, Alcuin's Auberge, Ligurio, Nauche-Fleur and Vexatores lie in the two regions. The Way of St. James runs through Tours, Poitiers, Melle and Saintes to the Dordogne crossing at Libourne, with branches by Angers and Niort and from Poitiers by Angoulême and Aubeterre; pilgrims from England, Normandy and Brittany often come by sea to the Gironde ports. Travelling in a band of pilgrims is a good way for careful magi to pass unremarked.

neighbours.name: Aquitaine
neighbours.summary:
The largest duchy of France, over two hundred and forty miles from the Bay of Biscay to the upper Loire: Poitou, Limousin, Périgord, Saintonge and the Auvergne. The west is wooded limestone plateau cut by rivers running to the Loire or the Dordogne; the east is the Central Massif, hard volcanic upland and puys where only sheep and goats thrive. South-facing limestone slopes carry vineyards, and wine, truffles and walnut oil go down the rivers; behind the coastal dunes lie wide marshes. Castles guard every road and river and churches stand almost everywhere, so little land escapes the lords and the Dominion.

Charlemagne made a kingdom of Aquitaine in 778; by the tenth century its barons were feuding behind their walls and ignoring any overlord. Eleanor of Aquitaine brought the duchy to Louis of France in 1137 and, after their divorce, to Henry of Anjou in 1154, since when it has been the prize between the kings of France and England. The present duke is Henry III, King of England.

The Tribunal counts Aquitaine north of the Dordogne as its own, though the southern folk speak Dordonha, a tongue of Oc. Nidi is the only covenant down there, and it is older than the Grand Tribunal's ruling of 1103; any covenant founded that far south now would belong to Provence.

In the cemeteries of Berry, Limousin and the Dordogne stand lanterns of the dead, slender stone towers six or eight times as tall as they are wide, with a lamp lit on top each night for the holy dead; the custom began with a novice of Charlieu shown such a tower in a vision by his dead uncle. Tradition-minded grogs ask for one over a covenant's graveyard, but an angel sees one torn down if those beneath are unworthy.

neighbours.name: Béhuard Island
neighbours.summary: An island in the Loire south-west of Angers, where a small Christian oratory was built over an ancient shrine of a sea goddess. Locals come to pray for the rivermen, and their devotion has raised a Dominion aura that swamps the shrine's Magic aura of 2.

neighbours.name: The Mayenne Valley
neighbours.summary: North of Angers the River Mayenne runs through a valley too steep to build in and unfit for cave homes, so it is one of the few places near the city with no Dominion aura: a possible refuge or site for magi.

neighbours.name: The Menhir of Le Mans
neighbours.summary:
A striped, pinkish standing stone at the south corner of the west front of Le Mans cathedral, pitted with a few holes; seen side-on in the right light it looks like a hooded figure. The site was pagan before the church, and folk still think it lucky to put their fingers in the holes. A Seeker might study it for what it shows of old fertility rites.

Story seed: the cathedral clergy, unwilling to involve rival clerics or to speak openly, ask the magi through a go-between to take the stone away quietly.
neighbours.secrets:
The menhir was the heart of a fertility cult whose true rite is forgotten: at each equinox a sheep was killed and its blood poured over the stone; once dry, it scrapes off as several pawns of Creo vis. The first Christians meant to move it, but whoever tried met with a nasty accident, so they built it into the church. Its Magic aura was once 6 round the stone; with the cult gone it would be 4, but the cathedral's Dominion smothers it.

A year ago some drunken local lads rediscovered what the holes were really for, and their wives and sweethearts bore strong, healthy babies nine months later. The story has spread, others are trying their luck, and the Church wants it stopped.

neighbours.name: The Gallo-Roman Tower by Tours
neighbours.summary: A windowless Roman brick tower west of Tours, high on a ridge over the Loire's north bank, sixteen feet square and about a hundred feet tall. No one locally knows what it was for. The Magic aura is 1 at its foot and rises to 5 at the top.
neighbours.secrets: Roman soldiers built it during the conquest of Gaul as a lookout for a magician of the Cult of Mercury.

neighbours.name: The Valley of Empty Caves
neighbours.summary: An enclosed valley about four miles south of Azay-le-Rideau on the Indre, south-west of Tours, where the people round about live in cliff caves of white tufa. Its many damp caves stand empty, it holds a Magic aura of 4, and a steady source there yields a little Aquam vis: a likely site for a new covenant.

neighbours.name: The Faeries' Cave
neighbours.summary: A dolmen deep in the forest some six miles north-west of Tours: eight great stones holding up three huge slabs over a chamber twelve feet long and four high, with a cross-stone closing off a small private space at one end. Its Faerie aura of 3 rises to 5 while the fae are there; they feast in it at least once a year.

neighbours.name: The Nymphs' Shrine at Gennes
neighbours.summary: Beside the Roman amphitheatre at Gennes, downstream of Saumur, lies a small Magic regio holding a Gallo-Roman shrine.

levels.name: The shrine of the water cult
levels.notes: Several nymphs live here (aura not given). They gladly talk about the water cult that honoured them under Rome and may give Aquam vis to visitors who amuse, honour or serve them. They are attentive, persuasive and loath to lose male company, so a man may find it hard to leave.

neighbours.name: The Dolmen of Bagneux
neighbours.summary: The largest of the many menhirs and dolmens hidden in the wooded hills round Saumur: a chamber sixty-six feet long and twenty-three wide, walled by sixteen upright slabs and roofed by four flat stones on a central pillar. It has a low Magic aura, as do the other megaliths far enough from the Dominion.

neighbours.name: The Sarcophagus Rock of Doué-la-Fontaine
neighbours.summary: An outcrop south-west of Saumur whose stone holds Creo vis and keeps flesh from decay. Merovingian masons cut thousands of stone coffins from it, but its virtue has been forgotten.

neighbours.name: Mount Mercury
neighbours.summary: The highest point of the Vendée, the thinly peopled forest, moor and marsh of north-western Aquitaine, whose trade goes to Nantes. Its village of St. Michael has a church on the site of a shrine to Mercury, patron of travellers. Since a maga who sought out such places identified the old dedication, Redcaps have come here as pilgrims to honour Mercury or the saint and to look out over the forest to the ocean.

neighbours.name: The Vendée Marshes
neighbours.summary: The greatest of the Vendée marshes, over eighty square miles, where a few people live by fishing and fowling. Marmoutier's monks have a priory on higher ground at Sallertaine and there is a Benedictine abbey at Chauvet. The lord of Montaigu rules it from La Garnache on its north-eastern edge. The covenant of Ligurio stood here for about a century; little is left of it, its buildings sunk into the marsh.

neighbours.name: St. Hilary's Demon
neighbours.summary: Past the pine-held dunes the Vendée coast turns rocky. At the end of one promontory a cleft runs down to a cave far below the sea, where a demon is imprisoned: as the surf surges up the cleft his wailing can be heard, and at high tide in a strong wind he roars and flings great bursts of spray over the cliffs. Long ago the sea drowned the low land; the people prayed, and St. Hilary found the demon behind the floods, caught him and drove him beneath the waves.

neighbours.name: Noirmoutier
neighbours.summary: A low island off the coast just south of the Loire mouth, marshy in the middle, its southern tail reaching toward the mainland across a dangerous current. The whole isle has a Magic aura of 3, rising to 5 at a sheltered north-western beach once sacred to Gallic druidesses, whose name still keeps people away. A covenant here would eat well on seafood and could sell salt from the marshes.

neighbours.name: The Marsh of the Sèvre
neighbours.summary: Wide marshland north of La Rochelle about the rivers Vendée and Sèvre Niortaise, with the fortress of Niort beyond it to the east and the oak and beech of the Argenson Forest on the hills to the east and south. Five local abbeys have lately joined to drain its northern part for farmland.
neighbours.secrets: The drainage will damage or destroy several vis sources the abbeys know nothing of: moulted tail feathers of pintails wintering at one pool (Animal, 4 pawns a year); the leaves of an aspen that quiver in still air (Auram, 3); the oversized cones of one alder (Creo, 3); plume feathers of egrets nesting in a certain grove (Imaginem, 2); and the bark of a white poplar whose black diamond marks are unusually regular (Rego, 4).

neighbours.name: The Bougon Tumuli
neighbours.summary:
Six grassy mounds of stone and earth hidden in the forest about halfway between Niort and Poitiers. Locals think them haunted and keep away; they are an undiscovered pagan burial ground of great interest to some magi.

Three stand together: a large round mound over a domed chamber twenty-seven feet across, split by a slab set on edge; a long barrow with two burial places at each end; and a smaller round mound seventeen feet high over a chamber with a rectangular platform. Beyond a low earth bank lie the other three, with banks enclosing a rectangle about two hundred and sixty feet long that holds two small oval mounds, each with a passage to a square chamber; the sixth mound is entered from the east by a low passage to two chambers.
neighbours.secrets: A tribe long gone built it for a chieftain, his family and the retinue that would guard and serve them. Animals or dark-loving fae may have moved into a mound, or all may be undisturbed. The large mound holds the scant bones of some twenty hunters and warriors among scattered stones; the long barrow is empty; the smaller round mound holds the broken bones of one dismembered man, a shaman, in a filled pit by the platform; each small oval mound holds the remains of a woman with jet bracelets, the chief's daughters or concubines; and the last mound holds the chieftain and his wife. At least one mound probably has a ghost.

neighbours.name: The Roman Baths of Chassenon
neighbours.summary: The ruins of a Roman spa town west of Angoulême. A stretch of wall and the overgrown temple and theatre can be found by searching; the baths are easy to find, roofless but with walls, pools, hypocausts and tunnels, and the whole sequence of changing room, warm, hot, steam and cold rooms, plunge pools and exercise hall can still be traced. The healing water holds Creo vis, but it flows weakly and fitfully.
neighbours.secrets: When Christianity came, the pagan statues were thrown into the gutters and sewers, then buried when invaders pulled the town down. If the right god's statue is dug out of the old drains under the baths and set back in its temple, the water will flow strongly and steadily again.

neighbours.name: The Spring of Vésone
neighbours.summary: A spring on the south side of the River Isle at Le Cité, sacred before Christianity. Some locals know of it; it yields Aquam vis.

neighbours.name: The Truffle Oaks of Périgord
neighbours.summary: On the limestone plateaus round Le Cité and south to the Dordogne, a knobbly fungus grows about the roots of certain oaks: purplish-black outside, pale and white-veined within, earthy when fresh and foul when overripe. It is prized as an aphrodisiac and dug from December to March with pigs or dogs. The fungus is common, but the rare potent nodules hold Herbam vis.

neighbours.name: La Coloubre's Cave
neighbours.summary: A cave on the south bank of the Dordogne at Lalinde, above Bergerac, where the river runs through rapids. The dragon La Coloubre lived here, preying on those who walked round the rapids, until St. Front killed it and burned the body on the hill above. A chapel marks the spot and fires are lit there every year, perhaps a warning that keeps other dragons from moving in.

neighbours.name: The Painted Caves of the Vézère
neighbours.summary:
The Vézère winds south-west between high limestone cliffs to join the Dordogne near Limeuil. Hardly anyone lives in the valley; the only sizeable settlement is St. Christopher's Rock, halfway along, where folk live on five levels up the cliff in part-cave houses on ledges reached by stairs.

A broad Magic aura lies under the lower valley, reaching out to Rouffignac to the west and along the Beune valley to the east, and touches the surface at 1 in a few places.

levels.name: The fresh paintings
levels.enter: Through a chain of small linked caves and low passages
levels.notes: There is light enough to see without a lamp, and the pictures on the walls look newly made.

levels.name: The painted land
levels.notes: A wide open country of rolling hills, grassy plains, dense forest and broad rivers, full of animals, some familiar and some known only from the pictures on the cave walls.

neighbours.secrets:
Undiscovered caves and passages run beneath, many painted or carved with deer, horses, mighty bulls and huge beasts with great curved tusks; where the pictures are most vivid the aura is 5 or 6, aligned with Animal. Other caves are hung with coloured stone, stalactites, stalagmites and crystal, the finest with auras up to 6, one or two aligned with Imaginem. Bjornaer of Clan Ilfetu know a cave here that is an ancestor site, fit for House rituals.

A string of small caves and low passages leads into a regio.

neighbours.name: The Druids' Grove of Clermont
neighbours.summary: All that is left of the druids' sacred wood where Clermont now stands is a clump of stunted trees south-west of the cathedral, beside a market, where a mineral spring soaks the soil.

levels.name: The living grove
