levels.enter: Only when the moon is full, both in and out
levels.notes: A healthy grove of trees. A spring inside yields Terram vis.

neighbours.secrets: Some Diedne magi knew of it and found a way into a regio here.

neighbours.name: The Puy de Dôme
neighbours.summary: An extinct volcano west of the road south from Clermont, its steep sides forested. The summit shrine was Lug's, then Mercury's, and is now St. Barnabas's. Locals believe the sorcerers of the Auvergne meet there at dead of night, a memory of the Mercurian magicians of Rome. What is left of a Roman road climbs to the top.

levels.name: The roofless temple
levels.enter: Climb on foot, staying exactly on the Roman road
levels.notes: The temple of Mercury stands abandoned and roofless.

levels.name: The whole temple
levels.notes:
Aura not given.

Secrets
No one has found this level yet: here the temple is intact.

neighbours.secrets: Climbing on foot and keeping exactly to the Roman road crosses into a small regio. A higher level, where the temple is whole, and an older route up to Lug's shrine are still undiscovered.

neighbours.name: The Auvergne Volcanoes
neighbours.summary:
The ancient volcanoes west of the Clermont road: the Puy de Dôme, the Puy de Sancy and the Cantal mountains. Before there were people, great magical creatures of air, water, earth and fire fought here and left the dramatic landscape behind them.

Many lovely lakes, waterfalls and strange rocks have low Magic auras, and some yield vis: a rock at Tuillière shaped like giant sheaves of wheat holds Creo vis; a polished black basalt stone cast into Lake Pavin on the longest night of the year stirs up a fierce storm that leaves several pawns of Auram vis to collect; at Bort-les-Orgues, pebbles like little loaves and fruits caught now and then in the hollows called giants' cauldrons hold Rego vis, and the echo off the grey columns of rock holds Imaginem vis when the right sound is made.

neighbours.name: The Hot Springs of the Auvergne
neighbours.summary:
Hot springs and hot vapours at Royat, le Mont-Dore and la Bourboule, warmed by a mighty fire elemental that has lived deep underground for ages. The water eases skin complaints and aching joints, the vapour chest ailments: half an hour in either gives +3 to a recovery roll, but longer harms, for the water and vapour are hot and noxious.

Aquam, Auram, Creo and Ignem vis are gathered here, and the Tribunal leases them as tropaea.

neighbours.name: The Bailli of Anjou
neighbours.summary: Since 1203 there has been no Count of Anjou: King Philip claims all the count's old rights and duties and governs Anjou, Touraine and Maine through professional royal officers, each bailli ruling a district in his name. They answer to the king, not to the local barons, and many castles had to be taken by force before they would.

neighbours.name: Count John IV of Montoire
neighbours.summary: Lord of the castle that looks down on Vendôme from its rocky spur. An old spear with a short dark shaft and an outdated plain iron head hangs on his wall; thrown, it has no lift and always lands flat. Two old folk of the castle believe it is one of the spears of the abbey's legend.
neighbours.secrets: It is. The second lies forgotten in an old chest in the darkest corner of the oldest part of the abbey crypt, and a farmer's wife a few miles out treasures the third as an heirloom. Each is an Arcane Connection to the other two, and once all three are together, each drips a drop of red flame holding a pawn of Divine-tainted Ignem vis on the first Sunday after Pentecost. Swapping the count's for a new spear is easy, but negotiation is safer than theft.

neighbours.name: Angers
neighbours.summary: Capital of the county of Anjou on the River Maine and long the seat of Plantagenet power, built of the pale tufa of White Anjou and the dark schist and slate of Black Anjou. Henry II loved its fortress and founded its Hospital of St. John. A long stair climbs from the quay to the cathedral of St. Maurice. The abbeys of Ronceray (Fulk Nerra's foundation), St. Serge and St. Aubin stand in the city.

neighbours.name: Cathedral of St. Maurice, Angers
neighbours.summary: The bishop's church of Angers; a long stair climbs to it from the quay. Pilgrims pray here for relief from gout and cramp.

neighbours.name: The Abbeys of Angers
neighbours.summary: Three religious houses of the city: Ronceray, founded by Fulk Nerra, and the abbeys of St. Serge and St. Aubin.

neighbours.name: Chinon
neighbours.summary:
A wine town on the River Vienne below the great castle Henry II built along the wooded north bank, a quarter of a mile end to end; below the slope the streets follow the line of the river. The church is St. Maurice's, the cliffs to the east hold cave homes and the cave Chapel of St. Radegonde, and the Forest of Chinon lies beyond. Henry II died here in 1189, John married Isabelle of Angoulême here in 1200, and the Treaty of Chinon gave the town to Philip II in 1214.

Six miles upstream, at Tavant, a small parish church with astonishingly lifelike paintings and carvings of griffins, sirens and a two-bodied monster is all that is left of the covenant of Sinapis.

neighbours.name: Le Mans
neighbours.summary: Capital of Maine on the River Sarthe, still ringed by its Gallo-Roman wall. Its cathedral of St. Julien has carving to rival Chartres, and a pagan menhir stands against its west front.

neighbours.name: Cathedral of St. Julien, Le Mans
neighbours.summary: The bishop's church of Maine, its sculpture second only to Chartres. The old standing stone built into its west front is an embarrassment its clergy would gladly be rid of.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St. Peter, Solesmes
neighbours.summary: An abbey south-west of Le Mans that keeps a Holy Thorn, one of the thorns of Christ's crown, which the Lord of Sablé carried home from the Holy Land; it has Faith 2.

neighbours.name: Tours
neighbours.summary:
A trading city on the south bank of the Loire, its fortress and great churches inside the repaired Roman walls and a newer quarter to the west built after the Viking raids. It is a centre of learning and pilgrimage, with the tomb of St. Martin in his basilica and the Abbey of St. Julien. Philip took it from the Angevins in 1205.

St. Martin was tricked into coming here in 371, hid from the crowd come to make him bishop, was given away by honking geese, and served twenty-six years while living simply at Marmoutier by the city gate. Gregory of Tours was cured at Martin's tomb in 563 and became bishop in 573. Alcuin of York became abbot of St. Martin's on leaving Charlemagne's court and founded its school and scriptorium.

The Redcaps moved their Mercer House here from Lixivia in 1124, beneath an enlarged pilgrim hostel; Alcuin's Auberge prospered until raiders took it in 1197. Some say Fudarus sent them; nothing was proved.

neighbours.name: Basilica and Abbey of St. Martin, Tours
neighbours.summary:
The tomb of St. Martin, one of the great pilgrim shrines of France, and the abbey whose school of the liberal arts and busy scriptorium Alcuin of York founded; the scriptorium still thrives.

The works of Gregory of Tours, the city's sixth-century bishop, are read here: the ten books of his History of the Franks (a summa on the Frankish royal house, level 4, quality 14, which also serves as a summa on the lore of France, level 3, quality 14; Magic Lore, level 3, quality 12; Divine Lore, level 2, quality 14; and Intrigue, level 2, quality 10), with much on the uncanny powers of the Merovingian kings; the Lives of the Fathers (a tractatus on Church Lore, quality 10); four books on the miracles of St. Martin, the last unfinished (a tractatus on Dominion Lore, quality 8); and On the Courses of the Stars, a psalm commentary that times the night office by the stars (tractatus on astronomy, quality 6, and on Church Lore, quality 12).

neighbours.name: Abbey of St. Julien, Tours
neighbours.summary: An abbey in the old walled quarter of Tours.

neighbours.name: Marmoutier
neighbours.summary: The monastery by the gate of Tours where St. Martin lived simply while bishop. Its monks keep a priory at Sallertaine in the Vendée marshes.

neighbours.name: Saumur
neighbours.summary: A town grown round a ninth-century fortified monastery built for the relics of St. Florent, long fought over by the counts of Blois and Anjou; perhaps in memory of that, tournaments are held here in the last week of July. Its often-battered castle was rebuilt again after Philip II took the town in 1203.

neighbours.name: Monastery of St. Florent, Saumur
neighbours.summary: The fortified monastery round which Saumur grew, keeping St. Florent's relics.

neighbours.name: Abbey of Fontevraud
neighbours.summary: A double abbey south of Candes-St-Martin, where a chapel marks St. Martin's death. A woodland hermit founded it in 1100 for the men and women who gathered round him, ruled by an abbess, usually of an Angevin noble house, who guides six separate communities: contemplative nuns, lay sisters, priests, lay brothers, lepers and the sick. The Plantagenet tombs are here; Eleanor of Aquitaine spent her last ten years here and was buried here in 1204.
neighbours.ruler: The abbess, of an Angevin noble family

neighbours.name: Church of Le Puy-Notre-Dame
neighbours.summary: A church far too big for its village south of Doué, a halt on the road to Santiago. It holds the Girdle of the Virgin, lately brought from Jerusalem, a help in childbirth with a Faith score of 1.

neighbours.name: Vendôme
neighbours.summary: A town laced with streams where the River Loir splits into braids, under a castle on the outcrop to the south. Many of the valley's people live in caves, above all at Trôo, where the poor live in damp caves at the cliff foot and steps cut in the rock lead up to the homes of the better-off.

neighbours.name: Abbey of the Trinity, Vendôme
neighbours.summary: Founded in 1032 by Geoffroy Martel, Count of Anjou, on the spot where three fiery spears he saw drop from the heavens struck the ground near a spring. He gave it the arm of St. George (Faith 2) and a tear Christ wept at the tomb of Lazarus (Faith 3). It is one of the most powerful religious houses in France. One of the three spears lies forgotten in its crypt.

neighbours.name: Lord of Montaigu-en-Vendée
neighbours.summary: The local lord of the great Vendée marsh, who lives in his castle at La Garnache on the north-eastern fringe of his watery lands.

neighbours.name: Hugh X of Lusignan, Count of La Marche
neighbours.summary:
Head of the house of Lusignan, kin of the old Counts of Poitiers, whose castle was raised by faerie magic. He is betrothed to Isabella of Angoulême, King John's widow. A cadet line holds Parthenay, in a castle the family's ancestress conjured for her second son.

Legend tells that Raymond, adopted son of a Count of Poitiers, killed his father by mischance while defending him from a cornered boar, fled through the forest and came on three beautiful women by a bubbling spring. One, Mélusine, married him on condition she spend each Sabbath alone. Their many children were fine people, each with some odd mark. Raymond learned she spent that day with a serpent's tail and kept silent, until, distraught when a son of theirs who was a monk was murdered in a Norse raid, he let slip that he knew, and she fled forever. A water sprite called Mélusine (more than one supernatural woman has taken the name) appears on the castle walls whenever a count is about to die or be born.

Story seed: Mélusine stands on the ramparts for days though the count is well and his wife not with child. A maga is asked to learn what she wants while the count is kept out of harm's way.

Story seed: people with the marks of Mélusine's children (drooping ears and odd-coloured eyes, a red face, one eye higher than the other, claw-like nails, a missing eye, or little tusks in the lower jaw) come to the covenant. Each has Undine Blood and could be worth recruiting; one bears his ancestress's curse and wants it lifted.
neighbours.secrets: Mélusine wants help to save her spring, which is being made into a well for a new convent.

neighbours.name: Isabella, Countess of Angoulême
neighbours.summary: The beautiful widow of King John of England, mother of King Henry III, who holds the county of Angoulême from her castle there and is betrothed to Hugh X of Lusignan, Count of La Marche.

neighbours.name: Count of Périgord
neighbours.summary: Lord of Le Cité, capital of Périgord. He and his city stayed loyal to King John as Duke of Aquitaine, while the rival pilgrim town of Le Puy-St-Front took Philip II's side. With the bishop of Le Cité he contends with the bishop of St. Front for prestige, influence and taxes.

neighbours.name: Count of Auvergne
neighbours.summary: The count whose castle at Montferrand, beside Clermont, the town grew up round. He is the bitter rival of the Lord Bishop of Clermont and is strengthening Montferrand's walls now.

neighbours.name: Lord of Couzan
neighbours.summary: Ruler of Forez from Couzan Castle: the granite mountains east of the Livradois forests, moorland summits often lost in mist, where women and children summer with the herds while the men farm the valleys.

neighbours.name: The de Castillon family of Aubeterre
neighbours.summary: Owners of the castle on the cliff above Aubeterre's monolithic church, joined to its gallery by a steep passage. The crusader Pierre de Castillon brought back relics of the Holy Sepulchre that are said to be kept in the church's hexagonal shrine.

neighbours.name: The de Born family of Hautefort
neighbours.summary: The castle of Hautefort, east of Le Cité. The troubadour Bertrand de Born, a favourite of Henry II, who gave him the castle in 1185, quarrelled over it with his jealous brother Constantine, who with the help of Henry's son Richard ruined it the next year.
neighbours.secrets: Bertrand's music had a supernatural gift; his brother had something darker and more destructive, and magic probably brought the fortress down.

neighbours.name: La Rochelle
neighbours.summary: A walled port trading with England and Flanders, chartered as independent in 1199. Its ownership is disputed between France and England; it is English for now (history has it fall to France after a siege in 1224). It has a castle, a mint, a Templar church and a nunnery of St. Catherine.

neighbours.name: Poitiers
neighbours.summary:
The city stands on a promontory between the Boivre and the Clain, the oldest Christian community of the region and still a great church centre: the fourth-century Baptistery of St. John, where until the last century every baptism in the city was held, its Dominion aura faded to 4; the splendid Church of Our Lady the Great; the unfinished Cathedral of St. Peter; the Cluniac abbey of Montierneuf; the Abbey of the Holy Cross; and the Church of St. Hilary, its most famous bishop, whose relics are venerated there.

North of the city Charles Martel turned back the Moors.

neighbours.name: Church of St. Hilary, Poitiers
neighbours.summary: Keeps the relics of St. Hilary, doctor of the Church and the most famous bishop of Poitiers, who in legend chained the demon of the Vendée coast under the sea.

neighbours.name: Cathedral of St. Peter, Poitiers
neighbours.summary: The bishop's church of Poitiers, still under construction.

neighbours.name: Abbey of Ligugé
neighbours.summary: Just south of Poitiers, the oldest monastery in the west, founded by St. Martin in 361 when he came to learn the faith from St. Hilary and stayed ten years. A tiny, very old basilica on the ruins of his Gallo-Roman villa has a Dominion aura of 5.

neighbours.name: The Five Abbeys of the Marsh
neighbours.summary: Five abbeys near La Rochelle that have joined to drain the northern part of the marsh of the Vendée and Sèvre for cultivation. They do not know the work threatens several vis sources.

details.wants: More farmland, and the wealth it brings

neighbours.name: Angoulême
neighbours.summary: A walled city on a promontory over the River Charente, with a cathedral of St. Peter built last century and the countess's castle; houses and workshops cluster round the little port outside the walls.

neighbours.name: Limoges
neighbours.summary:
Two rival settlements: the Cité, the church quarter round the Cathedral of St. Stephen near the Vienne, with a new bridge of 1210 and a temple of Jupiter under the cathedral; and the market town on the slopes round the castle and the Abbey of St. Martial, which got its own bridge in 1215.

South at Solignac is the great monastery St. Eligius founded in 632 (a Limoges goldsmith who became King Dagobert's adviser); west at Noblat is the Monastery of St. Léonard, Clovis's godson who lived as a forest hermit there.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St. Martial, Limoges
neighbours.summary: Built over the burial ground where St. Martial, who converted the region, lies; his relics are here, three more churches stand round his tomb for the pilgrim crowds, and its scriptorium is famed for splendid work.

neighbours.name: Saintes
neighbours.summary: A regional capital on the Charente, where the Roman bridge carries the votive Arch of Germanicus and a near-constant stream of traffic, many of them pilgrims to Santiago, who lodge west of the river at the Monastery of St. Eutrope or east of it at the Ladies' Abbey of St. Mary. The town clusters round the Cathedral of St. Peter west of the river; the Roman town lay on the hill to the east.

neighbours.name: St-Émilion
neighbours.summary:
A walled hillside town on the north bank of the Dordogne, founded in the eighth century by Émilion, a Breton monk who made his hermitage here, and ringed by vineyards making the best red wine in the land. Richard I made it a self-governing commune to protect the wine trade with England; the Jurade, an assembly of citizens, oversees justice, taxes, defence and the quality of the wine. By the market a church has been dug out round the hermit's cave, about a hundred and thirty feet long, sixty-five wide and up to thirty-five high, in three aisles of square pillars, and catacombs honeycomb the soft rock below.

North-west at Blaye on the Gironde is Rudel castle, birthplace a century ago of the troubadour Geoffroy Rudel, who sang of courtly love and lived it, devoted to the distant Countess Hodierna of Tripoli.

neighbours.name: Le Cité
neighbours.summary: Capital of Périgord in fertile wooded country on the River Isle, among the remains of the Roman city of Vesunna. St. Front converted the land and built St. Stephen's Cathedral over a temple of Mars. The city is fiercely at odds with neighbouring Le Puy-St-Front.

neighbours.name: Le Puy-St-Front
neighbours.summary: A town of pilgrims and trade grown up on the hilltop beside Le Cité where St. Front was buried, round a Byzantine-style basilica over his tomb. In the latest round of its rivalry with Le Cité it sided with Philip II.

neighbours.name: Basilica of St. Front
neighbours.summary: The Byzantine-style basilica over St. Front's tomb at Le Puy-St-Front, whose bishop vies with the bishop of Le Cité and the Count of Périgord for prestige, influence and taxes.

neighbours.name: Abbey of Brantôme
neighbours.summary: A rich abbey under the cliffs of the Dronne north of Le Cité, founded by Charlemagne in 769 with a relic of St. Sicaire. The monks have taken over the Fountain of the Rock, a pagan spring in the cliff caves, where pilgrims bathe sickly infants.

neighbours.name: Monolithic Church of Aubeterre
neighbours.summary: Beside the Dronne at Aubeterre (whose Church of St. Jacques has a zodiac carved round its west door), monks are finishing a church cut from a single block of rock; it has a gallery, side chapels holding tombs and a pool for baptisms. A six-sided shrine cut from the same rock is said to hold relics of the Holy Sepulchre.

neighbours.name: Bergerac
neighbours.summary: A crossing and wine port on the north bank of the Dordogne where the river opens into a wide valley, with vineyards behind the town; Nidi lies barely an hour's walk away. Upstream past the rapids of Lalinde and the two great loops, a chapel of St. Martin near Limeuil, finished in 1194, was paid for by Henry II in penance for Becket's murder and completed by Richard I.

neighbours.name: Clermont
neighbours.summary: A city of black local stone ruled by its Lord Bishop, with a basilica and a cathedral both of Our Lady and over thirty churches and chapels. The count's town of Montferrand stands beside it, and the two rulers are bitter rivals. South of it a road runs between vast upland forests: the Livradois and Forez to the east, the volcanoes to the west.

neighbours.name: The Lord Bishop of Clermont
neighbours.summary: Lord of Clermont as well as its bishop, from his cathedral of Our Lady. His feud with the Count of Auvergne in Montferrand is a trap for any magus or covenant caught misusing magic or breaking the law: each side would gladly buy silence with magical help against the other, and both may try it.

neighbours.name: Montferrand
neighbours.summary: The town grown up round the Count of Auvergne's castle beside Clermont, its walls being strengthened against the bishop.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St. Robert, La Chaise-Dieu
neighbours.summary: The most powerful lordship of the southern plateau: an abbey of some three hundred monks whose abbot answers directly to the Pope and heads more than two hundred priories in France, Spain and Italy.
neighbours.ruler: The abbot, answerable only to the Pope

neighbours.name: The Brabançons
neighbours.summary:
Bands of skilled, disaffected soldiers, named for the duchy of Brabant east of Flanders, who roam and blight the south of the Tribunal. In 1179 Pope Alexander III put freebooters under the ban against heretics, naming the Brabanters and excommunicating any who hired or harboured them; few heeded it. Philip of France used a troop against troublesome vassals such as the count of Sancerre, then sent it to aid the Young King Henry against his father; on the way to Limoges it massacred Noialle and took its wealth, and when the rebel could not pay, it turned to sacking monasteries.

Atsingani's turb is largely Brabançon.

details.wants: Pay, or plunder where there is none
details.offers: Hardened soldiers, horsemen and crossbowmen for hire

neighbours.name: The Capuchonnes
neighbours.summary: A movement begun in the 1180s by Durand, a freeman of Le Puy, to wipe out the brigands and bring peace. Its members wore a set hood and dress and swore to live soberly, without gambling or taverns; nobles, abbots and bishops joined, and it spread across southern France and southern Aquitaine, massacring three thousand brigands in the Auvergne in 1183, among them the father of Jacques of Atsingani. It soon turned to robbing the rich and keeping the spoils.

neighbours.name: The Isle of Oléron
neighbours.summary:
A small island in the Bay of Biscay known for its fishers and traders, many of whose sailors roam the coasts. Its people know the Apple Mile is there, over the north of the island and the sea about it, and generally keep clear of its folk.

The way in is an orchard of small, sour apples, long shunned as unlucky: the challenge ground where the Queen's champion is fought for.

levels.name: The Apple Mile
levels.enter: Through the orchard of sour apples, the challenge ground on the mortal side
levels.notes:
A summer that never ends: a splendid castle where the magi and their chief servants live, a harbour town for the lesser servants, fields running out into an endless orchard of sweet apples, and the covenant's own sea. Roads seem to lead away but loop back after long detours; only two go anywhere, one to the mortal world and one to the Stone Couches, the earth-covered stone cenotaphs of the Sleepers.

Secrets
The link to the mortal world fails if the champion does not answer a challenge by sunset of the next day.

neighbours.name: The Keepers of a Thousand Tales
neighbours.summary: A Merinita society devoted to seeing that stories live on in Arcadia, with a particular interest in Arabic tales. Caprican of Oleron is an active and controversial member: he does not share the Arabic focus, and those who know of the Stone Couches think them opposed to the society's aim, since they fix a story to one place and one version.

details.wants: Stories kept alive in Arcadia

neighbours.name: Lord Henri's Manor and Chase
neighbours.summary: A small castle and its manor in farmland an hour's walk from Bergerac, once lightly wooded and far from any town. South and east, the woods have been felled to make fields; to the west is the waste, woodland where peasants forage their beasts and gather wood; to the north is the chase, kept for the lord's hunting and patrolled by his men. In the chase stand wax statues of classical heroes.
neighbours.secrets: The chase hides a grove of oaks, perhaps druidic, overgrown by huge lilacs always in flower whose blossoms yield Herbam vis; the statues are the work of Regulus's bees.

neighbours.name: The Riverbank Laboratories
neighbours.summary: A clay bank on the river, half a mile north of the castle, once a water nymph's home, with a weak Faerie aura. A hollow tree full of bees stands there, and their stings keep the locals away.
neighbours.secrets: Nidi's laboratories are dug into the bank. Most entrances suit something smaller than a man; the one a human can use is through the bee-infested tree.

neighbours.name: Lord Henri
neighbours.summary:
A minor nobleman of Aquitaine whose small castle and manor near Bergerac shelter the magi of Nidi. His father was recruited as the covenant's nominal lord; Henri knows his guests are wizards and serves them as host and shield in return for a long and healthy old age. He keeps his pride: the magi make requests, never give orders.

Story seed: Henri has one child, his daughter Lila, and insists on her happiness. Young magi of Nidi might tour covenants that hide behind mortal families so she can choose a husband, or another covenant's magi might bring a servant to Nidi as a suitor.
neighbours.secrets: The covenant needs Lila to marry a man it can steer. Once Henri takes his longevity potion he will age too slowly: cosmetics will serve a few decades, then illusions, and in true old age he must be hidden away. Mythic Europe holds others like him, and the covenant could be asked to find a place for one who has become inconvenient.

neighbours.name: Atsingani's Camp
neighbours.summary: A large semi-mobile camp a little way inside a forest in the sparsely peopled uplands of the Auvergne: a half-ring of wagons, tents both opulent and shabby, a temporary barracks and a horse corral. Moving about, it has no aura of its own, though the magi settle in a Magic aura when they can find one.

neighbours.name: Atsingani's Council Tower
neighbours.summary: A ruined, windswept hilltop tower a couple of days from the present camp, given to Atsingani by Montverte as its council chamber. It is unfit to live in and neglected, but the magi must come every summer to hold council and gather the vis there, for the Tribunal's custom forbids moving a council chamber, and Quaesitors have more than once checked that they do.

neighbours.name: The Ile de France
neighbours.summary:
The middle of the Normandy Tribunal and the heart of the French crown: the old Capetian demesne round Paris, ruled directly by the king through a mesh of small, loyal baronies whose lords fill his army, his council and his offices of provost and bailiff. Hugh Capet was chosen king at Senlis in 987, and the court, once forever on the road, has now settled for good in Paris. Merovingian gifts made the Church a great landholder here; the royal abbeys cleared the wild land and pray for the kings, and the new cathedrals of St. Denis, Sens and Chartres have launched a building style that is spreading across France.

Most of the land is gentle, fertile farmland, among the richest in Europe, and only Flanders is more thickly peopled. The Seine and the Loire cross it from south-east to north-west. The forest of Cuise (Flanders and Picardy's) closes the north-east; south of Paris lie the forests of Yvelines and Fontainebleau, and below Orléans the marshy heath of the Sologne runs to Anjou. About a day out from Paris a ring of large towns stands on the radiating roads and along the Seine. South of the forests, the Loire valley holds the king's southernmost lands, two archbishops' sees and a handful of ancient schools.

Living covenants: Eboris in Paris and Lapis Crudus in the forest of Fontainebleau. The ruins of Caput Capra lie on the Loire near Fleury.

neighbours.name: The Île de la Cité
neighbours.summary:
The mile-long island in the Seine where the Parisii first settled: the oldest quarter of Paris and its ecclesiastical and administrative centre, a stifling maze of ancient timber houses round the grandest churches. Notre-Dame rises at the island's upstream end over the ruins of a Gallo-Roman temple: begun in 1163, its chancel consecrated in 1182 and its nave nearly done, it will be the greatest church in the West when finished. The stone Petit Pont of 1186 joins the island to the left bank, and two longer stone bridges cross the broader channel to the right.

The Seine is too shallow for sea-going ships, so there are no great docks, only busy small river craft; most long-distance goods travel by the road north to Rouen. Some parts of Paris have a high Divine aura (not given in numbers).
neighbours.secrets: Infernal auras lurk in the city's worst quarters, unmapped by the book.

neighbours.name: The Wooded Islets above the Cité
neighbours.summary: A couple of small, mostly empty islands a stone's throw upstream of the Île de la Cité, thick with copses of trees. Parisians think them places of ill repute; the book does not say why.

neighbours.name: The Left Bank of Paris
neighbours.summary: The south bank, centre of Roman Lutetia and now the city's scholarly quarter, where the cathedral and abbey schools have lately been recognised as a university. Its outer parts are less crowded, a string of village-like settlements with green ground between. Little of Rome survives: the forum and baths are built over and a Roman cemetery just south of the walls is buried and overgrown, but the amphitheatre of Lutetia still stands to the south-east. The abbey church of St. Geneviève crowns a prominent hill, and a little west of it is the abbey church of St. Germanus where most Merovingian kings lie.

neighbours.name: The Right Bank of Paris (Le Marais)
neighbours.summary:
The newest, largest and busiest quarter, home to about half of Paris and its commercial heart. It is called the Marais, the marsh, because it was swamp until the Capetians drained it and took much of it for themselves. Philip II enlarged and roofed the great market of Les Halles in 1183, and merchants come to it from far away; the Hanse Parisienne, the city's chief merchant league, wields great influence here. Just outside the walls to the west stands the Louvre, the king's tall square fortress of 1190, holding his residence, treasury and arsenal, with royal gardens and estates beyond. The Templars' great temple and treasury is also in Paris.

Philip's walls and moats enclose both banks in two half-circles, three miles north to south and two east to west, and perhaps a third of each bank's people live outside them in large villages and towns. Paris is less a single city than a dozen towns grown into one, broken by walls, moats and channels and stitched together by gates and bridges, beneath a forest of spires and a haze of smoke.

neighbours.name: Montmartre
neighbours.summary: The Mount of Martyrs, a hill a little over a mile north of the walls, named for the martyrdom of St. Denis there. It was once Mons Mercurius and carried a Roman temple; a new abbey now stands on its slopes.
neighbours.secrets: In the saga frame of the Boar King, the faerie courtier Salvirius asks a magus to carry a message to the Hill of Martyrs at an exact day and hour.

neighbours.name: The House of the Ivory Carvers
neighbours.summary:
Mathieus's great house on the Rue de la Tabletterie in a poor quarter of Paris: once a pilgrims' hostel, now three storeys over many levels of cellar, the office of an ivory-carving business, refronted in a style the local nobles sneer at as new money. It is the covenant of Eboris.

In its basement is a lacuna, a space with no aura at all, not even the Dominion's, which probably helped Mathieus choose it. The house is grand for its street, and its owner quietly holds shares in at least thirty taverns, breweries, brothels and other businesses round about.

neighbours.name: The Forest of Fontainebleau
neighbours.summary:
A rocky, varied wild about twenty miles across, on the Seine's left bank some thirty miles south of Paris: parallel sandstone ridges among limestone, a dry country of hillocks, small gorges and old druid groves. Most of it is open woodland rich in game, hunted now and then from a few lodges; a tiny hermitage is the only settlement, though Parisian criminals are said to hide here. Its wettest part is a moor of ponds and clefts. Another part is a barren waste strewn with oddly shaped boulders, some of which look like beasts or even people; these stones can be harvested for Animal and Corpus vis (amount and tenure not given).

At the forest's western end the bare sandstone massif of Les Trois Pignons hides the covenant of Lapis Crudus, and in the forest's middle lies the faerie regio of the Fountain of Fair Waters. The faerie Candidus dwells somewhere in the forest: a short man with chalk-white skin and hair, no eyes or sockets at all (yet he is not blind), dressed in dark blue, who grows in power by striking bargains with mortals and always asks a strange price.
neighbours.secrets: The man-shaped boulders may be hunters and hounds who pressed their chase into the nymph's domain and were cursed for it.

neighbours.name: The Fountain of Fair Waters
neighbours.summary: A Faerie regio at the heart of the forest of Fontainebleau, about the spring of Fontaine-Belle-Eau, with a Faerie aura of 6 within. The stone figures in the surrounding waste may be its work, and they yield Animal and Corpus vis.

levels.name: Fontaine-Belle-Eau
levels.enter: Rarely stumbled into; keen-nosed hounds sometimes find it by chance
levels.notes: The spring that names the forest, kept by a lovely nymph whom the ancients took for Diana, with a gentle white stag at her side and tame forest beasts, often boar, all about. Hounds and owners who come humbly may be tolerated or even rewarded; those who keep up the hunt are likely cursed and may never leave.

neighbours.name: Les Trois Pignons
neighbours.summary: A barren sandstone massif at the western end of the forest of Fontainebleau, cut by deep dry valleys that meet in star shapes among the boulders. In the middle of one such star, inside a Faerie regio, sits the covenant of Lapis Crudus. From outside all that shows is a few rough huts of apparent outlaws, who are really the covenant's grogs; one hut straddles the regio's edge and holds the mirror through which people pass. The surface aura is not given.

levels.name: The star valley of Lapis Crudus
levels.see: Through the enchanted mirror in the shack that straddles the boundary
levels.enter: Only by the mirror: two people of comparable social standing walk toward it from either side and change places, each carrying what he can
levels.notes: The covenant itself: a dozen sandstone buildings in a star of deep valleys, lit directly only at noon. Each arm holds a magus's sanctum and the hub the covenfolk's quarters; the Bleeding Stone lies in a cavern under the council chamber, and Herbam-rich vines hang down the cliffs.

neighbours.name: The Bridge of St. Cloud
neighbours.summary: An old timber bridge over the Seine at St. Cloud, six miles below Paris, many times patched and guarded by a tall wooden tower at either end. Here the Merovingian prince Clodoald cut off the long hair that marked his royal blood and swam the river to escape his uncles. Legend says that any king who steps onto the bridge falls dead; nobody knows whether it is true, and French kings take no chances, crossing here by boat. The curse may bind a faerie king as surely as a mortal one. Magic aura 2.

neighbours.name: The Forest of Yvelines
neighbours.summary: One of the sizeable forests south-west of Paris, at the centre of the realm, which with Fontainebleau marks the edge of the lands round the city and the start of the southern Ile de France. The book says little more of it.

neighbours.name: The Sologne
neighbours.summary: A marshy forest of heath south of Orléans, on the border with Anjou, the last of the Ile de France's great woods before the Plantagenet lands.

neighbours.name: The Old Well of Chartres
neighbours.summary: An ancient well on a low hill above the Eure, beside which the cathedral of Chartres now stands. It has been holy in turn to the druids, to a Roman mother goddess and, once missionaries read the goddess as the Virgin, to Mary; that devotion is why Charlemagne gave Chartres the Sainte-Chemise. When the Vikings sacked the town in 858 they threw the bodies of martyrs down the well. Its aura is not given; the cathedral's crypt beside it is the largest in France.

neighbours.name: The Druids' Grove at Fleury
neighbours.summary:
The ancient sacred grove beside the Loire, twenty miles above Orléans, where all the druids of Gaul once met each year, near the old heart of the Carnutes' land. Benedictines from Orléans founded the abbey of Fleury beside it in the seventh century, and St. Benedict's relics now draw pilgrims in their thousands. Its aura is not given.

The Diedne covenant Caput Capra was founded nearby in 981 to guard the site through the lawless late tenth century, and was the first of Normandy's Diedne covenants to fall, in 1005.

neighbours.name: King Philip II Augustus
neighbours.summary:
King of France, of the Capetian house, and the greatest power in the Tribunal. (He is entered as a duke because the app's titles stop there.) He rules the old royal demesne of the Ile de France directly, through loyal petty barons who supply his army, his advisers and the provosts and bailiffs who run his estates, and he has held Normandy since 1204. His court no longer wanders: it has settled in Paris, and the great nobles of France and of some small neighbouring states have built palaces there to be near him.

Much of Paris is his work: its walls and moats, the Louvre (1190), the roofed market of Les Halles (1183), paved streets, and the progress of Notre-Dame. He finished the vast walls and Great Tower of Bourges in 1190, his one stronghold south of the Loire, and chartered the University of Paris in 1200. In 1214 he won the battle of Bouvines in Flanders under the Oriflamme and took Count Ferdinand of Flanders prisoner.

Kings of France never set foot on the bridge of St. Cloud. Magical war under the noses of the king and the abbey of St. Denis is a crime few magi would risk, and the Tribunal treats any meddling with the potentates of Paris as a grave matter.
neighbours.ruler: Philip II Augustus, King of France

neighbours.name: Barons of the Royal Demesne
neighbours.summary: The many small baronies of the Ile de France, wholly loyal to the king: they raise much of the royal army, sit on his council and serve as the provosts and bailiffs who manage his estates when he is away. They are a sketch for the many minor lords a saga may need round Paris.

neighbours.name: Archbishop of Sens
neighbours.summary: Metropolitan over most of the sees of the Ile de France, Paris among them, and several in Champagne and Burgundy. His cathedral of St. Étienne, begun in the 1130s and now mostly complete, was the second church built in the new French style after St. Denis, and other builders have copied it, William of Sens among them at Canterbury. A rich episcopal palace and treasury hold many relics, including the alb of St. Thomas Becket.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Paris (Notre-Dame)
neighbours.summary:
The bishop of the greatest city in the North, whose new cathedral of Notre-Dame rises at the upstream end of the Île de la Cité on the site of a Gallo-Roman temple: begun in 1163, its chancel consecrated in 1182, its nave all but finished, and much still to build. The bishops also hold the town of St. Cloud. The book does not name the present bishop.

In the last century the canon Fulbert, uncle of Héloïse, served this cathedral; his revenge on Peter Abélard is still a Parisian scandal.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St. Denis
neighbours.summary:
The great royal abbey six miles north of Paris (twice that by the winding river), built over the grave of St. Denis, martyr and patron of France. Dagobert I founded it in the seventh century and Pepin the Short enlarged it; nearly every French king since the seventh century lies in its crypt, with Clovis and his son Childebert. Its most famous abbot, Suger, schoolfellow and confidant of Louis VII, became abbot in 1122 and ruled the kingdom justly as regent during the Second Crusade, earning the name father of the land.

Suger's basilica of the 1130s, built after his vision of the heavenly Bethlehem, is the first church in the new French style: soaring pointed arches and slender columns that make room for stained glass on a scale never seen before. A great spire was recently added to one tower. Peter Abélard was a monk here late in life.

Its greatest treasure is the Oriflamme, the flame-coloured royal banner taken by Clovis from Syagrius at Soissons and later carried by Charlemagne. It may fly only in the king's presence, at the head of his army on a lance; it heartens and strengthens his troops and seems to overrule any other supernatural effect nearby. It flew last at Bouvines in 1214. Magi cannot tell whether it is Divine or Magical, and none admits to having tried his powers against it.
neighbours.secrets: The Oriflamme's true nature is left open by the book; a storyguide may decide.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St. Geneviève
neighbours.summary: The abbey church on its hill on the left bank, dedicated to Paris's patron. Geneviève, a pious peasant girl, turned Attila away from the city with her prayers in 451 and later broke Childeric's siege by bringing food in by boat; she died in 512 and many miracles followed. The book places her tomb in the Benedictine church of St. Peter and St. Paul that Clovis founded, which this record also stands for.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St. Germanus
neighbours.summary: An abbey church a short way west of St. Geneviève on the left bank, the burial place of most of the Merovingian kings; Clovis, notably, is not among them.

neighbours.name: Abbey of Montmartre
neighbours.summary: A new abbey on the slopes of Montmartre, where St. Denis was martyred and where a Roman temple to Mercury once stood.

neighbours.name: Nunnery of Argenteuil
neighbours.summary: A convent near Paris, where Peter Abélard sent his secret wife Héloïse to spare her the strain of their hidden marriage. Fulbert took her departure for desertion and had Abélard castrated, after which both took vows.

neighbours.name: The Temple of Paris (Knights Templar)
neighbours.summary:
The Templars' great house in Paris and its immensely rich treasury, which works as a bank. It began by sparing pilgrims to the Holy Land the danger of carrying coin: a pilgrim pays the whole cost of his journey into a local commandery and takes a coded parchment receipt, draws credit at Templar houses on the way, and can withdraw at the Order's other great treasury in Jerusalem.

The service now reaches far past pilgrims. The Order takes deposits and moves money for merchants, nobles, kings and the Church, and it lends, getting round the ban on usury by charging rents on the money borrowed. With the fortune this has built, the Templars pay for wars, crusades, trading ventures and great buildings.

A covenant short of money may get a very large loan here. Missed payments, or magic the knights notice, will make a powerful enemy that is quick to stir up trouble at court or with arms.

neighbours.name: Cathedral of Chartres
neighbours.summary:
The cathedral of Our Lady on the hilltop beside the old well, keeper of the Sainte-Chemise, the tunic the Virgin wore at Christ's birth, given by Charlemagne. Lightning started the Great Fire of 1194, which burned most of the town and nearly all the church (fires had also ravaged the town in 1020 and 1134); only one great steeple survived. Three days later priests were found shut safe in the treasury with the relic, and a papal legate called it a miracle and a sign to build greater.

Gifts poured in from afar and the townsfolk hauled stone from the quarry themselves; in 1220 the vast new nave, modelled on St. Denis, is just finished, and a still greater steeple is planned. Its crypt is the largest in France. On the four great feasts of the Virgin the streets about it become a fair packed with pilgrims come to see the relic.

neighbours.name: Abbey of Fleury (St. Benedict)
neighbours.summary:
The Benedictine abbey on the Loire twenty miles upriver of Orléans, founded in the mid seventh century beside the druids' grove, which soon received the relics of St. Benedict from Monte Cassino. Their many healing miracles bring pilgrims in thousands. The lofty white-stone basilica of St. Benedict, in the older style, was finished in 1218 after a century and a half and keeps his shrine in its crypt.

Theodulf, the Goth poet-scholar of Charlemagne's circle and bishop of Orléans, founded its school, famous for its manuscripts; he fell from favour after Charlemagne died, and Vikings later raided the abbey. Abbot Abbo, confidant of Robert II, restored it in the late tenth century and enlarged its library.

Its library holds the History of the Franks written here by the monk Aimon in Abbo's day (not Gregory of Tours's older work), now treated as the semi-legendary official chronicle of the Capetians. It is a single book that serves as three summae: Organization Lore: French Royalty, level 3, quality 9; Area Lore: Ile de France, level 2, quality 9; and Divine Lore, level 3, quality 9.

neighbours.name: Archbishop of Bourges
neighbours.summary: Primate over much of Aquitaine, seated in the king's fortress city of Bourges. The cathedral, begun in the new style in 1195 under Archbishop Henry de Sully, is meant to proclaim the might of the Capetians and the archbishops alike. Work slowed when his successor William de Donjon died in 1209, but William was made a saint in 1218, and the pilgrims and gifts that followed have set the building going again at speed.

neighbours.name: Paris
neighbours.summary:
The largest city of northern Europe, with more than fifty thousand people, built where the Seine is crossed at an island: royal capital, seat of churchmen and scholars, and a market town. The right bank holds about half the people; the Cité and the left bank share the rest. Many Parisians are serfs who farm the king's rich fields for miles about, so Paris is no city of industry like Ghent, though it has a vast trading quarter and every craft. Since the court and the university came, it teems with rich young men who fear no officer of the law; by night the city boils with lust and brawling, by day it trades and argues philosophy.

It is a melting pot of greed, heresy, petty crime, vice and sickness, with every pleasure and luxury for sale. The Brethren of the Free Spirit hold secret masses all over town, and the King of the Beggars rules its underworld. Writers accuse Parisians of idolatry and sorcery, mostly without cause: most are more or less devout.

History: the Parisii fished here first; Roman Lutetia grew on the left bank and declined from the late third century. Geneviève's prayers turned Attila away in 451. The city burned at the end of the sixth century; Vikings sacked it in 845 and had to be bought off, and in 885 a far greater Viking host besieged it for ten months until Count Odo broke the siege. Peace came in 911, and in 987 Hugh Capet, elected king, made Paris his capital; it has thrived ever since.

Hermetic: Eboris is the senex of Paris under the ruling of 1200, so proxy wars between covenants' masks here are now illegal, and Eboris may pursue the sponsors of masks it can identify. Many covenants keep agents in the city: Confluensis among the Seine shippers and the law faculty, Fudarus through many independent agents, Montverte in the Hanse Parisienne. Folk magicians whose Gifts the Order missed are hidden among the crowds, and Parisian magi must buy them, warn them off, or kill them.
neighbours.secrets: Hidden Infernal auras fester in the seediest parts of the city.

neighbours.name: St. Denis
neighbours.summary: A rich royal town about six miles north of Paris on an old Roman site, where the Paris-to-Beauvais road passes a wide bend of the Seine, grown up round the abbey. Each October the abbey's Lendit fair, begun in 1109 to raise money, fills the fields outside town with hundreds of stalls and draws merchants from abroad; parchment and writing materials are its speciality, bought up by the university's agents.

neighbours.name: St. Cloud
neighbours.summary: A small town on the Seine six miles below Paris, once called Nogent. Clodoald, grandson of Clovis, fled here in the sixth century after his father Clodomir fell in battle and his brothers were murdered; he cut off his royal hair to escape their fate, founded a monastery and was its abbot until his death in 560. His tomb drew pilgrims and the town took his name. It now belongs to the bishops of Paris; its old bridge is cursed for kings.

neighbours.name: Chartres
neighbours.summary: A town on the Eure in the rich plain of the Beauce, named for the Carnutes; the counts of Champagne hold the land. Burned in 1020, 1134 and 1194 and sacked by Vikings in 858, it lives largely on the pilgrims and the four fairs held on the Virgin's feasts round its cathedral and relic.

neighbours.name: Sens
neighbours.summary: Named for the Gaulish Senones and capital of Roman Senonia, Sens stands mostly on the right bank of the Yonne beside an island, inside old ramparts and a moat. It is above all the seat of the archbishop, with his cathedral of St. Étienne, palace and treasury.

neighbours.name: Orléans
neighbours.summary: A town on the Loire at what was once the centre of Gaul and the Carnutes' country, near the druids' yearly meeting place at Fleury. The Romans named it Aurelianum. In 451 a Visigothic and Roman army lifted Attila's siege at the last moment, and early in the sixth century it was the capital of Clodomir's Merovingian kingdom of Burgundy. Its cathedral school is its glory.

neighbours.name: Bourges
neighbours.summary:
A heavily fortified city at the southern tip of the Ile de France, seat of an archbishop with primacy over much of Aquitaine. The count of Bourges sold it to Philip I in 1100 to pay for his crusade. When Henry II married Eleanor of Aquitaine, Bourges became the crown's only domain south of the Loire, so the kings spent thirty years walling it, a work Philip II finished in 1190: a great stone wall with earthworks and a moat round the whole city, fortified bridges, and in the southern wall the Great Tower, a moated keep that served as the model for the Louvre. It is a plain warning to the duke of Aquitaine, King Henry III of England.

With pilgrims flocking to the tomb of St. William and money flowing to the cathedral, its population is growing fast.

neighbours.name: University of Paris
neighbours.summary:
The cathedral and abbey schools of the left bank, lately raised to a university; the king chartered it in 1200. Its students are mostly rich young men whose connections put them beyond the reach of the watch, and Paris's nights show it. In 1219 Pope Honorius III banned the teaching of law in Paris, sending a wave of students to Orléans. The heresy of the Brethren of the Free Spirit began among its theologians. Mathieus chose his poor quarter partly to keep away from the university's fools; some of the law faculty keep in touch with Confluensis.

Its most famous master was Peter Abélard, the brilliant and quarrelsome philosopher born at Le Pallet in Brittany in 1079, who studied at Chartres and came to Paris in 1118. Hired to tutor Héloïse, niece of the canon Fulbert, he fell in love with her; she bore a son, Astralabe, and they married in secret. Fulbert had him castrated and both took vows. Abélard fled to St-Gildas-de-Rhuys in Brittany, where the monks tried to poison him and he escaped by a secret passage in 1132; he later became a monk of St. Denis and died at Cluny.

neighbours.name: Cathedral School of Orléans
neighbours.summary: One of the oldest schools of the West. Burgundian kings sent their sons here in the sixth century, Bishop Theodulf built it up in the eighth, and the eldest sons of both Charlemagne and Hugh Capet studied here, with students from across Christendom since. The papal ban of 1219 on teaching law in Paris has brought a new flood of law students. In history it becomes a university in 1235.

neighbours.name: The Hanse Parisienne
neighbours.summary: The chief league of Paris's merchants, powerful in the city and in its great market of Les Halles. Montverte has several contacts among them, who do well supplying those rich magi with luxuries.

details.wants: Trade, privilege and the custom of the rich.
details.offers: Luxuries of every kind, and influence in the city.

neighbours.name: The Court of the King of the Beggars
neighbours.summary:
A great gang of beggars, cutpurses and burglars that dominates, though it does not wholly own, the Paris underworld. Its king, also called the Grand Coësre, is rumoured to pay the city's officials to look away. Under him the cagoux, master thieves, act as his nobles; under them the archisuppôts, mostly fallen clergy, teach the rules. Both may beg as they like, untaxed.

The rank and file, the argotiers, speak a secret cant and are licensed by trade: marcandiers play robbed merchants, francs-mitoux fake fainting fits, malingreux paint their faces with fat and ash to feign disease, piètres hobble on crutches, sabouleux smear on blood and froth with soap, polissons beg naked for clothes, courtauds-de-boutanche carry tools and plead lack of work, hutins claim mad-dog bites, coquillards show forged pilgrim papers, calots sit gaping like simpletons, capons cheat at cards, narquois are old soldiers who extort with threats, millards run rackets in the countryside, and orphelines cut rich men's purses.

Seeds: a grog who has shown his mettle in Paris is kidnapped to be made one of the cagoux; visitors are caught up in a turf war between the king and a pretender.

details.rules: The king takes a share of every subject's takings; the cagoux collect it, enforce his edicts and drive interlopers from his pitches; the archisuppôts teach his law and train apprentices. Each court of argotiers is licensed for one trick and kept small so as not to glut the market.
details.wants: Every good begging pitch in Paris, and freedom from the watch.
details.offers: Thieves, spies and hired hands for any job, and every rumour in Paris, for coin or vis.

neighbours.secrets: The present king is the magus Anacrôn of House Ex Miscellanea. Each year he enslaves a band of fighting men with The Irresistible Pressgang to serve as cagoux; when the spell ends, the Warping often leaves them witless and they sink among the calots. Two of his Hermetic forebears, crippled by age and Warping, live hidden among the beggars, kept alive against their will.

neighbours.name: The Brethren of the Free Spirit (Paris)
neighbours.summary: Among the biggest and best-loved heretical cults in Paris, begun by theologians of the schools and now loved by many common folk. They believe themselves heralds of a coming age of the Holy Spirit and beyond sin, and so indulge their pleasures without shame; their secret meetings and masses are held all over the city.

details.wants: The new age of the Holy Spirit, and freedom from sin and its rules.

neighbours.name: The Itinerarium
neighbours.summary: House Jerbiton's grand tour of the cities of art, meant to give senior apprentices and young magi taste, polish and enough experience of life to resist the pull of the laboratory. Before 1204 they were sent to Constantinople; since its fall the tour usually runs from Paris over the Alps to Valnastium and on into Italy. Eboris hosts its first stage, and Mathieus keeps the rich, nearly-magi young merely foolish rather than disgraceful, or hides their mistakes; he is well paid in favours. Its leading figures are Antigones, the rising generation of Jerbiton who mean to mend the Order, and the tour lets them meet nearly every aspiring Jerbiton.

details.rules: Masters stay answerable under the Code for their apprentices' conduct, and some travel with them.
details.wants: Taste, manners and a lived life for the young of House Jerbiton.
details.offers: Favours and social contacts to its hosts.

neighbours.name: Candidus, the Chalk-White Faerie
neighbours.summary:
A powerful faerie of the forest of Fontainebleau who gains power by making pacts with mortals: the mere making of a bargain seems to give him the power to keep it. His name, Latin for chalk-white, was given by Lapis Crudus, who do not know his true one. He looks like a short man with chalky skin and white hair, dressed in dark blue, with smooth skin where eyes and sockets should be, yet he sees.

In 1118 Aries of Flambeau tricked him into hiding and protecting Lapis Crudus. Candidus kept his word by moving the covenant into a regio, then sealed it in out of resentment. Since Aries's Final Twilight in 1215 he has allowed the exchange of the mirror.

details.rules: Every bargain must be paid in full, at a price as strange as the wish is great.
details.wants: Pacts with mortals, and odd payments: a stone's breath, a man's reflection, a dying dragon's lament.
details.offers: Almost any wish, through a pact.

links.note: Bound to it by Aries's pact

neighbours.secrets: His limitless power may be borrowed: he may get the wishes he grants from other faeries or from humans through yet more pacts. Mnemon owes him an unknown and fearsome task.

neighbours.name: Flanders
neighbours.summary:
The small, flat, low-lying county between the North Sea and the Scheldt, the Tribunal's northern corner, with the Rhine Tribunal beyond the river. It matters far beyond its size: it is crowded with people and sprawling cities, and alone in Mythic Europe it lives by industry rather than farming, weaving fine woollen cloth from English wool. It cannot feed itself, and trades cloth and linen for imported grain.

Once it was empty coastal marsh and creeks. Monasteries came first, and from the seventh century their monks drained and diked the land; Baldwin Ironarm, son-in-law of Charles the Bald, was given the county in 866, and later counts organised landowners into drainage societies, the Wateringues, and fortified the coast against the Vikings. Peace in the eleventh and twelfth centuries brought the wool trade, chartered towns, belfries, and comital castles in every great city: the chief palace is at Lille, and the keep of Douai, ringed by huge ramparts, has walls twelve feet thick.

Serfdom is fading fast here. Patrician families and merchant gilds run most cities and the wool trade and have wrung power from the counts, who in turn side with the weavers, spinners and dyers against them; beneath both seethe the poorly paid workers, so every level of Flemish society is tense. Most folk speak Flemish, a Low German tongue.

For the Order this is a backwater dominated by Florum and its vassals, who keep apart from the rest of the Tribunal and back the Lotharingian movement. Vis is scarce.

neighbours.name: Picardy
neighbours.summary:
The poorer cousin of Flanders, Normandy, the Ile de France and Champagne, which surround it: rolling hills and plains with scattered woods and, in the south-east, most of the Forest of Cuise. It has neither great trade nor great farmland, but rich sees, the mighty archbishopric of Reims among them, and many wealthy abbeys; several of its old Carolingian cities are raising cathedrals in the new French style.

No single lord rules it. King Philip's hand lies heaviest: since 1180 he has taken Valois, Clermont, Artois and lands about Amiens, and bishops rule most of the remaining counties. Flemish workers fleeing their masters have swelled the northern towns, bringing a young cloth trade and also unrest, which the bishops and the King put down harshly.

Its few wild places, the Boulonnais coast, the Somme valley, the Forest of Cuise and the Montagne de Reims, hold most of the region's vis.

neighbours.name: Bavacum and the Seven Roads
neighbours.summary:
Deep in the Hainault forest where Flanders meets Brabant and Picardy, a crumbling milestone stands where seven overgrown Roman roads meet, and nearby lie the forest-buried ruins of Roman Bavacum, a supply town and garrison sacred to Mercury, sacked and left at the end of the third century. A Magic aura of 3 covers the junction and the ruins.

On any day one of the seven roads is open: whoever takes it walks clear through the forest and, after a single morning, comes out within sight of the city at its far end; the other six are the slow, tangled tracks they look. Which road is open follows the seven planets, perhaps by some forgotten Mercurian working; the southern road, to Reims, opens when Mars is ascendant, coming out of the Forest of Cuise in view of the Porte de Mars. Going clockwise from due south the roads lead to Reims, Soissons, Cambrai, Boulogne, Utrecht, Cologne and Trier. Predicting the open road takes Intelligence + Artes Liberales against 12.

On the Mercuralia, the fifteenth of May, every road is open at once, and old footprints show in the road surface; each imprint, carefully dug up, is a pawn of Rego vis.

neighbours.name: The Boulonnais coast
neighbours.summary: The hills north of Boulogne that make the coast: a windswept wild country of chalk cliffs, headlands and dry valleys, from whose clifftops England can be seen on a clear day. One of the region's few wildernesses of interest to magi.

neighbours.name: The marshes of the Somme
neighbours.summary: For a dozen miles below Amiens the Somme crawls through a swamp of peat bog and water meadow too shallow for much river traffic, home only to a few hamlets of peat-cutters and hunters.

neighbours.name: The Blue Springs of the Somme
neighbours.summary:
Enchanted pools scattered about the edges of the Somme marshes, some beside little-used roads, each with a Faerie aura of up to 3. Turning shafts of blue light rise from them, and a close look, unwisely taken, shows laden carriages and other riches circling slowly in the depths.

Water sprites are said to keep whatever falls in or is caught by the pools and to beguile travellers; yet a small child who slips in comes out with lovely blue eyes, and gifts freely given to the water may be repaid.

neighbours.name: The Caves of Naours
neighbours.summary:
A few hundred peasants farm dull fields about the village of Naours, on a limestone plateau six miles north of Amiens, but half their village lies a hundred feet underground: the muches, a cave town of hundreds of rooms that can shelter over a thousand, with more than a mile of streets, a smithy, brewery, bakeries, stores, byres, stables and a square, reached by chimneys, two stairways and a steep road. A Magic aura of 2 fills it.

Hiding here from the Vikings, the villagers met a powerful cave spirit, a genius loci, and swore a pact of mutual protection with it that both sides still keep. The villagers are shy of showing their caves to anyone, but they are no pagans and go to the small church above ground.

neighbours.name: The Montagne de Reims
neighbours.summary: A wild, hilly forest beginning at the edge of Reims and running fifteen miles south to the Marne and twenty-five miles across: dense trees on a broken limestone plateau of small lakes, underground streams and chasms. It is poor hunting country, and the archbishops do not hunt anyway, so wild beasts roam freely. Several odd sites and vis sources lie within it.

neighbours.name: The Grove of St. Lie
neighbours.summary: On a ridge at the forest's northern edge, looking out over Reims and the plain, an old Gaulish burial mound stands in a ring of oaks, with a tiny chapel to St. Lie, a hermit saint of the fifth century. The pale flowers on the mound yield a few pawns of Creo vis, a tropaeum of the Tribunal.

neighbours.name: The Faux de Verzy
neighbours.summary: A dark grove of twisted, stunted black beeches in the east of the forest, with a Faerie aura of 4, which the local peasants avoid.
neighbours.secrets: The wilder stories say a dark, dwarfish folk carry off villagers who stray in; those who come back bear some deformity and will not speak of what happened.

neighbours.name: Nanteuil
neighbours.summary: A remote vale near the heart of the forest where the Knights Templar keep a priory, an odd site for one, hard to reach and leading nowhere. The magus Norlanus wrote that he found it to be a regio, perhaps Divine: leaving the priory as a guest, he came out into a brighter version of the forest. Others say he merely had a strong Twilight episode.

levels.name: The lighter forest
levels.enter: Leaving the priory as a guest, by Norlanus's account
levels.notes: A brighter, different version of the forest; its aura and realm are not given, and whether it exists at all is disputed.

neighbours.name: The Forest of Cuise
neighbours.summary: A great finger of woodland south of Compiègne, some seventy miles long, reaching from the edge of the Ile de France toward the Ardennes. Much of it is the French kings' hunting chase: sunny, open woods of beech and oak over gentle hills, with winding rivers and ponds, full of deer, wolves and boar, and crossed by a few roads, many hunting paths and the odd village and monastery. The abbey of Prémontré lies in a hidden valley within it.
neighbours.secrets: The Tribunal knows of no real faerie presence here; if the forest has a faerie ruler, it is shy and kindly to mortals.

neighbours.name: The cliffs of Laon
neighbours.summary: The rocky flanks of the great mount of Laon, where the eremite Norlanus of Jerbiton has hidden his sanctum and harvests a small source of Terram vis, his legacy by the Tribunal's grant for many years.

neighbours.name: The Farm, Ghent
neighbours.summary: A district on Ghent's southern edge, once a flax farm a mile out of the city that Florum bought fifty years ago, foreseeing the city's growth; Ghent has since swallowed it. Almost three hundred people live there, in good tenements round a great factory. It stands over an ancient kabouter workshop, which gives it a Faerie aura (its strength is not given); Prunellie of Merinita chose the site.

neighbours.name: The Spider's Palace
neighbours.summary:
Florum's original site, a little more than two days' journey north of Ghent (Florum's history puts the old covenant between Bruges and Ghent). Here stood the thousand-year-old oak spirit that guarded the local people and led their ancestress to wed the spider prince, and here the spider built his bride a palace, which in time slipped out of the mundane world. The magi use it as their covenant building.

It was raided several times in Florum's early days.

levels.name: The palace of the spider prince
levels.notes: The faded palace the magi live in, with excellent laboratories; the aura and the way in are not given.

neighbours.name: The ruins of old Nesle
neighbours.summary:
The deserted ruins of the old town of Nesle on the plains of central Picardy, about an unconsecrated graveyard where the Donatores fought their last great battle against the restless dead early in the twelfth century. The magic unleashed there left a Magic aura of 5. A new Nesle has been built a couple of miles away, and the locals think the ruins haunted.

Beneath the graveyard the Donatores dug catacombs that hold most of their covenant.

neighbours.name: Joan, Countess of Flanders
neighbours.summary:
Countess of Flanders since 1205, niece of King Philip. Her father Baldwin IX was chosen Emperor of Constantinople in 1204 on the Fourth Crusade and died a captive a year later. Her husband Ferdinand, a prince of Portugal, was taken at Bouvines in 1214 and has sat in a Paris prison for six years; Joan, who has little love for him, refuses her uncle the ten thousand pounds he asks as ransom and governs alone, which Philip seems not to mind.

Her house's main castle and palace is at Lille, with castles in every great city. The counts police the cloth fairs and keep the roads and waterways safe, and side with the craft gilds against the patricians. She commissioned two continuations of Chrétien's Perceval, partly to show herself the rightful heir of Philip of Flanders. Arms: or, a lion sable.

neighbours.name: Bruges
neighbours.summary:
Brugge, Flanders' greatest port and a leading wool and weaving city. Baldwin Ironarm built a castle here against the Vikings in the ninth century, and Robert the Frisian made it his capital in 1093; the old channel to the sea silted up and the town stagnated, until the great tidal wave of 1134 scoured a deep channel in the Zwin. A harbour was built at Damme, five miles off, and joined to Bruges by canal, and the city boomed again.

Rival merchants asked the Church to look into the wave, some claiming the patricians of Bruges had it conjured; several magi suspected Florum or Infelicitas, but the Quaesitores never had evidence enough to investigate.

The castle sits at the centre within brick ramparts that also hold a broad market square and St. Donatius, the largest church. Among the other churches is the Basilica of the Holy Blood, whose reliquary holds Christ's Blood, brought back from the Second Crusade by Count Thierry of Alsace. There is a large cloth market. The patrician council grants tax immunities and trading privileges and lets foreign merchants, though not local craftsmen, buy property; their enclaves lie outside the walls. The fair cycle ends here.

neighbours.name: Basilica of the Holy Blood, Bruges
neighbours.summary: A church of Bruges holding a reliquary of the Blood of Christ, which Thierry of Alsace, Count of Flanders, carried home from the Holy Land after the Second Crusade. A potent relic.

neighbours.name: Ghent
neighbours.summary:
Gent, at the meeting of the Scheldt and the Lys: the largest city in Flanders and in northern Europe after Paris, with perhaps forty thousand people, bigger than London or Cologne, and home of Florum. It grew round the abbeys of St. Bavo and St. Peter that St. Amand founded in the seventh century; plundered twice by Vikings, it recovered after Baldwin II built a stone castle in the tenth.

Many trade routes meet here. Wool and cloth rule, but almost anything can be bought in its huge markets, including Eastern and Mediterranean luxuries via the Champagne fairs; Italians, Jews and the Templars run a young banking trade, and the wool workers' guild grows stronger. The rich merchants have built stenen, fortified stone town houses, and in 1180 Count Philip of Alsace answered by rebuilding his castle on the model of the crusader castles: a strong keep with a ring of turrets and a moat from the Lys. The great church of St. Nicholas is half-built, and the Graslei docks run through the city's heart.

The city is spreading fast with newcomers and foreigners into suburbs, one of which, the Farm, is Florum.

neighbours.name: Abbeys of St. Bavo and St. Peter, Ghent
neighbours.summary: The two monasteries founded by St. Amand, apostle of Flanders, in the seventh century, round which Ghent grew; they now stand at the centre of the city. (The founding year is approximate.)

neighbours.name: Ypres
neighbours.summary:
Ieper, on an old Roman site refounded in the tenth century, now one of Flanders' largest cities. It lives by woollen cloth, with a great cloth market near the church of St. Martin, and also weaves linen, for the Lys is good for retting the flax grown all round. South of it the Heuvelland, Flanders' thinly peopled uplands, rises in wooded hills up to five hundred feet that overlook the lowland.

Many cats live in the Cloth Hall, welcome in winter for keeping the mice from the cloth. In spring the superstitious townsfolk, who think them witches' creatures, bag every cat they can and throw them to their deaths from the top of the belfry beside the cloth market: the Kattenfeest. The cleverest cats hide and survive to hunt next winter's vermin.

Hook: a clever cat, perhaps a familiar, begs the magi to stop the killing, and the cats would be grateful for ever. Hook: a sinister man in motley stirs the crowd and leads the march to the belfry laughing, then is seen picking over the dead cats, perhaps an urban hedge wizard collecting vis.

neighbours.name: Antwerp
neighbours.summary:
A harbour on the Scheldt estuary, smaller and less notable than the great Flemish cities, that thrives on fish, grain and salt and on English raw wool. It grew from a Roman fort and was converted by St. Amand in the seventh century.

Legend says the giant Druon Antigon once preyed on the estuary, wrecking ships and cutting off the hands of any who would not pay his toll or whom he disliked, until the soldier Silvius Brabo beat him, cut off his hand and flung it in the river. Brabo was given the land, and the city's name means hand-throwing; its arms show two severed hands before a castle.

neighbours.name: Tournai
neighbours.summary:
The seat of the bishopric of Flanders, an old, learned and pious city unlike the busy cloth towns. St. Piat converted the Roman town; under the Frankish kings it was a capital, where Chilperic is buried and Clovis was born, who founded the see. Since 1187 it has been free of the counts and answers directly to the French crown.

The cathedral of Notre-Dame and its belfry dominate it. The Scheldt divides it, but the walls cross the river on stone arches and make boats stop and pay toll. Its artisans, and above all its gold- and silversmiths, are famous.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Tournai
neighbours.summary: The see of Flanders, founded by Clovis, seated at the cathedral of Notre-Dame in Tournai with its great belfry.

neighbours.name: Lille
neighbours.summary: Seat of the Counts of Flanders, with their chief castle and palace, and the first town of the Flemish cloth fair cycle each year.

neighbours.name: Douai
neighbours.summary: A Flemish town with one of the counts' grandest castles: a great keep inside huge ramparts, its walls twelve feet thick.

neighbours.name: Steenvoorde
neighbours.summary:
A Flemish town whose hero is Yan den Houtkapper, John the Woodcutter, a clever giant who made everlasting boots for Charlemagne and was given a huge suit of armour in return. The townsfolk dress a giant figure in that armour and carry it through the streets in procession every year.

Hook: the armour may be blessed or magical, and would fit only someone with Giant Blood; stealing the town's dearest treasure would enrage it.

neighbours.name: Archbishop of Reims
neighbours.summary:
The most powerful archbishop in France, who anoints and crowns its kings with the holy phial of oil a dove brought from heaven for the baptism of Clovis by St. Remigius, the kings' proof of their divine right. The archbishops have used that privilege shrewdly, acting as arbiters between claimants to the throne and keeping Reims prosperous.

Their opulent palace keeps the coronation relics: the phial; Charlemagne's talisman, thought to hold a piece of the True Cross; a coronation chalice; and the reliquary of the Holy Thorn. The new cathedral of Notre-Dame, in the French style, has been rising at the south end of the city since 1210. Archbishop William of the White Hands granted the city its charter late in the twelfth century.

neighbours.name: Reims
neighbours.summary:
The largest city of Picardy, where the kings of France are crowned. Capital of the Gaulish Remes, then a rich Roman city with roads to its gates, it saw Clovis baptised one Christmas at the end of the fifth century. Its cathedral school has been a beacon of the liberal arts for centuries, and the city has grown since its charter.

At the north end stand Roman remains: the Porte de Mars, a triumphal arched gate in the wall, a ruined temple of Mars and an ancient forum. In the centre is the eighth-century monastery of St. Remigius, its basilica rebuilt grandly over his grave of 533. The wild Montagne de Reims begins at the city's southern edge.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St. Remigius, Reims
neighbours.summary: The eighth-century monastery of the patron saint of Reims, who baptised Clovis; his basilica, raised over his grave of 533, has been rebuilt on a far grander scale.

neighbours.name: Cathedral school of Reims
neighbours.summary: For centuries one of the great schools of the liberal arts. Hautvillers Abbey is a branch of it.

neighbours.name: Hautvillers Abbey
neighbours.summary: Founded in 660 by St. Nivard near the north bank of the Marne, a large abbey church in a quiet, lovely spot among vineyards, now a branch of the Reims school whose scriptorium makes some of the finest illuminated manuscripts anywhere. A few miles upstream is Ay, an old Gaulish village of vintners with a royal residence the kings seldom visit.

neighbours.name: Templar priory of Nanteuil
neighbours.summary: A priory of the Knights Templar in a remote vale in the middle of the Montagne de Reims, oddly placed, hard to reach and on the road to nowhere; Norlanus believed it stands at a regio.

neighbours.name: Soissons
neighbours.summary:
A city amid rich farmland in the Aisne valley. It was the capital of Syagrius's Roman kingdom of Soissons until Clovis beat him at its gates; when a defiant soldier smashed a vase Clovis wanted returned to Reims, the king killed him a year later at a review of his troops, reminding him of the vase. For a time it was the Frankish capital under Chlotar, son of Clovis.

Its cathedral of St. Gervais and the abbey church of St. John of the Vines are forever being enlarged with the abbey's wealth.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St. John of the Vines, Soissons
neighbours.summary: Founded in the eleventh century, it has grown under royal patronage into one of the richest abbeys in France, and its money builds both its own great church and the cathedral of Soissons.

neighbours.name: Arras
neighbours.summary:
Seat of the county of Artois on the Flemish border, now the King's, once capital of the Atrebates and Roman Atrebatum. Its large grain market draws Flemish traders exchanging woollen cloth for grain.

It is full of renowned troubadours and entertainers, a tradition begun in the twelfth century by its most famous trouvère, Gautier d'Arras, best known for Eracle, the romance of Heraclius who becomes Emperor of Constantinople.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St. Vaast, Arras
neighbours.summary: Founded by St. Aubert in the seventh century on the slopes of the Baudimont hill, it keeps the relics of St. Vaast, first bishop of Arras.

neighbours.name: Count of Boulogne
neighbours.summary: Lord of an important county on the Channel; the present count, not named, has begun rebuilding the ruined walls and ramparts about the old Roman castle of the upper town.

neighbours.name: Boulogne
neighbours.summary: Roman Bononia, between two hills where the Liane meets the sea: Claudius's base for invading Britain and then the chief port linking the province to the Empire. Now a county seat, a busy port and fishing town, and a place of pilgrimage. The upper town has grown round the old Roman castle.
