neighbours.name: Notre-Dame de Boulogne
neighbours.summary: In 636 the Virgin appeared to a small congregation in the chapel of Boulogne and sent them to the shore, where a boat with neither sail nor crew grounded gently, bearing her statue. The statue, a famous relic, is kept in the cathedral and draws pilgrims, for it is believed to keep travellers safe; the kings of France customarily make the pilgrimage, and English kings have come too.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Amiens
neighbours.summary: Keeper of two great relics: half the cloak St. Martin of Tours, then a Roman horseman, cut in two for a freezing beggar, and the greater, the head of John the Baptist, which came back with the Fourth Crusade in 1206. The church burned in 1218, and the bishop and his flock have already begun a much larger cathedral worthy of the relic.

neighbours.name: Amiens
neighbours.summary: The historical capital of Picardy, chief town of the Gaulish Ambiani and Roman Samarobriva, where St. Martin shared his cloak. Lands about it have lately passed to the King. Downstream the Somme spreads into marsh.

neighbours.name: Abbey of Corbie
neighbours.summary:
The leading monastery of northern France, in a quiet spot of the Somme valley above Amiens, founded in 657 by St. Bathilde, wife of Clovis II, and raised to greatness by Charlemagne's cousin St. Adalard. Hundreds of monks lived here; it was famed for theology and its library, where the Carolingian script was first written, and the last Lombard king, Desiderius, was exiled here. At its height it was perhaps the heart of western Christendom and founded many daughter houses.

St. Ansgar, Apostle of the North, was born here in 801, carried its ways to Corvey in Saxony, became archbishop of Hamburg and preached in the Norse lands.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Laon
neighbours.summary: A see founded by St. Remigius, who was born in Laon. A century ago Bishop Gaudry bought from the King the revocation of the commune his weakness had let the townsfolk win, and took cruel revenge; the town rose, burned the palace and the old cathedral, and killed him and his men. Bishops and people have been uneasy ever since, the kings ruling now for one, now for the other. The new cathedral of Notre-Dame is nearly finished in the French style.

neighbours.name: Laon
neighbours.summary:
A city on a rocky ridge over a mile long and a quarter wide, rising three hundred feet from the plain: Roman Laudunum, which held out against the Germanic invaders, and under the Carolingians in the ninth and tenth centuries for a while the capital of France, richly endowed by Charles the Bald. Hugh Capet plotted with its bishop to take it from the Carolingians and then ruled from Paris, and Laon lost its political weight.

It is still a centre of learning, its cathedral school famous since Anselm of Laon in the eleventh century. Spires and towers climb to the new cathedral; beside the old church of St. Martin is a Templar chapel and commandery. Roads wind down slopes of vineyards to the lower town. The eremite Norlanus of Jerbiton lives here, his sanctum hidden in the cliffs.

neighbours.name: Cathedral school of Laon
neighbours.summary: A renowned school, at its height under Anselm of Laon in the eleventh century, where Norlanus of Jerbiton spends much of his time and is respected for his wisdom.

neighbours.name: Compiègne
neighbours.summary: A small, ancient city on the Oise in southern Picardy, born of the country palace Charles the Bald built in imitation of Charlemagne's at Aachen; the town grew round the royal abbey of St. Cornelius founded after it. The Forest of Cuise stretches south of it.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St. Cornelius, Compiègne
neighbours.summary: The royal abbey that keeps St. Cornelius's relics, the burial place of the old Carolingian kings before St. Denis took that role.

neighbours.name: Abbey of Prémontré
neighbours.summary:
Mother house of the Premonstratensians, in a hidden valley of the Forest of Cuise, ten miles from Laon to the west. St. Norbert, a German born near Cleves, gave away his goods and vowed himself to poverty after a revelation, when a storm threw him from his horse. In midwinter 1120 he came with the bishop of Laon to a clearing where a monastery had once failed, was ordained there, and founded his own; he became a friend of St. Bernard of Clairvaux.

His order, also called Norbertines, was modelled on the Cistercians and approved by the Pope in 1126: strict canons in white habits who preach and follow the rule of St. Augustine. It now has several hundred houses across western Europe, most in northern France, Germany and England.

neighbours.name: The Flemish patricians and merchant gilds
neighbours.summary: The powerful merchant gilds and patrician families who run most Flemish cities and the lucrative wool trade, and have gradually forced power out of the counts' hands. The richest have built fortified stone town houses.

details.decides: Councils of the leading families in each city
details.wants: Control of the cities and the wool trade, and more power from the counts
details.offers: Wealth, trade privileges, property for foreigners

neighbours.name: The Flemish craft gilds
neighbours.summary: The weavers, spinners and dyers, rivals of the merchants and friendlier to the counts, who often ally with them. The wool workers' guild of Ghent is growing in power, and many Spinnen sit in the city's Weavers' Guild. Below them the mass of grimy, barely paid workers nurses resentment.

details.wants: A check on the merchants, and better lives for the workers
details.offers: The counts' alliance against the patricians

neighbours.name: The Flemish cloth fairs
neighbours.summary: A cycle of trade fairs from February to November, held in turn at Lille, Mesen, Ypres, Torhout and Bruges, given over to fine woollen and linen cloth rather than general trade. Most goods travel by water.

details.rules: The counts guard the fairs and keep the roads and waterways safe

neighbours.name: The Beguines
neighbours.summary:
A movement that has sprung up of itself among widows and single women, who are beginning to gather in convents in the towns. They take their name from St. Begga, a seventh-century abbess in Andenne in Brabant. Unlike nuns they take no vows and may still marry. Most come from wealthy families, for piety, family trouble, the wish for a simple shared life with some freedom, or all of these, and they nurse the sick or sew and weave.

A beguinage is a small walled town at the edge of a larger one, rows of cottages round one or more square courts about a church. They are just beginning to flourish in Flanders; by the middle of the century there will be large ones in Ghent, Bruges and other cities of Flanders, Brabant and northern Picardy.

Hook: a new beguinage near the covenant draws away its discontented women, leaving it short-staffed. Hook: a beguinage oppressed by a harsh landlord asks the covenant's protection and would work for it to be freed of its debt, at the cost of the landlord's enmity.

details.rules: No vows and no renouncing of marriage, but a common rule; chosen poverty, not harsh; manual work, charity and cottage crafts
details.wants: A pious, simple common life with some independence
details.offers: Care of the sick, sewing and weaving, labour in return for protection

neighbours.name: The Spinnen
neighbours.summary: A Ghent family of faerie blood, descended from a maiden whose ancestral oak, at the end of its thousand years and as the Church came, summoned faerie and mystic princes to woo her. She refused them all, and the oak told her to wed Spin Head, the last and ugliest, whose dowry would replace the dying forests. The oak died, the spider passed a simple test and took human shape, and he gave his bride the first flax plant, weaving her wedding dress from it with his fingers.
neighbours.ruler: Piet de Spinnen (the de Spinnen family, a front)

details.wants: To live well and stay hidden
details.offers: Cloth spun by touch: tents, ropes and sails too

neighbours.secrets: A few in each generation can turn their own weight of fibre into cloth each day by touch (the Virtue Faerie Blood (Spinnen)), or unweave old cloth within the same limit; some make tents, ropes or sails instead. Pelagius of Jerbiton found a dozen soon after the Order's founding; in 1220 there are almost thirty, all employed by Florum and living far better for it. They hide in plain sight, many in the Weavers' Guild of Ghent, and their relatives weave by ordinary means in the covenant's workshop. Their flax legend is widely known, so the wary might guess the truth.

neighbours.name: The kabouters of the Low Countries
neighbours.summary: A dwarfish faerie folk who sided with the coming Church: they gave a hundred bells to the missionaries they approved of and sang the first carillon of the Low Countries under a gnome's baton. A tribe of them is firmly allied with Prunellie of Merinita, and an ancient kabouter workshop lies under Florum's Farm, giving it its Faerie aura.

neighbours.name: The Donatores Requietis Aeternae
neighbours.summary: The Givers of Eternal Rest, an Ex Miscellanea tradition born of the hedge wizards, clergy and others who fought the plague of restless dead in Picardy and won the battle of Nesle; the Quaesitor Muirgheal brought them into the Order in 1109. Their spiritual home and library are at Requies Aeterna, but most have scattered across western Europe to wherever the dead walk; one, Philip, has lately joined Atramentum Renatus. Some magi have always distrusted them.

details.wants: To give the restless dead their rest, and to banish those that will not go
details.offers: Expert banishers of the dead

neighbours.name: Champagne
neighbours.summary:
The Romans' Campania, the land of plains: rolling, rich farm country between the upper Seine in the south and the wooded heights of the Ardennes and the Argonne to the north and east. Apart from the swamp of St. Gond, the great forest of Orient and a few lesser woods it is all good tillage, and it is known for a red wine with a faint sparkle.

Its wealth and fame in 1220 come from the cycle of trade fairs at Provins, Troyes, Lagny and Bar-sur-Aube, where the goods of the north and the Mediterranean change hands. A century of Cistercian houses founded by St. Bernard has filled it with busy monks and their cottage trades.

The great road the Romans built from Lyon to Boulogne runs through it, and with it the Redcaps' route between the Rhine, the Greater Alps and Rome; the Mercer House at Cunfin sits on that road, close to the fairs, where Redcaps quietly pitch their own trading tents. The Church is strong here and covenants are few.

neighbours.name: Burgundy
neighbours.summary:
The south-eastern corner of the Tribunal and the old heartland of the Gauls, thick with their hill-towns and with Roman ruins. The duchy dates from the partition of Charlemagne's empire at Verdun in 843, when the north-western part of the old Burgundian kingdom fell to Charles the Bald; in the eleventh century Henry I of France gave it to his brother Robert, whose junior Capetian line has stayed loyal to the crown and, through crusading in Iberia, is kin to the royal houses of Castile and Portugal.

Where Champagne lives by trade, Burgundy lives by pilgrims, and the Church is mightier here than anywhere: Cluny and Citeaux, the mother houses of their orders, Vezelay with the relics of St. Mary Magdalene, and Pontigny, Molesme, St. Seine, St. Benigne and Fontenay besides, with Clairvaux on the northern edge. The monks' vineyards make Burgundy one of the great wine lands of Europe.

The duchy is not the larger kingdom of Burgundy (Arelat) to its south-east, which is shared between the Greater Alps and Provencal Tribunals.

neighbours.name: The Forest of Orient
neighbours.summary: The largest forest of Champagne, an island of woodland among the plains east of Troyes. The book names it but gives it no aura or inhabitants.

neighbours.name: The Swamp of St. Gond
neighbours.summary: The one stretch of Champagne that is not good farmland, a wide marsh south of Chalons. The book names it without detail.

neighbours.name: The Bishop's Meadow at Chalons
neighbours.summary:
A broad, quiet riverside meadow just south of Chalons, part of the bishop's estate and lightly grazed by sheep. St. Bernard and Pope Eugene III both preached here.

Travellers of every sort now treat it as a lucky and handy place to meet, and not all of their business is pious: a natural spot for a rendezvous, a hand-over or an ambush on the road between the fairs and the north.

neighbours.name: The Catalaunian Fields
neighbours.summary:
About a dozen miles from Chalons lies the field where, in 451, the Roman general Aetius with Theoderic's Visigoths and the Franks of the sorcerer-king Merovech turned back Attila and his Ostrogoth allies at midsummer, after the Huns had sacked Reims and besieged Orleans. Theoderic fell; Attila escaped to his camp and away. More than forty thousand died, and an old chronicle tells of a brook swollen with blood that the wounded drank from.

Today it is empty scrub and fallow, walked by a few thin sheep and grimy peasants, under a Malevolent Infernal aura of 3. A dark stream runs below the ridge in the middle of the field. On the night of the summer solstice, the battle's anniversary, it runs red, and the cries of dying men and horses are heard; whoever climbs the stream that night enters an Infernal regio where the ghosts of both armies fight forever, driven on by demons, among heaps of the dead and dying. A magus who braves it may harvest a great deal of Perdo and Corpus vis; the book gives no tenure for it.

levels.name: The Endless Battle
levels.enter: Climb the blood-red stream below the central ridge on the night of the summer solstice.
levels.notes: The shades of Huns, Goths, Romans and Franks fight on, goaded by warrior demons; Perdo and Corpus vis in quantity, some of it tainted. Its aura is not given.

neighbours.secrets: Some of the Perdo and Corpus vis gathered in the regio carries an Infernal taint, and nothing marks which.

neighbours.name: Attila's Camp
neighbours.summary: A few miles east of the battlefield, the overgrown remains of the camp where Attila's household guard held out after the battle, still ringed by a low wall.

neighbours.name: The Caesar Tower
neighbours.summary: The great square watchtower and prison crowning the fortifications of Provins's upper town, beside the counts' hilltop castle. Folk say Julius Caesar himself raised it.

neighbours.name: The Valley of Cunfin
neighbours.summary:
A deep, well-watered valley in Champagne holding the village of Cunfin and its Cistercian abbey: plain buildings with almost no ornament, one low tower, undivided windows of clear glass and wooden crosses. The monks keep a Dominion whose temper Eloi's holy power has made Calm. The Dominion's strength is not given.

Over the abbey and its surroundings lies a Magic regio of a single level, unseen by most of the mundane folk. It was once a ruined Roman fort; Celeres has rebuilt it as a miniature castle with pennons flying, and most of the covenant's members live there. Anyone carrying a charm cut from the fort's stones can pass in. How a Magic regio survives inside so strong a Divine aura is unknown, and several Bonisagus magi have studied it.

levels.name: Celeres's Castle
levels.see: A miniature castle where the Roman fort stood.
levels.enter: Carry a charm made from the old fort's stones.
levels.notes: The covenant proper; its aura is not given. Eloi lives mostly at the abbey and Angelus in his cave.

neighbours.secrets: Rumour, perhaps true, says the abbey was founded in 1136 by Valoran, a pupil of St. Nerius; Eloi believes Valoran was Angelus's parens.

neighbours.name: Angelus's Cave
neighbours.summary: A small cave in the hills a stone's throw above the abbey of Cunfin, where the hermit Angelus has lived alone in prayer for decades. The monks know a holy hermit dwells there and count themselves blessed.

neighbours.name: The Morvan
neighbours.summary:
Burgundy's only real wilderness, the Black Mountain of its Celtic name: a basalt upland a little above the country round it, often lost in rain, snow or mist, its rivers quick to rise in sudden spate. Oak, hornbeam and beech cover most of it, with conifers on the high rocky slopes. It is poor, rolling land without fields or vines, and the few peasants who scratch a living there are shunned by their neighbours.

Magi know of several vis sources in the Morvan, most of them disputed, for dark faeries haunt its lakes, streams and woods. Its aura is not given. The ruins of Bibracte lie on Mont Beauvray in the south, near Autun, and Moles Magna once stood on its edge.

neighbours.name: Mont Auxois (Alesia)
neighbours.summary:
A peak of about 1,300 feet a short way north-east of the Morvan and some six miles south of Fontenay abbey, crowned by the ruins of Alesia, the Gallo-Roman hill-fort where Caesar's siege forced Vercingetorix to surrender; he was taken to Rome in chains and strangled years later.

Among the empty ruins are old bronze forges and an underground temple to the Gallic mother goddesses, the Matres. The hilltop keeps a Magic aura (strength not given) and could suit a new covenant, though the ghosts of the pagan dead haunt it.

neighbours.name: The Fountain of St. Reina
neighbours.summary: On the south-western edge of Mont Auxois, under a Divine aura, a spring rose where the young Christian Reina was beheaded for refusing to marry Olibrius, Roman governor of Alesia. Its water was said to heal, and drew pilgrims for a while before it was forgotten; the old fountain hides among trees beside a ruined Merovingian chapel to the saint.

neighbours.name: The Cave of Sabinus
neighbours.summary:
A hidden cave some ten miles south of Langres, beside the forest spring where the Marne begins, home to a powerful genius loci. Sabinus, a chieftain of the Lingones who rebelled at Langres after Nero's death in 70 AD, fled here and bargained for the spirit's protection; it hid him for nine years before it wearied of him, and he was found and taken to Rome to die.

Aquam vis can be drawn from the spring if the spirit allows. Because the spirit is so hard to please, the Tribunal counts the source a luctatio, open to any magus who dares.

neighbours.name: The Temple of Janus at Autun
neighbours.summary: The remains of a Roman temple to Janus, the god with two faces who rules gates and doorways, of beginnings and endings, in a meadow across the Arroux outside Autun. No aura is given.

neighbours.name: The Pyramid of Autun
neighbours.summary: A strange ruined pyramid some fifty feet high standing in the fields about a mile south-east of Autun cathedral, most likely the tomb of some forgotten Roman notable. No aura is given.

neighbours.name: Atramentum Renatus
neighbours.summary: The site of the covenant Atramentum Renatus in Burgundy, built about a vis source that was once a legacy of Fudarus. The book does not say where in the duchy it lies, nor its aura; its magi's interest in Bibracte suggests the Morvan's edge.

neighbours.name: Count of Champagne
neighbours.summary:
Theobald IV, a charming young count of nineteen, holds many lesser counties and baronies in Champagne and is overlord of Blois and Chartres in the Ile de France and Auxerre in Burgundy. His mother, Blanca of Navarre, loyal to King Philip, rules as regent. He cares little for hunting or building castles; he is a gifted young poet and musician who loves books and travel, and his romantic, wandering ways so trouble his mother that she is already arranging a political marriage for him. His court spends long seasons at Provins, which is becoming a home of the arts under him.

If history holds, he comes of age in 1222 and his early reign is troubled by money, politics and three marriages, until in 1235 he inherits Navarre through his mother, daughter of King Sancho VI. He will be remembered as one of the finest troubadours of his age, the Chansonnier, and will bring Syrian roses to Provins.

His arms are azure, a bend argent with potent cotises or; the shield here shows the bend alone.

neighbours.name: Duke of Burgundy
neighbours.summary:
Hugh IV, the Capetian Duke of Burgundy, is only eight; his mother Alice de Vergy rules as regent and, like Champagne's regent, is loyal to the French crown. The dukes descend from Robert, brother of King Henry I, to whom the duchy was granted in the eleventh century, and are kin to the kings of Castile and Portugal. Robert I moved the ducal seat from Autun to Dijon in 1051; the dukes are now buried at Citeaux, not Autun, and hold the walled hill-town of Avallon as a stronghold.

Their arms are bendy or and azure, a bordure gules; the shield here shows the bendy field without the border.

neighbours.name: Chalons-en-Champagne
neighbours.summary:
An ancient city on the Marne where the roads from the fairs head north to Reims, Picardy and Flanders; Roman Catalaunum. It matters more to the Church than to trade: its bishops take part in the coronations at nearby Reims, and two great churches dominate it.

The basilica of Notre-Dame stands on the pilgrim road south through Burgundy to Compostela and draws pilgrims of its own, for shepherds found a statue of the Virgin there in a burning bush. Newly built Notre-Dame-en-Vaux, a collegiate church, has the pointed vaults of the new French style and two Romanesque towers, and a famous arcaded cloister of sixty column-statues of prophets and saints. The bishop's meadow lies just south of the city, and the Catalaunian Fields a dozen miles out.

neighbours.name: Provins
neighbours.summary:
One of Champagne's chief cities, grown rich under Count Henry I in the later twelfth century. It holds two fairs a year, from May to June in the upper town and from September to October in the lower, when it swells into a vast market of southern and northern visitors: merchants, innkeepers and moneychangers, with many clothmakers, dyers and weavers and a sizeable Jewish community. Count Theobald's court stays here for long spells.

The lower town grew round a Benedictine priory of the eleventh century, built where St. Ayoul's relics were found by a miracle; the upper town round the counts' hilltop castle, crowned by the Caesar Tower.

neighbours.name: Troyes
neighbours.summary:
Champagne's other great fair town, with two fairs a year (late June to early August, and November to mid-December), older than Provins and built on a Gaulish fortress. Its early bishop St. Lupus saved it from Attila by giving himself as a hostage and came home only after long captivity. The fairs' weight is such that Troyes has set its own measure, the Troy ounce.

It has two quarters, the cathedral district, which has hosted great Church councils, and the commercial quarter round the old castle where the fairs are held. Henry I the Liberal founded thirteen churches and thirteen hospitals here. The poet Chretien de Troyes lived here for much of his life, and the great Jewish commentator Rashi (1040 to 1105) was born and taught here. If history holds, Jacques Pantaleon, a local cobbler's son, will become Pope Urban IV in some forty years.

neighbours.name: Lagny
neighbours.summary: A Champagne town holding one of the six great fairs of the cycle; the book gives no more.

neighbours.name: Bar-sur-Aube
neighbours.summary: A Champagne town holding one of the six great fairs of the cycle. Clairvaux abbey keeps a townhouse here.

neighbours.name: Auxerre
neighbours.summary:
Roman Autessiodurum on the road from Lyon to Boulogne, a holy place since the fifth century, when St. Germanus was its bishop: a proud, worldly nobleman and governor of Gaul whom bishop St. Amator turned to prayer by burning his hunting trophies and tonsuring him against his will. Its school was famous under the Carolingians; the town has declined since, though the Pope named it a Holy City in the twelfth century.

Its oldest house is the Benedictine abbey of St. Germanus, and the new cathedral of St. Etienne, begun in 1215, is still little more than a building site.
neighbours.ruler: The Count of Auxerre, under the Count of Champagne

neighbours.name: Avallon
neighbours.summary: A walled town on a granite hilltop over terraced slopes above the Cousin, on the site of the Roman citadel of Aballo. Sacked by the Goths, fortified after raids by Moors and Normans, it is now a formidable stronghold of the dukes that has seen off more than one siege. Pilgrims come to its church of St. Lazarus, a little over a century old, for a piece of the saint's skull that protects against leprosy.

neighbours.name: Vezelay
neighbours.summary: A thriving town in the valley below the hilltop abbey of St. Mary Magdalene, on the edge of the Morvan above the valley of the Cure, living off the steady stream of pilgrims; one of the great roads to Compostela begins here. In 1096 its peasants rose against the abbot's taxes for a new church and killed him.

neighbours.name: Autun
neighbours.summary:
Roman Augustodunum, after Lyon the greatest Roman city of Gaul, on the main road from Lyon to Boulogne, with the most complete Roman remains in the Tribunal. It became one of the earliest bishoprics in France and hosted Church councils, one of which regulated the Benedictines in the seventh century. It has faded since the dukes moved to Dijon.

Two Roman gates still serve, St. Andrew's in the east and the Porta Senonica over the Arroux to the north; the vast Roman theatre, which held twelve thousand, is quarried for stone. Miles of ramparts and aqueducts surround the walls, with the temple of Janus across the river and a ruined pyramid in the fields to the south-east.

neighbours.name: Langres
neighbours.summary: A walled hill-town, the northern gate of Burgundy, named for the Lingones whose capital it was; as Roman Andemantunum it stood where twelve roads met. Its influential bishops rule it now. St. Didier, an early bishop, was beheaded defending it against barbarians, picked up his head and rode away; a chapel marks where he finally died. The Cave of Sabinus lies ten miles south.

neighbours.name: Dijon
neighbours.summary: The ducal seat since 1051 and now Burgundy's largest town, fat on the court: a centre of art and trade full of poets, craftsmen and visiting minor nobles with their hangers-on. A riot and fire in 1137 burned nearly all of it; Duke Hugh II rebuilt it with wider walls and a grand palace. In 1220 the foundations of a great new church in the French style were lately laid. St. Benignus's abbey church keeps the tomb of its founding patron saint.

neighbours.name: Cluny
neighbours.summary: A large, wealthy town beside the great abbey, there mostly to supply the monks with the luxuries they want: jewellers, goldsmiths and other fine craftsmen, with a steady flow of visitors besides.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Chalons
neighbours.summary: Lord of Chalons and a part of every coronation at Reims. The city's great churches are the pilgrim basilica of Notre-Dame, on the road to Compostela where a statue of the Virgin was found in a burning bush, and the new collegiate church of Notre-Dame-en-Vaux with its cloister of sixty statue-columns. The bishop owns the meadow south of the city where St. Bernard and Pope Eugene III preached.

neighbours.name: Priory of St. Ayoul
neighbours.summary: The eleventh-century Benedictine priory at the heart of Provins's lower town, where the relics of St. Ayoul were miraculously discovered.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Troyes
neighbours.summary: The see of St. Lupus, who saved Troyes from Attila. Its cathedral quarter has hosted important Church councils in past centuries.

neighbours.name: Clairvaux Abbey
neighbours.summary:
The clear valley, founded by St. Bernard in 1115, is among the greatest and most influential Cistercian houses in France, on the northern edge of Burgundy. Austere quadrangles of lodgings and workshops sit inside a strong wall with watchtowers; its 300-foot church, a Latin cross, has no stained glass, carving or steeple. Gardens, orchards, a spring and carefully kept fishponds fill the precinct. The whole abbey has a Divine aura of 6.

It is the model for many other Cistercian houses. Its workshop turns out a great many manuscripts, it has lately built an iron-smelting forge at Wassy, and it keeps a townhouse at Bar-sur-Aube. Eugene III, who became pope in 1145, had been a monk here.

St. Bernard (1090 to 1153), a nobleman's son who entered Citeaux at twenty-one and founded Clairvaux at twenty-five, kept his monks on boiled vegetables, water and bare pallets; that they survived seemed a miracle, and the hard life drew followers. He rose to lead the Church of his day, preached the Second Crusade at Vezelay in 1146, prosecuted Abelard for heresy, and is the patron saint of farms and farmhands.

neighbours.name: Abbey of Cunfin
neighbours.summary: A plain Cistercian abbey in a deep valley of Champagne, close to the fair roads, whose monks keep open house for the many travellers. Its prior, Brother Eligius, is revered for his piety and wisdom, and the monks believe the holy hermit in the hills above blesses them twice over. Its abbot, Martin, is a man in middle age with considerable influence in the Cistercian Order.
neighbours.secrets: Brother Eligius is Eloi of Jerbiton, and the abbey shares its valley with the covenant of Cunfin. Martin, the cellarer and a few brothers know and help the magi, and Martin uses his influence in the Order on their behalf.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St. Germanus, Auxerre
neighbours.summary: Auxerre's oldest house, a Benedictine abbey founded in the sixth century by Clotilda, wife of King Clovis. Beneath it a great Carolingian crypt painted with magnificent frescoes holds St. Germanus's tomb, a place of pilgrimage.

neighbours.name: Church of St. Lazarus, Avallon
neighbours.summary: Avallon's pilgrim church, just over a hundred years old, keeping a piece of St. Lazarus's skull, a relic that grants divine protection against leprosy.

neighbours.name: Abbey of Vezelay
neighbours.summary:
The Benedictine abbey keeping the relics of St. Mary Magdalene, Burgundy's greatest pilgrimage since the eleventh century and the start of a main road to Compostela. St. Bernard preached the Second Crusade here, Philip II and Richard the Lionheart met here before the Third, and the exiled Thomas Becket excommunicated Henry II's supporters here in 1166.

Founded by Gerard de Roussillon and destroyed by the Normans in the ninth century, it was rebuilt on a hilltop on the edge of the Morvan. Its history is chequered: peasants killed the abbot over taxes for a larger church in 1096, and in 1120 the new church burned on the feast of the great pilgrimage, 22 July, with a thousand pilgrims inside. The Basilica of St. Mary Magdalene has since been rebuilt.
neighbours.secrets: The relics' origin is unclear: one story says St. Badilo brought them from the Holy Land in the ninth century, another that the saint's tomb was found at St. Maximin in Provence, identified by a carving of the anointing at Bethany. The monks do not doubt them.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Autun (Cathedral of St. Lazarus)
neighbours.summary: One of the oldest sees of France. The cathedral of St. Lazarus at the south of the city keeps that saint's relics, brought from Provence in the tenth century by Gerard de Roussillon in a failed bid to rival Vezelay. It is the dukes' chapel, and the episcopal palace beside it was their seat before Dijon; the dukes were buried here until Citeaux.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Langres
neighbours.summary: The bishops who now rule Langres, heirs of the martyr St. Didier, whose chapel marks where he died after riding off with his head in his hands.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St. Benignus, Dijon
neighbours.summary: The abbey church in Dijon whose crypt holds the tomb of St. Benignus, founder and patron of the city.

neighbours.name: Citeaux Abbey
neighbours.summary:
The mother house of the Cistercians, founded in 1098 by Robert of Molesme, who left his lax abbey with twenty monks for a dreadful reedy swamp a dozen miles south of Dijon; the reeds gave the abbey its name. The monks drained it through great hardship, and under St. Bernard it flourished; it now mothers more than five hundred Cistercian houses across Europe.

For all its sprawl of buildings it keeps its austerity, discipline and manual labour. Its great church, finished in 1193, is the new burial place of the dukes of Burgundy. Since 1147 the attached house of La Trappe has kept its monks in solemn contemplation.

neighbours.name: Cluny Abbey
neighbours.summary:
Founded in 910 by William I of Aquitaine, the most powerful monastery there has ever been: mother of a thousand Cluniac houses whose priors meet here every year, its abbot answering to the Pope alone. Closely tied to the papacy since the Gregorian reforms, it has given the Church several popes; Urban II called it the light of the world, and St. Bernard asked whether the light needed a golden candlestick. A little waned by the Cistercians' rise, it still arguably rivals Rome and leads western monasticism.

It is everything Citeaux is not: wealth and splendour, with abbots who live like kings. Its abbey church of Sts. Peter and Paul, built under St. Hugh and Peter the Venerable, is the largest building in Christendom, nearly 600 feet long with two transepts, four aisles and five belfries, lavishly adorned. Its library is among the richest in Europe, and the abbots keep a fine townhouse in Paris. Its Divine aura is strong (strength not given).
neighbours.secrets: Optionally, dark powers may be working Cluny's slow corruption through the monks' love of luxury: servants of the Devil hidden in its hierarchy, Infernal auras pocketed inside the Divine one, or places where the Divine aura is weaker than it should be.

neighbours.name: Pontigny Abbey
neighbours.summary: A notable Burgundian abbey where Thomas Becket spent part of his exile from England.

neighbours.name: Fontenay Abbey
neighbours.summary: A notable Burgundian abbey some six miles north of Mont Auxois and the ruins of Alesia.

neighbours.name: Molesme Abbey
neighbours.summary: The Benedictine abbey whose laxity drove its abbot Robert to leave with twenty monks in 1098 and found Citeaux.

neighbours.name: The Merchants of the Champagne Fairs
neighbours.summary: The six great fairs of the Champagne cycle (Provins and Troyes hold two apiece, Lagny and Bar-sur-Aube one each), with lesser fairs in other towns, are among the main meeting places of northern and southern trade: Flemish wool against Eastern spices and luxuries, with merchants from as far as Constantinople and Scotland. Their weight gave Troyes its own measure, the Troy ounce.

details.wants: Safe roads, fair dealing and the count's protection for the fair cycle.
details.offers: Goods from Constantinople to Scotland, credit, and news from every road.

neighbours.name: The Temporary Mercer Houses of the Fairs
neighbours.summary: At most of the Champagne fairs Redcaps, organised mostly from Confluensis and Cunfin, put up temporary Mercer Houses, quietly trading vis, books and other Hermetic goods and swapping news and messages. Hervé le Brun of Cunfin has taken over their running from his father Évrard, a post his foster brother Renaud wanted.

details.wants: Profit, news and the Redcaps' standing at the fairs.
details.offers: Vis, books and Hermetic goods for sale, letters carried and news traded.

neighbours.name: The Jews of Troyes
neighbours.summary: A Jewish community settled at Troyes in the eleventh century under the counts' protection; there is another sizeable one at Provins. Its most famous son is Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki, Rashi (1040 to 1105), who studied at Worms and Mainz, came home at twenty-five, and wrote the great commentaries on the Tanakh and the Talmud, weaving literal reading with allegory and symbol. Copies are found in Troyes and other leading Jewish communities; each commentary is a Theology (Judaism) tractatus of Quality 13.

details.wants: The counts' continued protection.
details.offers: Learning, and copies of Rashi's commentaries.

neighbours.name: The Priory of St. Nerius
neighbours.summary: Followers of St. Nerius, a holy man who reconciled Magic and the Divine, who seek his recognition by the Latin Church. Eloi of Cunfin is close to them without being a member, and rumour says Cunfin abbey was founded in 1136 by Valoran, Nerius's pupil. Realms of Power: The Divine describes them.

details.wants: St. Nerius recognised as a saint by the Latin Church.
details.offers: A bridge between the Magic and the Divine.

neighbours.name: The Cotentin marshes
neighbours.summary: More than 2,500 acres of brackish, untamed swamp that all but cut the Cotentin peninsula off from the rest of Normandy, so that people call it an island. With no good roads across, the peninsula is thinly peopled and holds no great lordships, and outsiders seldom bother with it. Confluensis lies hidden in the tidal reaches, where the rivers meet the sea; strangers crossing the fens risk the fen ague, a fever Hermetic magic can cure. The marsh's own aura is not given.

neighbours.name: The Confluence
neighbours.summary: The site of Confluensis, in the swamp's tidal zone at the very middle of the band where the rivers' fresh, fertile water pushes back the barren salt. Under the covenant's raised floors creation and destruction wrestle with every tide, and on spring tides they spin up dancing whirlpools that the magi catch in enchanted nets for vis. The book calls the Magic aura powerful but gives no score. A ring of magical mist and contrary currents hides the place: the covenfolk learn the currents' usual pattern, which a device in the council chamber can change; the watch carry items that see through the mist and the turb captain one that thickens or thins it; and a ring of active defences, which the magi say they change often, lies beyond.

details.tethers: The tide, where fresh river water turns back the salt

neighbours.secrets: One of the covenant's founders had a flaw in her Gift that made building on the tide necessary; only a few magi know it.

neighbours.name: The Orchard
neighbours.summary: An island north-east of Coutances where many of Confluensis's covenfolk live, taken from a faerie court soon after the site was settled because of its aura and its vis. Its trees bear small, sour apples full of Intellego vis. Folk say that when a virgin peels one with her left hand the peel forms her future husband's initial, and its taste foretells how sweet the marriage will be, but the hedge wizards who knew the custom could not write it down and the magi will not waste the vis. The island's Faerie aura has slowly turned to Magic (its score is not given), though a weak Faerie aura returns at each solstice. The Orchard of Sour Apples, the vassal covenant whose site Confluensis took over in 1051, was named for it.

neighbours.name: The Hospitallers' City of God
neighbours.summary: A new Hospitaller settlement near Confluensis, meant to grow into a City of God: a perfect town ruled by the Church, where everyone is devout and sin does not happen. For now it is a grant of land and a hospital kept by three elderly knights of the Order. In effect a small monastery, it has a Dominion aura of 4. The knights often have True Faith or relics, are sworn to obey their Order's master, and are so pious that moving against them may draw demons to help in secret. Many such cities fail and end as homes for old crusaders, who could train grogs and may have fought djinn, demons and faeries. Confluensis wants it gone from the peninsula, but must set no precedent other covenants could abuse.

neighbours.name: The statue of St. Giles
neighbours.summary: A statue of St. Giles in the Cotentin that local people use as a fertility charm. It has been given a large phallus, from which they shave slivers of wood for a healing drink, and they say the wood grows back by a miracle. That may be God at work in a way the Church does not teach, a demon or faerie using the statue, or a magical device. A phallic saint is heresy, and the Hospitallers nearby may call in the preaching friars if they hear of it. Its realm and aura are not given.

neighbours.name: The lair of the Gargouille
neighbours.summary: A drowned cavern in the estuary swamps near the Seine's mouth, where the river bends on its north bank, once the lair of the dragon Gargouille, which rose from the river in the seventh century spewing floods until St. Romanus of Rouen stopped it with the sign of the cross and a condemned prisoner dragged it to Rouen to burn. Confluensis stood here from 810 to 1051; raided a dozen times in a century, its magi grew skilled in battle magic, and much of the Order's early guessing about the Order of Odin came from contacts here. Dragon's Rest holds it now. Its aura is not given.

neighbours.name: The Boar King's Hall
neighbours.summary: A timber stronghold in a faerie regio, reached from several dark, damp groves deep in the Tribunal's forests where the air is close and the sun hardly reaches the ground. From outside the groves show only gloom and rot; it takes days of travel to reach the forest's heart.

levels.name: The Boar King's fortress
levels.enter: Through one of the dark groves, if the King allows it
levels.notes: The King has barred Hermetic hoplites from entering.

neighbours.secrets: The hall is the Boar King's, and his court of faerie knights and courtiers camps there between hunts. Some of the plenty the court offers guests is glamour. The King learns each day roughly where and how many humans are in his forest, so visitors are expected long before they arrive.

neighbours.name: The Ships of Flame
neighbours.summary: Three small magical regiones along the Seine, each holding a Viking longship that burns without end as the pyre of a dead warlord. A regio opens only to someone drifting down the river in a burning boat on the day that warlord died; leaving needs only a swim to the bank. The fire needs no fuel and never consumes the ship, but it burns away anything brought in that magic does not protect, and anyone on deck suffers +20 fire damage each round, a magical attack of Penetration 30. A strong Perdo Ignem effect could put a fire out, and would probably destroy the regio with it.

levels.name: The first burning ship
levels.enter: Drift down the Seine in a boat aflame on the death-day of the warlord it holds
levels.notes: Queen Skuld's laboratory is on its deck.

levels.name: The second burning ship
levels.enter: Drift down the Seine in a boat aflame on the death-day of the warlord it holds

levels.name: The third burning ship
levels.enter: Drift down the Seine in a boat aflame on the death-day of the warlord it holds

neighbours.secrets: Queen Skuld, Hierophant of the Children of Odin, lives here alone and keeps her laboratory on the deck of one ship. A cult initiate's first Quest is to reach a deck unaided and take an axe from a fallen warrior. Few others visit, as the days are hard to time, so Skuld speaks to her cult through Haunt of the Living Ghost.

neighbours.name: The Court of the Boar King
neighbours.summary:
A faerie the Gauls once worshipped, the Boar King is a big man with a boar's head and two great tusks that thicken his speech; his bare arms and chest carry abstract tattoos and bronze rings, and he wears hide trousers and a cloak and rides a wild horse bareback with faerie knights and courtiers at his side. He claims the Tribunal's forests, as other powers also do, hunts boar each autumn, and turns the hunt on hunters who take too much.

Centuries ago House Diedne helped him guard his woods. He knows the House fell, has watched men and the Divine eat into the forest, and has decided that killing the odd greedy hunter changes nothing; he now looks for new Hermetic allies, most likely among Merinita and Bjornaer, to halt and undo the clearing of the forest. His offer copies the Forest Paths of the Rhine; whether it is a true one hardly matters given what his court can supply an ally.

In brief, as the book gives him: Faerie Might 40 (Animal), Size +1, Reckless +3, Proud +2, Wrathful +1, known locally as King of the Forest and in the Order as an ally of House Diedne. He fights with boar spears and his tusks, is a master hunter and woodsman, and speaks Gaulish, Latin and Breton. His powers let him command the forest's beasts and plants, sense the human intruders in his forest each day, fall into a day-long rage that will not retreat or spare anyone, pin a victim helpless with a thrown spear until it is pulled out (a Heavy Wound), and appear anywhere in his forest. Each tusk holds 4 pawns of Animal vis.

details.rules: Take no more from the forest than it can spare; the King's word is law.
details.wants: Hermetic allies to replace House Diedne as wardens of his forests, and the advance of men and the Church driven back
details.offers: A share of the forest's power, Virtues through Salvirius's quests, and the court's resources, some of them glamour

neighbours.secrets: Salvirius, his subtle adviser, sounds out the magi the King approaches and sets the quests by which the court grants Virtues. A Diedne magus thought dead in the Schism War is rumoured to ride with the court.

neighbours.name: The Children of Odin
neighbours.summary:
A secret Mystery Cult whose magi call themselves heirs to the magic of the ninth-century Viking raiders. The pedigree is claimed, not real: the cult is barely ten years old. It is small, probably no more than half a dozen magi, and the Order has not found it. Members need a good Ignem score to survive their first Quest, which suits Flambeau, and Montverte magi descended from that covenant's Scandinavian founders are likely recruits. It is not the Order of Odin, only a cult claiming to have found some of its secrets.

Initiation Scripts. The cult can initiate three Virtues: Life Boost (Minor Hermetic), Minor Magical Focus in shape-shifting (Minor Hermetic) and Life-Linked Spontaneous Magic (Major Hermetic). The Ordeals that go with them may leave the initiate with Blood Haze (Minor Hermetic: within a dozen paces of blood shed in violence the maga takes -10 to Formulaic magic and -3 to Concentration), Flawed Parma Magica against Vim (Minor Hermetic) or Deficient Technique in Creo (Major Hermetic).

Initiation. Without the Mystery Cult rules, the Mystagogue sets the initiate a Quest of about a year, during which they suffer an Ordeal (a Flaw) and gain the Mystery (a Virtue); the instructions are an Initiation Script, a special Laboratory Text. The first Quest is to reach the deck of one of the Ships of Flame unaided and bring back an axe from a dead Viking. Raiding with Nordic Triumph has served as another.

Nordic Triumph is the cult's ritual (MuMe(He)(Te) 65; Touch, Moon, Structure): cast aboard a ship, it turns her into a dragon-prowed longship and her crew into Viking warriors who follow the caster as their chief, fighting as a trained band though they gain no Abilities they lacked.

details.rules: Secrecy; obedience to the Hierophant; advancement by initiation, a Quest and an Ordeal for each Mystery
details.wants: Normandy taken from the French crown, with Skuld crowned its maga-queen
details.offers: Viking magic: Life Boost, a shape-shifting Focus, Life-Linked Spontaneous Magic, and the ritual Nordic Triumph

neighbours.secrets:
Queen Skuld is Hierophant and has been Mystagogue at every initiation. Her aim is power: Normandy back in Norman hands and herself crowned its maga-queen as Rollo's heir. What draws other magi is not her politics but the Viking secrets she says she found in wrecks and ruins as a young maga.

Thormod of Montverte is a leading member who practises the cult's Viking magic and uses his influence for it; he may be Skuld's kin or lover. If the cult truly descends from the Order of Odin, it may know rune magic, or a researcher may one day bring the runes into Hermetic theory; if it does not, Skuld may be lying to her followers.

neighbours.name: The Cabal of Frankish Gold
neighbours.summary: A Tytalan cabal working to make the Lotharingian Tribunal happen. Like every Tytalus cabal its members are anonymous to one another, meet in disguise or not at all, and may come from more than one Tribunal; they share the goal, not the reasons. Some honestly want the new Tribunal as a utopia for magi, Tytali above all, free of the weight of their old Peripheral Codes, and mean to found a new covenant there whether or not their own covenants join.

details.rules: Membership anonymous; meetings in disguise or by letter and spell
details.wants: A Lotharingian Tribunal founded, each member for their own reasons
details.offers: Tytalan wit, gold and connections in two or more Tribunals

neighbours.secrets: Augustina of Confluensis, the Traitor, belongs: she thinks the new Tribunal doomed but likes the principle that unhappy magi may break from an old Tribunal, and wants to see how the Order answers a challenge in its heartland. Prima Buliste joins only to keep her brother Harpax busy. At least one member is a saboteur, quietly souring relations between the movement's covenants.

neighbours.name: The Cabal of the Golden Coin
neighbours.summary: A cabal that fixes the Hermetic Tourney so its members take the best prizes. Tytali began it, but most members now come from other Houses. Several of the changes to the prize levels, put forward as points of tradition, were its work, meant to open gaps in the prizes it can exploit.

details.rules: Members anonymous to outsiders; agreements made in secret and kept
details.wants: The Tourney's prizes, the tropaeum leases above all
details.offers: A contest fixed for a modest bribe of vis

neighbours.secrets: Members agree in secret which contests to throw so their teams place best. Some leave their covenant's team to field a separate one, which places remarkably well: a team of three young magi, each of a different covenant and House, has come fourteenth at the last three Tourneys. Late in a Tourney a member may quietly offer a covenant a fixed contest for a little vis.

neighbours.name: The Lotharingian Movement
neighbours.summary:
Covenants of the north and west of the Rhine and the neighbouring part of Normandy that want to revive the Lotharingian Tribunal, which the Grand Tribunal of 865 created and that of 898 dissolved. Four Rhine covenants back it in whole or part (Triamore, Fengheld's supporters, Waddenzee and Oculus Septentrionalis) with three of Normandy (Florum, its vassal Spider's Palace, and Requies Aeterna, also Florum's vassal). Florum and Triamore conceived it.

Their aim is a Tribunal where magi need not hide what they are, brought about slowly with help from churchmen in the Rhine cities, using their arts for mankind's good without breaking the Oath's ban on meddling. Writing their own Peripheral Code, they would allow more than the Rhine and less than Normandy, and they think the consortium strong enough to keep nobles from dragging them into war and politics. They mean to put the proposal to the Grand Tribunal of 1228 and found the Tribunal only later, expecting resistance.

details.rules: Each covenant pledges support in whole or in part
details.wants: A new Lotharingian Tribunal with its own Peripheral Code, proposed at the Grand Tribunal of 1228
details.offers: Freedom from Normandy's raiding and its rulings on meddling, and openness with the mundane world

neighbours.secrets: Their reasons differ: Daria la Gris wants Triamore to matter; about half of Fengheld's 23 magi agree in theory and plan chapter houses beyond Cologne; Waddenzee wants a Code that permits its piracy; Oculus Septentrionalis wants open trade and may plant a covenant to counter Waddenzee. Requies Aeterna expects a Lotharingian Code to dissolve its oath to Florum and would not mind. Montverte and Waddenzee plan for Waddenzee to join and then defect as Montverte's vassal, crippling the new Tribunal.

neighbours.name: The Boar King's Hunt
neighbours.summary: The Boar King, a faerie lord of the old Gaulish forests, has decided that hunting down greedy hunters no longer holds back the plough, the axe and the Church. He wants Hermetic wardens for his woods, as House Diedne once was, and is ready to court them, with Salvirius to make the offers. Whether he exists in this saga is the troupe's choice.

details.antagonist: The Boar King, faerie lord of the forests

stages.title: Hunters hunted
stages.clues: Each autumn the boar hunts end badly for those who took too much: poachers and lords' huntsmen are found speared deep in the forest. Charcoal-burners speak of a rider with a boar's head leading faerie knights through groves where the sun never reaches.
stages.ignored: The killings go on and foresters and settlers stay out of the deep woods.
stages.stopped: The covenant warns the locals to take less; the hunt passes them by, and the King notices who gave the warning.
stages.turned: The covenant learns the court's customs and earns a cautious welcome.

stages.title: Master of the Hunt
stages.clues: A Merinita or Bjornaer magus travelling alone through the forest is met by the King and a quieter courtier, Salvirius, who tests his feeling for the wild and, if he likes the answers, offers a share of the forest's power for a sacrifice and a quest, perhaps the destruction of a new settlement cut into the woods.
stages.ignored: The King finds another magus, perhaps one of a rival covenant.
stages.stopped: The offer is refused; the court counts the covenant among the men of the axe.
stages.turned: A magus of the covenant becomes the King's ally and forest warden, gaining Virtues from Salvirius at the price of a Flaw each, and owing the court his help.

stages.title: The desecrated temple
stages.clues: Missionaries once pulled down the Boar King's temples, and now a revived cult is trying to consecrate one again. The cultists may come to the covenant asking help against the Church, or local churchmen may come asking help to put the cult down, and to be sure the covenant has no part in it.
stages.ignored: Cult and Church clash, blood is spilled, and the Church looks for wizards behind the pagans.
stages.stopped: The cult is broken up; the Church is satisfied and the King enraged.
stages.turned: The covenant brokers a quiet peace: the old rites kept deep in the wood, out of the bishop's sight, or covenant members lead the cult themselves.

stages.title: The hidden enemy
stages.clues: A Quaesitor of the Tribunal visits, raising hoplites to look, by force if need be, into word of a Diedne magus seen with the Boar King. The King meets the hoplites outside his regio, orders them gone and refuses them entry.
stages.ignored: The Quaesitores go in without the covenant, and anyone who dealt with the King may later be asked why.
stages.stopped: The hoplites force the regio and break the court; the King, in his ancient rage, turns on every settler in his woods.
stages.turned: A magus allied with the King defends his realm against the Quaesitor, setting himself against his own sodales, or brokers terms that spare both.

stages.title: The forest pushed back
stages.clues: With Hermetic allies at last, the King moves openly against new clearings and villages, as he once did with Diedne at his side; nobles and abbots who own the assarts complain of wizards in the woods.
stages.ignored: Villages burn, the Church and the nobles blame the Order, and the Tribunal asks who let it happen.
stages.stopped: The King is humbled or bound by treaty, and the plough moves on into the forest.
stages.turned: A lasting compact keeps some forests the King's and gives the covenant a faerie ally, and perhaps his tusks' vis in time.

neighbours.secrets: A Diedne magus believed killed in the Schism War is rumoured to ride with him, and the Quaesitores will come. Salvirius is not what he seems: he can teach Diedne Magic, and his last offer marks the magus who takes it for an unknown watcher in Paris.

neighbours.name: Queen Skuld and the Ships of Flame
neighbours.summary: Raiders out of the Viking age appear on a coast that has not seen them in two hundred years. Behind them is the Children of Odin, a young and secret Mystery Cult, and its Hierophant Queen Skuld, who wants Normandy back from the French king and herself crowned its maga-queen. Whether the cult exists in this saga is the troupe's choice.

details.antagonist: Queen Skuld, Hierophant of the Children of Odin

stages.title: A Norman conquest
stages.clues: A covenant magus of strong Norman blood is visited by a relative who wants backing for an Anglo-Norman attack on mainland France. The relative is controlled by a Child of Odin, sounding out how the magus feels about the French holding Normandy.
stages.ignored: The cult tests other Norman-born magi until one bites.
stages.stopped: The control is found and broken; the cult learns it has been noticed.
stages.turned: The magus seems keen, is approached by the cult with its 'more realistic plan', and may be initiated through its degrees.

stages.title: Attack ships
stages.clues: Vikings raid a string of monasteries on the Normandy coast and merchant ships go missing. The covenant, being near, is asked to investigate. Hermetic magic is plainly involved, but the casting sigils are shrouded. The raids are a cult initiate's Quest, carried out with Nordic Triumph.
stages.ignored: The raids go on; the Church and the king's officers look for the wizards behind them.
stages.stopped: The responsible cultist is found and the raids end; a case at Tribunal may bring the cult to the Order's notice.
stages.turned: The culprit is bargained with and the secret kept, for a price; or the culprit is a player magus already in the cult.

stages.title: The tapestry
stages.clues: A band of Vikings appears at the gates of Bayeux, hacks its way into the cathedral and makes off with the Tapestry; or a cult member is sent to fetch it quietly. The Church asks the covenant to recover it, or its magi are in the town when the raiders come.
stages.ignored: The Tapestry vanishes into a burning regio on the Seine.
stages.stopped: The Tapestry is recovered, and the Church is grateful.
stages.turned: The covenant keeps the Tapestry, a bargaining piece both the cult and the Church want back.

stages.title: The burning ships
stages.clues: The trail leads to the Seine and to three burning longships in regiones that open only to a burning boat drifting downstream on a warlord's death-day. The fire on deck kills the unprotected.
stages.ignored: Skuld finishes her preparations undisturbed.
stages.stopped: Skuld is confronted on her ship and the cult laid before the Quaesitores; quenching the fires would end the regiones too.
stages.turned: The covenant strikes a bargain with the Hierophant or joins her.

stages.title: The maga-queen of Normandy
stages.clues: With the Tapestry as her link, Skuld casts at the French king; risings in Normandy and Norman relatives across the Channel are stirred to strike at once.
stages.ignored: Magic strikes the King of France; if it is traced, the Order is blamed and ruin follows.
stages.stopped: The cult is broken and Skuld slain, Marched or driven back into the North.
stages.turned: Skuld is unmasked as someone else entirely, or her cult is turned to a quieter search for the true magic of the Order of Odin.

links.note: A leading member of the cult

neighbours.secrets: Thormod of Montverte is a leading member. Skuld wants the Bayeux Tapestry to help her spell get through to King Philip, Normandy's duke in law. She may be an impostor, and the cult's magic may not be the Order of Odin's at all.

neighbours.name: The Traitor's Game
neighbours.summary:
House Tytalus keeps a Traitor: a volunteer exiled from the House and counted the loser of all her contests, beneath any Tytalus's notice as a rival, whose one duty to the House is to restart its struggles when they stall. Since the time of Tasgillia the Traitor has carried a magical key; most think it once weakened Fudarus's defences, and some think it now only a symbol.

The present Traitor, Augustina of Confluensis, a hoplite trained by the last Traitor, serves Proctor, who trusts no Tytalus and gives her the riskiest work. Meanwhile the House's two Primi, Harpax and Buliste, have been deadlocked for twenty years, and only one can take the House's seat at the Grand Tribunal of 1228.

stages.title: A stalled feud
stages.clues: Decimi wearing Harpax's sigil and Fideli under Buliste's purple banner shout down mediators, who come away feeling they were the joke. Harpax holds Fudarus, its vis and its Rod; Buliste holds the House's web of spies and suppliers. Nothing moves, and Augustina is seen asking after both.
stages.ignored: The deadlock holds and the Traitor decides the game needs waking.
stages.stopped: Proctor keeps Augustina busy elsewhere, for now.
stages.turned: The covenant becomes Augustina's confidant and hears what she plans.

stages.title: The dangerous device
stages.clues: Fudarus offers new vassals generous terms. Sworn vassals are sent to find the pieces of a powerful pre-Hermetic item for Harpax, not knowing it is a Diedne relic, that Buliste led him to want it, or that she means to frame him with it. A trusted merchant vanishes on false charges laid by Harpax, and a spirit from Buliste offers help.
stages.ignored: The covenant is left holding a relic that is dangerous both magically and politically.
stages.stopped: The relic is hidden or destroyed, and both Primi are cheated.
stages.turned: The covenant plays the Primi against each other for its own gain.

stages.title: Gold for Lotharingia
stages.clues: The Cabal of Frankish Gold puts its weight behind the Lotharingian movement, while someone sours the movement's covenants against one another. Augustina's name surfaces where the Traitor has no business.
stages.ignored: The movement and its enemies grow bitter; the Traitor watches the Order react.
stages.stopped: The saboteur, or Augustina's part, is exposed; Proctor must answer for his Traitor.
stages.turned: The covenant uses the cabal's gold and secrets for its own ends.

stages.title: A third contender
stages.clues: Porphyrion of Tytalus, an archmagus who came from Rome three years ago, asks to join a young covenant. Local Tytali think he wants the House for himself; Harpax and Buliste close ranks against him.
stages.ignored: Porphyrion settles elsewhere and waits for one Primus to fall.
stages.stopped: He is refused, and both Primi are quietly grateful.
stages.turned: His power transforms the covenant, and makes it the target of both Primi.

stages.title: The seat at Durenmar
stages.clues: The Grand Tribunal of 1228 nears and the feud escalates: whoever sits in the House's seat will have shown they are the stronger. If Buliste sits alone, Harpax may arrive on the last day with news of a threat to the Order, perhaps one of his own making.
stages.ignored: The feud spills into the Tribunal, and the Order may face a danger Harpax manufactured.
stages.stopped: One Primus yields, and the House settles under a single head.
stages.turned: A third contender takes the House, steadying it and restoring Fudarus's power in Normandy.

links.note: Prima, holding the House's web of spies
The House's seat the Primi contest

neighbours.secrets: Augustina sits in the Cabal of Frankish Gold, backing the Lotharingian Tribunal she expects to fail, to see how the Order answers a challenge in its heartland. She was trained by Buliste's own mater. Buliste is in the cabal only to keep Harpax busy, and a saboteur in it works against the movement. Each of the feud's ends is open: one Primus yields, one dies or disappears (neither will commit a High Crime), or a third contender beats both.

neighbours.name: The Lotharingian Secession
neighbours.summary:
A Tribunal needs twelve magi from four covenants. Florum and Triamore lead a movement to carve a new Lotharingian Tribunal from the north and west of the Rhine and the neighbouring part of Normandy, to be proposed at the Grand Tribunal of 1228. The last new Tribunal was Novgorod in 1008, but this one would take land the Rhine and Normandy have held for centuries, and the traditionalists, most of the Rhine among them, are horrified. Both losing Tribunals have their critics, and the distant ones do not care.

For Normandy the loss is serious: the region holds great mundane wealth and some of the Tribunal's best vis, and without it Brittany, Tytalus country, would produce more vis than the rest of the Tribunal together. A covenant in Flanders, Picardy or Champagne must watch closely, and so must any covenant holding legacies there, which a Lotharingian Code might not honour.

details.antagonist: The Lotharingian movement, led by Florum and Triamore

stages.title: Speculative missions
stages.clues: Magi are sent into the region to weigh vis sources, mystical places and other resources that may become bargaining chips. Florum airs its grievances over raiding and meddling at every meeting.
stages.ignored: Others survey the land first and know its worth.
stages.stopped: The covenant keeps what it learns to itself.
stages.turned: What the covenant learns buys it a voice with either side.

stages.title: Choosing sides
stages.clues: Each covenant must declare itself. A vassal of Florum is expected to follow its liege; a vassal of another liege must weigh support against its oath. Requies Aeterna quietly hopes the new Code will free it of its oath.
stages.ignored: The covenant is counted undecided, and courted or threatened by both sides.
stages.stopped: The covenant stands with Normandy, and the movement loses a hope.
stages.turned: The covenant pledges to the movement and may lose its Normandy legacies, or its liege's goodwill.

stages.title: Soured friendships
stages.clues: Someone works to spoil relations between the movement's covenants and their neighbours. Waddenzee's pirates court Montverte's council, and Oculus Septentrionalis talks of a covenant of its own in the region.
stages.ignored: The movement fractures from within before it reaches Durenmar.
stages.stopped: The saboteur is unmasked, and the movement's members trust again.
stages.turned: The covenant feeds the quarrels to its own advantage.

stages.title: Riches and vis
stages.clues: Confluensis sends agents inside and outside the Tribunal to talk the covenants out of independence or rally the Grand Tribunal's voters against it, and quietly scouts a site for a Quaesitorial covenant and Mercer House in the new Tribunal's lands.
stages.ignored: Proctor's agents shape the outcome without the covenant.
stages.stopped: The movement's supporters are won back one by one.
stages.turned: Player magi found a frontier covenant as 'the new law' in the new Tribunal.

stages.title: The Grand Tribunal of 1228
stages.clues: The proposal goes before the Grand Tribunal at Durenmar, with the House leaders lobbied hard by both sides.
stages.ignored: The vote goes as the powerful wish; the political map of the western Order may be redrawn without the covenant's say.
stages.stopped: The proposal fails and Lotharingia stays divided between the Rhine and Normandy.
stages.turned: The proposal passes; a new Tribunal follows with its own Peripheral Code, and vassal oaths and legacies there may be void.

links.note: Plots with Waddenzee to wreck it

neighbours.secrets: The Cabal of Frankish Gold backs the movement, with a saboteur inside. Montverte and Waddenzee plan for Waddenzee to join and then defect as Montverte's vassal, leaving the new Tribunal hemmed in by predatory Normandy covenants. Provençal may welcome the new Tribunal and try to merge with it, or fear for its own old Lotharingian lands; with all eyes on Lotharingia, Normandy's Tytali may try to win back ground lost to the Provençal Flambeau.

neighbours.name: The Fixed Tourney
neighbours.summary: The Hermetic Tourney after each Tribunal decides the tropaeum leases for seven years, the Tribunal's books and other prizes. The Cabal of the Golden Coin rigs it.

details.antagonist: The Cabal of the Golden Coin

stages.title: Points of tradition
stages.clues: Proposals to adjust the prize levels come up at Tribunal, each presented as old custom; together they open odd gaps in who wins what.
stages.ignored: The changes pass, and the gaps grow.
stages.stopped: The covenant argues them down at Tribunal.
stages.turned: The covenant proposes changes of its own that suit it.

stages.title: The lucky fourteenth
stages.clues: A team of three young magi from three covenants and three Houses has come fourteenth at three Tourneys in a row; some magi skip their covenant's team to enter one of their own.
stages.ignored: The pattern is noticed by no one, or no one says so.
stages.stopped: The covenant shows the tallies to the Redcaps who keep them.
stages.turned: The covenant asks the team, quietly, how it is done.

stages.title: An offer in the lists
stages.clues: Late in the Tourney a member of the cabal, perhaps one of the fourteenth-place team, approaches the covenant and offers to fix a contest for a little vis.
stages.ignored: The covenant ranks lower than it should, and a rival higher.
stages.stopped: The offer is refused and reported; the Quaesitores take an interest.
stages.turned: The covenant pays, places higher, and is now the cabal's accomplice.

stages.title: Fair play
stages.clues: The cabal now chooses who holds the tropaeum leases; covenants that lost out begin to wonder aloud.
stages.ignored: The Tourney becomes a sham, and the Tribunal's vis drifts to the cabal's members.
stages.stopped: A case at Tribunal breaks the cabal, the prizes are restored and the Tourney's rules mended.
stages.turned: The covenant joins the cabal and shares its prizes, and its risk.

neighbours.secrets: The cabal's members trade thrown contests, field 'lucky' separate teams, and shaped the prize levels to suit themselves. Members of the Cabal of the Crushed Viper, who hate the chivalric ideal, may want the Tourney ended altogether.

neighbours.name: A Romantic Saga
neighbours.summary:
A saga frame. The romances sung by trouvères (noble poets who collect their songs in chansonniers) and jongleurs (lower-born minstrels) shape the Tribunal's culture: chivalry, courtly love, and more and more often wizards, faeries and devils. Their two great cycles are the Matter of Britain, which Chrétien de Troyes and his followers made French, and the Matter of France, Charlemagne and his twelve paladins, with Roland's fall at Roncevaux the best known of all. In Mythic Europe the Arthurian tales lack Galahad, and Camelot does not fall through Lancelot and Guinevere.

The songs hide true lore: monsters, regiones, treasures, vis sources and faerie places, and many cite old books, perhaps lost Hermetic works, such as the ancient Breton book Geoffrey of Monmouth claimed and the book Meister Kyot found in Toledo. Magi read them as clues, Grail-seekers such as the Knights of the Green Stone as maps, and a few, like Celeres of Cunfin, as a code to live by. In a high-fantasy telling, the magi keep stumbling into faerie regiones where faerie knights guard every crossroads.

details.antagonist: The romance's own peril: the gap between the ideal of chivalry and its practice

stages.title: A song worth hearing
stages.clues: A jongleur's chanson names a place the magi recognise; some trouvères know of the Order and sing magi's deeds for Hermetic patrons. A knight errant who looks exactly like one of the magi arrives at the gate: a twin, and an Arcane Connection, that the magus's parens never mentioned.
stages.ignored: Rivals mine the songs first, and the twin's resemblance is noticed by others.
stages.stopped: The covenant keeps its secrets and the knight rides on.
stages.turned: The songs lead to a vis source or a faerie place; the twin becomes a companion.

stages.title: The unbreakable blade
stages.clues: Grogs back from Compostela bring a sliver of metal full of magic, sold near Roncevaux as a chip of Durendal, Roland's relic-hilted sword that would not break. Is the sword at Rocamadour, as the locals say, or elsewhere?
stages.ignored: Others follow the sliver to the sword.
stages.stopped: The fragment proves a fake, or is laid to rest with the relics.
stages.turned: The search for Durendal begins in earnest.

stages.title: The strange fate of Chrétien de Troyes
stages.clues: Celeres of Cunfin faints over a book a Redcap brought him: Chrétien's own journal, planning a trip to Brittany's Arthurian sites to finish Perceval and fearing knights who shadow him, knights who match Wolfram's Grail Templars. It ends as he sets out.
stages.ignored: The journal's trail goes cold, or someone else follows it.
stages.stopped: The mystery is solved: an ordinary death, or a faerie regio, as Merlin's was.
stages.turned: The magi find what Chrétien was looking for in Brittany.

stages.title: The Grail in Iberia
stages.clues: A covenant knight brings home Wolfram's Parsifal, rumoured to be the work of the Rhine magus Gunnar von Falster. Its margins name a book by 'Flegetanis the heathen' found in Toledo, and beside the Grail castle someone has written 'Montserrat', the jagged mountain above Barcelona where a covenant once vanished.
stages.ignored: Others go to Montserrat first.
stages.stopped: Montserrat holds only the lost covenant's ruins.
stages.turned: The quest for the Grail leads south.

stages.title: Courtly love
stages.clues: A maga finds herself the subject of love songs the covenfolk now hum. The trouvère, a powerful lord with a relic in his ring, comes to court her, thinks her a noblewoman, writes verses about her 'court', and may propose marriage. An old knight friend of the covenant, ruined, rides to a tournament for ransoms he cannot win, with a magus watching from the stands.
stages.ignored: The suitor's songs draw eyes to the covenant; the old knight is maimed or killed.
stages.stopped: Delicate diplomacy or a clever ruse sends the suitor away content.
stages.turned: The suitor becomes a patron; the old knight wins, helped covertly, and the watching magus is fooled.

stages.title: The Grail quest
stages.clues: The lost books, Durendal and Chrétien's road all point to the Grail, as the troupe has chosen to see it.
stages.ignored: The Grail is found by others, or lost again for an age.
stages.stopped: The quest fails, as the knights of the romances so often do.
stages.turned: The Grail, or the perfection it stands for, is won.

links.note: Lives by the code of chivalry

neighbours.secrets: The troupe should decide early whether the Grail is a thing to be found, as in the early romances, or a symbol of spiritual perfection, as in the later ones.

neighbours.name: The Boar and the Dragon
neighbours.summary: A saga frame. The boar stood for the kings of Gaul a thousand years ago, the dragon for the Vikings who ruled the region three centuries back. The lion and the lily eclipse both now, but leftovers of those courts remember their greatness and plot its return: the Boar King and the Children of Odin, antagonists for a hoplite saga or any other, or courts the characters may join.

details.antagonist: The Boar King and Queen Skuld, old courts seeking revival

stages.title: Old courts stirring
stages.clues: Hunters vanish in the deep forest; Viking raiders are reported on the coast. The troupe chooses which court, if either, is real.
stages.ignored: The courts grow in strength unseen.
stages.stopped: The rumours are run to ground early.
stages.turned: The covenant makes contact with one court or both.

stages.title: The boar's offer
stages.clues: The Boar King, through Salvirius, courts a Merinita or Bjornaer magus as the new Diedne of his forests.
stages.ignored: He finds his warden elsewhere.
stages.stopped: He is refused, and the forest turns hostile.
stages.turned: A covenant magus joins the court.

stages.title: The dragon's call
stages.clues: The Children of Odin sound out Norman-blooded magi and send initiates raiding as Vikings.
stages.ignored: The cult grows and its raids multiply.
stages.stopped: The cult is exposed to the Quaesitores.
stages.turned: A covenant magus is initiated.

stages.title: Lion and lily answer
stages.clues: The Church, the king and the Quaesitores react to pagan rites in the woods and raiders on the coast, and look for the wizards behind both.
stages.ignored: The Order is blamed for the old courts' revival and must answer to mundane powers.
stages.stopped: Both courts fall back into legend.
stages.turned: The covenant stands between the old courts and the new powers, bargaining with each.

neighbours.secrets: One, both or neither may exist in a given saga; the troupe decides. Begin The Boar King's Hunt or Queen Skuld and the Ships of Flame alongside this frame for their detail.

neighbours.name: The Tradition of Kings
neighbours.summary:
A saga frame for a covenant with ties to the nobility. Philip Augustus rules France absolutely under a divine mandate, yet several plots aim at the throne or at the holy oil of anointing kept at Reims. The characters meet each plot in turn through their noble kin, oaths and the Order, and the ending is best saved for when several ripen at once.

Where does kingship lie: in the oil, in the oil with the Church's blessing, in the crown or throne, or in the blood of Merovech, whose long hair and beard the Frankish kings still wear in their images? A magus who solved it might turn the secret to power in the Order. Saints linked to the Frankish kings (Clotilde, Martin of Tours, Remi, Riquier, Valery, Vedast) may answer a prayer with guidance. If history holds, Louis IX, now five, becomes king in 1226 and is canonised in 1297, and diviners may try to help or hinder that.

details.antagonist: The plotters against the oil and the throne of France

stages.title: Does it depend on the oil?
stages.clues: A powerful magus, one bad Twilight past sense, prepares spells to walk into Reims Cathedral and anoint himself, sure it will make him Primus; he may visit to consult a history or let a clue slip at Tribunal. German nobles plan to steal the oil to stop Philip anointing his son, and crown an East Frankish heir of Charlemagne, wrongly thinking the seven generations' grace of Pope Stephen II's ruling is nearly over.
stages.ignored: The oil is taken, and the wrath of the mundane powers falls on the Order.
stages.stopped: The magus is exposed without the characters being charged with scrying, though a senior magus makes a dangerous enemy.
stages.turned: The characters guard the oil at Reims, and meet the German plot there.

stages.title: Does it depend on the man?
stages.clues: French nobles plan a 'hunting accident' for Philip, meaning to shape his young son into a proper king, and the characters' closest noble contact asks for help. A learned, striking young man asks the covenant for a permanent, scarless tattoo of a red cross, for another plot to replace Philip's line. The king is said to be badly advised: clerks pack the court with kin, keep him from the crusade, and feed him lies. Has he kept divine favour?
stages.ignored: The king dies or falls under worse counsel.
stages.stopped: The plotters and the false counsellors are exposed.
stages.turned: The characters gain the gratitude, and the secrets, of the court.

stages.title: Does it depend on the bloodline?
stages.clues: A Jerbiton maga has taken as apprentice an un-Gifted boy of Merovech's line, who wins every brawl, understands animal calls, divines a little, has the Purifying Touch and never cuts his hair; she means to bring him near the throne. A lone Ex Miscellanea peregrinator of the Rhine, Merovech's heir and perhaps Gifted with the Quinotaur's legacy, plots to take the throne herself.
